title: Build with Foundry
summary: Turn a build plan into durable tasks, isolated work, review evidence, and a controlled release.
body:
## Learn the tool connection concept

Curious about MCP? Read [how AI connects to tools and context](/guide/mcp-fundamentals) to distinguish the connection protocol from Foundry work coordination and application permissions.

## Start with the complete setup tutorial

New to Foundry? Follow [Foundry from zero](/guide/foundry-repository): create and open a GitHub repository, install the Python tool, initialize native configuration, register owner trust, start sessions, run a first task, and understand release/CI/recovery. Each step identifies where to type it and what to verify.

## Where Foundry fits

Foundry is my primary engineering workflow for building applications. It surrounds the development process: plans become tasks, work is assigned to workstreams, implementation produces artifacts, and release decisions use evidence tied to a candidate revision.

It is a development control plane. The running application still consists of the browser, API, database, workers, and delivery infrastructure. Foundry does not authenticate an application's users or check their report permissions. Those are runtime responsibilities described in the [security guide](/guide/security-boundaries).

## The build and release system

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  Owner[Anthony - outcome and release authority]
  Plan[Build plan and acceptance criteria]
  Orchestrator[Orchestrator - interpret and coordinate]
  Control[Foundry control plane - durable tasks and policy]
  Work[Workstream branch and worktree]
  Agent[Worker agent - implementation within scope]
  Artifact[Candidate commit and attributable artifacts]
  Review[Independent QA and security evidence]
  Approval[Required human approval for candidate]
  Main[Integrated main revision]
  Build[Static handbook build]
  Netlify[Netlify delivery]
  Browser[Reader browser]
  Owner --> Plan
  Plan --> Orchestrator
  Orchestrator --> Control
  Control --> Work
  Work --> Agent
  Agent --> Artifact
  Artifact --> Review
  Review --> Approval
  Owner --> Approval
  Approval --> Main
  Main --> Build
  Build --> Netlify
  Netlify --> Browser
```

**Text alternative:** Anthony defines the outcome and acceptance criteria. An orchestrator coordinates tasks through Foundry. A scoped workstream produces a candidate and artifacts. Review evidence and required human approval support integration. The resulting handbook builds into static assets served by Netlify to readers.

The diagram shows the intended governed path. The first handbook deployment was a direct manual Netlify deployment, not a completed Foundry-governed release. Initializing Foundry alone does not establish all the gates in this diagram.

## Native repository structure

This repository uses the native layout created by `foundry init`. Foundry's older documentation also describes `.claude/state/`; do not mix that legacy layout into this project by copying examples blindly.

| Location | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| `.foundry/foundry.yaml` | Project identity, branches, provider and runtime configuration |
| `.foundry/project/` | Project component and architecture descriptions |
| `.foundry/policy/` | Capabilities, evidence requirements, and gates |
| `foundry/state` branch | Durable control-plane state, separate from application history |
| `.foundry/state/` | Local worktree attached to the state branch |
| Workstream branches/worktrees | Isolated candidate changes and reviewable diffs |
| `content/` and `src/` | Handbook product content and browser application |

Current project settings identify the task prefix as `ENG`, the main branch as `main`, the state branch as `foundry/state`, and the level as local. Providers are configured as Claude and runtime engine as auto; these settings are configuration, not proof that a worker is installed, authenticated, running, or container-isolated. Sessions are currently configured off.

## Start with facts, then define the task

Use the installed CLI to reconstruct state before relying on an old conversation. On this machine the CLI is available in the sibling Foundry virtual environment; a normal tool installation exposes it as `foundry`.

**Terminal · project repository root, installed Foundry required**

```bash
# Step 1: Reconstruct local facts without changing task authority.
foundry boot
# Step 2: Inspect work and next actions.
foundry status
# Step 3: Validate repository and state consistency.
foundry validate
# Step 4: Inspect recovery facts without applying changes.
foundry recover
# Step 5: Discover the installed task commands before creating work.
foundry task --help
```

Write an outcome with observable acceptance criteria. For this handbook, “add diagrams” should mean rendered runtime and request-flow diagrams, structured text alternatives, correct guide links, and no diagram rendering failures. “Add security” should specify the trust model, permission matrix, negative tests, and which deployed headers must be observed.

## Workstreams and artifacts

Assign bounded ownership and agree on the contract before implementation. A content workstream and a frontend renderer workstream can share the Mermaid fence convention without editing each other's files. An isolated branch makes changes inspectable; a worktree provides a separate checkout, not an automatic security sandbox.

Artifacts are attributable outputs such as a candidate commit, a handoff, test output, or a review. Foundry distinguishes submitting an output from accepting it. A worker's statement that a task is complete should not satisfy its own release gate.

Discover exact command arguments with `foundry workstream --help`, `foundry artifact --help`, and `foundry run --help`. Do not copy invented task identifiers or invocation syntax into a production workflow.

## Evidence belongs to the candidate

A passing test report is evidence for the revision it tested. Changing the candidate afterward can invalidate that evidence. Security review must examine the actual diff and relevant negative paths; QA must verify the actual application behavior. Human approvals in configured native projects are bound to exact commits rather than a general permission to ship whatever comes next.

For a frontend handbook, validation should include metadata and internal links, typechecking, a production build, diagram rendering, keyboard interactions, responsive reading, and hosted deep links. Foundry's installed test help describes governed .NET and Django evidence; do not claim that running `npm run build` automatically creates governed frontend evidence. Inspect the actual evidence contract before integrating JavaScript checks.

## Development security versus application security

| Concern | Foundry development control | Application runtime control |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scope | Agent path and capability policy | Tenant membership and object permissions |
| Identity | Agent sessions and human principals | Selected Django session, JWT, Clerk, or Gait contract |
| Isolation | Worktrees and configured supervised runtimes | Scoped queries and infrastructure boundaries |
| Secrets | Protected paths and runtime environment limits | Server-side secret storage and least privilege |
| Approval | Candidate review and release authority | Authorized user actions and workflow transitions |
| Evidence | Revision-bound artifacts and reviews | Audit events, metrics, and denial tests |

Declared agent identity, a worktree, or an orchestrator prompt does not provide the same enforcement as a configured container boundary or verified signed approval. Required GitHub checks also need actual branch protection. Treat each control as configured, observed, or still proposed; do not infer enforcement from the diagram.

## Recovery and release

After interruption, inspect Git and Foundry state before restarting work. `foundry recover` is read-only by default; applying recovery is a separate deliberate action. Check dirty worktrees, candidate revisions, and pending artifacts so a restarted agent does not overwrite or repeat work.

`foundry checkpoint --help` describes narrative checkpoint recording. Use it to persist what is done, the remaining gaps, evidence, and the next action; a checkpoint does not grant task authority or replace a release approval.

Before using `foundry release`, inspect its help and project evidence policy. The installed command describes checking evidence, trial integration, approval, and publication. Netlify publication remains a separate delivery concern unless an actual configured integration connects it. A Foundry merge does not prove a Netlify deployment succeeded.

## Current handbook adoption and next steps

Foundry initialization is complete, and the native configuration/state layout exists. This chapter's source inspection confirms the available concepts and commands. It does not establish signed principal registration, policy adoption, required branch checks, worker sandboxing, or a governed release for this handbook.

The next adoption step is to map content/frontend ownership and validation commands into the project configuration, inspect capability and evidence requirements, and establish the human authority and review workflow required by the selected policy. That setup should be a concrete adoption task rather than an implied guarantee attached to `foundry init`.

title: My build workflow: from repo to release
summary: The starting point for my engineering manual: choose a layout, build with Foundry, verify the boundaries and ship.
body:
## Use this as the starting checklist

This is my master manual for building. The goal is a repeatable path from an idea to a working application, with the structure, decisions and checks easy to find. Not every application needs every tool.

Use the [interactive project checklist](/guide/project-starter-checklist) to track your next steps, and the [recipe directory](/guide/build-recipes) for common implementation tasks.

## 1. Establish the repository and project shape

Start with [Git basics and pull requests](/guide/git-basics). Keep the [Git command reference](/guide/git-command-reference) nearby when staging, branching or reviewing a change.

For a documentation site or browser-only tool, start with the [frontend structure](/guide/frontend-folder-structure). For an application with its own API, start with the [Django + React structure](/guide/full-stack-folder-structure): one repository, backend and frontend directories, three ignore files. Define what belongs to the browser and what requires server authority before choosing libraries.

## 2. Establish the work

Use the [Foundry setup tutorial](/guide/foundry-repository) for repository creation, installation and initialization. Write the intended outcome, scope and acceptance checks before assigning work. Keep human release authority explicit. Foundry helps coordinate building; the application's runtime remains a separate system.

## 3. Build a small vertical slice

Follow the [Django learning path](/guide/django-toolkit) from environment setup to a protected REST endpoint. Connect the [React transport and query layer](/guide/react-api-connection). Get one real operation working through the interface, API and database before adding more subsystems.

For a frontend-only project, deliver a complete reading or interaction flow and verify static hosting instead of creating an unnecessary backend.

## 4. Add the boundaries the product needs

Choose [authentication](/guide/authentication-options), apply [tenant isolation](/guide/tenant-isolation) where needed, and define roles around actual operations. Choose [views](/guide/django-views), [services](/guide/services-and-selectors), [Channels](/guide/django-channels) or [background jobs](/guide/reliable-job-lifecycle) because a requirement calls for them.

For AI, keep authoritative calculations and permissions outside the model. Use [deterministic context](/guide/deterministic-ai), scoped documents and explicit fallback behavior.

## 5. Verify failures before release

Check ownership, permissions, invalid inputs, retries, concurrent work and recovery. Exercise loading, error and empty states in the interface. Use the [Django delivery checks](/guide/django-testing-delivery), [Reports walkthrough](/guide/reports-verification) and [failure drills](/guide/auth-and-document-drills) to select checks appropriate to the change.

Reference examples and completed handbook exercises are not executed application tests. Record what actually ran and what remains unverified.

## 6. Deploy and keep it running

Choose the [deployment platform](/guide/deployment-platforms) for the processes the application needs. Use the [CI/CD map](/guide/ci-cd-release-workflow) to separate checks, approval and deployment. Follow [Django on Heroku](/guide/heroku-django-deployment) and the [Heroku operations reference](/guide/heroku-operations) when that is the selected host. Configure migrations, secrets, storage and static delivery deliberately. Define [scheduled work and backups](/guide/backup-and-scheduled-tasks), then verify recovery through the [runbook](/guide/recovery-runbook).

## 7. Feed real experience back into the manual

Use the [project case studies](/projects) to compare real boundaries and tradeoffs. When a project changes, update the relevant guide and its source evidence. Label a new idea as proposed until it has been implemented and checked. Keep the default path simple enough to follow, and put optional tools where their requirements become relevant.

## When something fails

Open the [troubleshooting desk](/guide/troubleshooting-desk) to start from a symptom and find the failing boundary before changing configuration.

## Keep the reference useful

Define [API contracts](/guide/api-contracts), plan [database changes](/guide/safe-database-migrations), select a [testing strategy](/guide/testing-strategy), and prepare [operational runbooks](/guide/operational-runbooks). Save frequently used guides in [My library](/guide/my-library); bookmarks and recent visits stay in your browser.

## Keep learning deliberately

Use the [Learning roadmap](/guide/learning-roadmap) for the few skills you want to practice next. Suggested topics, self-reported learning and executed project evidence remain separate.

## Find a specific answer

Open [All guides](/guides) to search a command or filter by topic. The sidebar follows the same topic names; previous and next links stay within your current topic or project. Use [Git worktrees](/guide/git-worktrees) when separate Foundry tasks need separate directories.

title: Start a project: my build checklist
summary: Choose frontend-only or full-stack and track the steps from repository setup to release.
body:
## Make the next step visible

Choose the project type above, then work through its checklist. Progress is saved in this browser when storage is available, separately for each project type. It is a reusable personal checklist, not a per-repository tracker: export your notes before resetting it for another project.

A checked box records your own completion claim. This handbook does not run commands, inspect your repository or verify a deployment. Exported notes preserve that distinction.

## Use the right amount of architecture

A frontend-only build needs a reliable reading or interaction flow, accessibility, a production build and static hosting. A full-stack application adds identity, permission boundaries, a database, API contracts and backend operations. Add workers, WebSockets and AI when a requirement calls for them—not as mandatory startup dependencies.

## Build one useful slice

Begin with the smallest end-to-end action that proves the application works. For a full-stack example, follow the [Tasks API](/guide/django-first-api) and [React connection](/guide/react-api-connection). For feature operations, use the [recipe index](/guide/build-recipes).

title: Build recipes: find the task, follow the steps
summary: Short implementation paths with file locations, copyable excerpts and checks.
body:
## Use a recipe while building

Search the task list above and open the relevant recipe. Each gives prerequisites, file locations, an integration excerpt, and checks to run in the real application. Examples reuse the manual's Tasks and Reports domains; a snippet is not a complete application scaffold.

## Keep the deeper guide nearby

Recipes handle a narrow task. The linked chapters explain architecture, failure behavior and alternatives. Start a new application with the [project checklist](/guide/project-starter-checklist), then return here when you need an implementation path.

## Verification stays explicit

These are reference instructions. Copying an example or marking a checklist item does not execute a backend test, establish authentication or prove a release is ready.

## When something fails

Open the [troubleshooting desk](/guide/troubleshooting-desk) to start from a symptom and find the failing boundary before changing configuration.

title: Troubleshooting desk: start with the symptom
summary: Find the failing boundary, collect useful evidence and verify the correction.
body:
## Diagnose before changing the system

Use the desk above to choose a symptom and open its investigation path. Search and category filters are linkable; copyable notes are an **unexecuted diagnostic plan**, not evidence that the application was checked.

## Capture the minimum useful context

Record the affected environment, application/infrastructure revision, time window, operation and a safe correlation identifier. Distinguish one user's failure from a tenant-wide or service-wide incident. Compare the first failing request with its preceding login, preflight, mutation or job attempt.

Never paste access tokens, cookies, database credentials, patient records or private file links into a troubleshooting note. Use synthetic reproduction data and approved diagnostic access.

## Change one cause and recheck

A browser error, an HTTP status and a server exception describe different layers. Identify which one failed before changing configuration. Avoid making a private service public, disabling CSRF or broadening permissions to see whether the error disappears.

After correcting the cause, repeat the original failure and a relevant denied case. A successful authorized request does not prove unauthorized requests remain blocked. Record actual outcomes in the application's evidence, not as assumptions in this manual.

## Keep incident response separate

If there is suspected credential compromise or data exposure, follow the response plan rather than repeatedly reproducing the issue against real records. See [Lumen's planned incident/recovery controls](/guide/lumen-aws-security) and the [recovery runbook](/guide/recovery-runbook). Lumen AWS examples remain proposed; no live infrastructure is diagnosed by this page.

title: Learning roadmap: what I want to learn next
summary: Choose a few priorities, practice deliberately, and define what learning looks like.
body:
## Keep learning separate from established practice

This is a personal learning plan. A topic being listed here does not mean you lack the skill, and marking it Learned does not establish production readiness. The initial topics are suggested exercises based on the manual's existing projects; edit or remove them to reflect your own priorities.

## Use three simple states

**Next** means you intend to focus on the topic. Keep that list to roughly three–five priorities. **Practicing** means you are actively working through an exercise. **Learned** records your own assessment after meeting your completion criteria; it is not an automated competency check or certification.

Each topic has a reason, a practical exercise, completion criteria and an optional related guide. An exercise should produce something you can explain or inspect: a synthetic test result, a design decision, a small implementation or a recovery walkthrough.

## Make the exercise safe and concrete

Use disposable environments and synthetic data. A cloud exercise here does not provision infrastructure or authorize changes to another project. Record actual checks where the application keeps its evidence, and avoid putting credentials, clinical records or private links into a personal learning note.

## Save and export your plan

Edits and status changes are stored in this browser when storage is available. There is no account or cross-device sync. With blocked storage, changes last only while this page stays open. Export the roadmap before clearing browser data if you want a portable copy.

The export identifies statuses as self-reported and says that no exercises or application checks were executed by the handbook. The roadmap never changes the review status of source-based chapters or marks a planned Lumen AWS deployment as complete.

title: My library: saved and recently viewed guides
summary: Keep frequently used material close with local bookmarks and reading history.
body:
## Your browser, your shortcuts

Save a guide using its bookmark button, then return here to reopen it. Recently viewed lists the latest distinct guide visits, newest first. Both lists are stored locally in this browser when storage is available; there is no account, cross-device sync or server-side reading telemetry.

## Keep control of the list

Remove individual bookmarks or clear a list when it is no longer useful. Clearing history does not clear bookmarks. Private browsing, cleared site data or blocked storage can prevent persistence. If storage is unavailable, the lists work only for the current open application session.

This library stores guide identifiers only, not clinical data, credentials or the contents of another project. Reading a guide does not mark an application check as executed.

## Plan your next skill

The [Learning roadmap](/guide/learning-roadmap) keeps editable practice goals alongside your saved reading, with an exercise and completion criteria for each topic.

title: Skills needed: the engineering gap map
summary: The infrastructure and platform skills underneath my apps, ranked by where they show up in real projects.
body:
## What am I learning?

My handbook is strong on application code: Django services and selectors, React data flow, authentication, tenant isolation, CI/CD, Foundry and observability. It is thin on the layer underneath, meaning the machines, networks and data systems my code runs on.

That gap stays hidden on Heroku and Netlify, because the platform handles it. It becomes visible as soon as a project leaves the platform. Lumen's AWS design assumes I can reason about an ALB, private subnets, RDS and a worker tier. This section is the list of what to learn, and why, in order.

## The map

| Priority | Skill | Why I need it | Where it shows up | Lesson |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Containers | The unit of packaging and deployment almost everywhere off-platform | Lumen on AWS, local dev parity, CI builds | [Containers](/guide/containers-fundamentals) |
| 2 | Networking and load balancers | Every request crosses DNS, TLS and a proxy before Django sees it | Lumen's ALB, Heroku's router, WebSockets for Channels | [Networking and load balancers](/guide/networking-and-load-balancers) |
| 3 | PostgreSQL performance | Slow pages and connection errors are usually database problems | Moneta dashboards, EstateIQ ledgers, every Heroku app | [PostgreSQL performance](/guide/postgres-performance) |
| 4 | Caching and rate limiting | Speed without leaking tenant data; protection without false security | Redis tier in Lumen, login endpoints, AI calls | [Caching and rate limiting](/guide/caching-and-rate-limiting) |
| 5 | Infrastructure as code | Cloud resources clicked by hand cannot be reviewed, repeated or recovered | Lumen's AWS topology | [Infrastructure as code](/guide/infrastructure-as-code) |
| 6 | Linux and the shell | Debugging a server means processes, files, permissions and logs | EC2 hosts, containers, CI runners | Not yet written |
| 7 | Performance and load testing | Knowing capacity before users find the limit | Any launch, AI features | Not yet written |
| 8 | Web performance and accessibility | Core Web Vitals and WCAG decide whether real users can use the frontend | Every React app | Not yet written |
| 9 | Software supply chain | Dependencies and images are code I did not write but still ship | npm, pip, base images, CI | Not yet written |
| 10 | Data privacy and retention | Health and financial data carry obligations beyond security | Lumen (clinical), Moneta (financial) | Not yet written |

The order follows dependency. Containers come first because load balancers route to them, IaC provisions them, and supply-chain checks scan them. Database performance comes before caching because a cache that hides a slow query only postpones the problem.

## How each lesson works

Every lesson follows the same structure, so I always know where I am:

| Part | What it gives me |
| --- | --- |
| Lesson card | Level, time, prerequisites, and what I'll be able to do afterward |
| Core concepts | The vocabulary, in one table |
| Modern patterns | Current practice: the problem each pattern solves and when to use it |
| Anti-patterns | Common mistakes and why they hurt |
| Build it step by step | A worked example on my own stack, with a checkpoint |
| Exercise | A task on a real project, with a clear "done means" |
| Check your understanding | Questions to answer before reading the answer key |
| Go deeper | Official documentation for the next level |

## How to use this section

1. Read one lesson and answer its self-check without looking.
2. Do its exercise against a real project: Moneta, EstateIQ or a throwaway repo.
3. Add the skill to my [learning roadmap](/guide/learning-roadmap) with the exercise as the success criterion.
4. When a "Not yet written" skill becomes urgent, write its lesson here.

## What this section is not

These lessons teach concepts with official sources. They are not claims that I have deployed ECS, Terraform or Redis in production. [Deployment platforms](/guide/deployment-platforms) records what I have actually run.

## Check your understanding

- Why does this gap stay invisible while I deploy to Heroku and Netlify?
- Why learn containers before infrastructure as code?
- What is wrong with caching a slow query instead of fixing it?

## Answer key

The platform runs the containers, router, TLS and database operations for me, so I never touch them. Infrastructure as code mostly provisions things that run containers and route traffic to them, so it makes sense only once those parts are understood. A cache hides the slow query until the cache misses, expires or is wrong, and then the original problem returns under load.

title: The system, end to end
summary: Follow a request through the browser, application, and durable data.
body:
## How the system gets built

[Foundry is the primary engineering workflow](/guide/building-with-foundry): it coordinates tasks, workstreams, artifacts, evidence, and release authority. It governs development of the code delivered to these runtime components. It does not replace the application API, identity provider, or hosting platform.

## Start with boundaries

A useful system map separates code organization from running processes. A Django service is a Python function that owns a business operation. A worker is a separate process that executes queued work. Moving a function into a service does not make it asynchronous.

The baseline application has a React browser, a Django API, and PostgreSQL. Add a worker, broker, and private object storage when slow jobs or durable files require them. The handbook itself is a static frontend; this map describes the applications it teaches.

## The platforms behind the diagram

My main application host is Heroku; I have used Vercel for frontend delivery and AWS S3 for file storage. This handbook runs on Netlify. [Deployment and storage](/guide/deployment-platforms) maps those responsibilities, while [backups and scheduled tasks](/guide/backup-and-scheduled-tasks) covers recurring operations. Broader AWS infrastructure is proposed learning material rather than deployed experience.

## The complete runtime map

The diagram separates the public browser, identity provider, and project-owned runtime. Dashed edges represent asynchronous or supporting flows. It is a proposed reference architecture; these services are not provisioned by the handbook.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  subgraph public[Public browser and delivery]
    Browser[React browser]
    CDN[Static frontend delivery]
    CDN --> Browser
  end
  subgraph identity[Selected identity boundary]
    Gait[Django auth, Simple JWT, Clerk, or Gait]
    IdentityDB[(Identity data - local or provider owned)]
    Gait --> IdentityDB
  end
  subgraph project[Project application boundary]
    API[Django API - authorization]
    DB[(Project PostgreSQL)]
    Outbox[Durable job outbox]
    Broker[Message broker]
    Worker[Background worker]
    Storage[Private object storage]
    API --> DB
    DB --> Outbox
    Outbox -. Publish with retry .-> Broker
    Broker --> Worker
    Worker --> DB
    Worker --> Storage
    API --> Storage
  end
  Browser -->|Sign in and refresh| Gait
  Browser -->|Authenticated HTTPS requests| API
  API -. Key and session policy .-> Gait
  Worker -. Delivery adapter .-> Email[Email provider]
  API -. Provider adapter .-> External[External integrations]
  API -. Redacted telemetry .-> Monitor[Logs and monitoring]
  Worker -. Job correlation .-> Monitor
```

**Text alternative:** Static delivery serves React. React signs in through Gait and calls the project API. Identity ownership depends on the selected mechanism; project-managed Django identities and external-provider identities have different data boundaries. The diagram separates identity/session truth from business data logically; Django-managed identity tables may share the project database. The project API owns authorization and project PostgreSQL. A durable outbox feeds a broker; workers consume jobs, update business status, and create private files. Provider adapters connect email and integrations; redacted telemetry connects web and worker processes to monitoring.

[React responsibilities](/guide/frontend-architecture), [Django boundaries](/guide/services-and-selectors), and [security controls](/guide/security-boundaries) explain the components in detail.

## Application layers versus processes

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  UI[Page and presentational parts] --> Controller[Controller hook]
  Controller --> Query[Query and mutation hooks]
  Query --> Transport[Typed API module]
  Transport --> View[Django view - request orchestration]
  View --> Selector[Selector - scoped reads]
  View --> Service[Service - workflow writes]
  Selector --> Model[Models and database constraints]
  Service --> Model
```

**Text alternative:** UI parts emit intent through a controller and server-state hooks to a typed API module. Django views orchestrate scoped selectors for reads and services for writes. Both reach models and database constraints. These are code layers; selectors and services normally run inside the same web process. Workers are separate runtime processes.

## Authentication and authorized reads

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant B as React browser
  participant G as Selected identity mechanism
  participant A as Project API
  participant D as Project PostgreSQL
  B->>G: Authenticate using inspected integration contract
  G-->>B: Session and access credentials
  B->>A: Request report with selected organization
  A->>A: Verify selected session or token contract
  A->>D: Resolve active membership and role
  D-->>A: Trusted organization scope
  A->>D: Retrieve report within trusted scope
  D-->>A: Authorized report or no scoped match
  A-->>B: Representation or policy-defined denial
```

**Text alternative:** The browser establishes a session or credentials through the selected identity mechanism. The API verifies the selected session or token credential, resolves active membership from project data, and retrieves a report inside that scope. Authentication alone does not grant report access. Fresh-session checks depend on the actual integration contract and required revocation policy.

## Follow a read

1. The browser resolves the frontend domain and downloads versioned JavaScript and CSS.
2. A user action selects an organization and report. The frontend sends an authenticated API request.
3. The API verifies identity, resolves active membership, and checks report access.
4. A selector queries PostgreSQL with the trusted organization scope.
5. A read serializer shapes the result. React renders loading, error, empty, or successful data.

The browser's organization identifier is a request for scope. It is never proof of authority. The server must establish membership before retrieving data.

## Follow a write

A write serializer checks input shape. A service checks workflow rules and commits the change inside a database transaction. Database constraints protect durable invariants even when two requests arrive together. The API returns the authoritative representation, and the frontend updates or invalidates the affected cache.

For report generation, return an accepted job identifier after recording durable intent. A worker generates the file and updates job status. The frontend polls or subscribes to an actual supported status mechanism. Completion should refresh report data rather than merely close a modal.

## Who owns what?

| Component | Durable responsibility | Boundary |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gait | Identity and sessions | Authentication |
| Project API | Memberships and domain rules | Authorization |
| PostgreSQL | Reports, tenant relationships, job status | Durable business truth |
| Object storage | Private generated files | Authorized downloads |
| Browser | View state and local preferences | Untrusted client |

The identity provider shown is selected per project; Django auth and Simple JWT may use project-managed identity data, while Clerk and Gait introduce an external identity boundary. Gait integration contracts have not been inspected for this handbook. Treat these roles as a proposed architecture, not verified endpoint behavior.

## Failure and recovery

An API timeout does not tell the browser whether a write committed. Use an idempotency contract for operations that cannot safely be duplicated. A broker outage can strand work between a database commit and message publication; a durable outbox records work for retry. A worker may receive the same job twice, so state transitions and file publication must tolerate duplicate execution.

## Verify the boundaries

Trace one synthetic report with a request identifier. Confirm the organization filter reaches every query and related-object lookup. Repeat the request with a different organization's report identifier and expect denial. Observe durable status after a worker restart rather than inferring success from a queued message.

Continue with [Django setup](/guide/django-setup) and [frontend architecture](/guide/frontend-architecture).

title: Django: the learning path and toolkit
summary: Start a project, build a REST API, then choose the tools your system needs.
body:
## Start here

This is my curated path through Django: how the pieces fit together, the choices I make, and the mistakes to test for. The examples use a small personal Tasks API before introducing organization-scoped systems. They are reference code for a separate application; this handbook runs no backend.

### Getting started

1. [Choose the full-stack folder structure](/guide/full-stack-folder-structure).
2. [Create the Django workspace](/guide/django-setup).
3. [Install REST Framework and build a first endpoint](/guide/django-first-api).
4. [Connect React using Axios and TanStack Query](/guide/react-api-connection).
5. [Verify the backend and prepare deployment](/guide/django-testing-delivery).

### Core tools and decisions

| Tool | Reach for it when | Keep the boundary clear |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [ORM and migrations](/guide/django-models-orm) | Modeling durable records and relationships | Database constraints protect invariants |
| [Views and ViewSets](/guide/django-views) | Mapping HTTP requests to operations | Transport should not hide domain workflows |
| [Serializers and permissions](/guide/django-rest-boundaries) | Validating input and enforcing API access | Valid input is not permission to act |
| [Services and selectors](/guide/services-and-selectors) | Sharing writes and scoped reads | Application workflow stays explicit |
| [Middleware](/guide/django-middleware) | Establishing request-wide context | Selecting a tenant does not authorize it |
| [CORS](/guide/django-cors) | React and Django use different origins | Browser response access is distinct from authentication and CSRF |
| [Signals](/guide/django-signals) | Connecting small, decoupled event handlers | Required workflow should remain visible |
| [WebSockets](/guide/websocket-design) | Designing a live connection and recovery contract | Transport delivery is not durable application completion |
| [Channels](/guide/django-channels) | Bidirectional live interactions | Authenticate, authorize and recover connections |
| [Jobs and schedules](/guide/reliable-job-lifecycle) | Work must outlive the HTTP request | Durable state and retry policy own completion |
| [Authentication](/guide/authentication-options) | Selecting sessions, JWT, Clerk or Gait | Identity and application authorization differ |
| [Operations](/guide/backup-and-scheduled-tasks) | Backups, periodic work and recovery | A schedule is not evidence of success |

## Learn from the projects

[Gaming](/guide/gaming-multiplayer-flow) shows Channels and server-owned multiplayer state. [EstateIQ](/guide/estateiq-domain-map) shows tenancy, financial workflows, documents and AI boundaries. [Gait](/guide/gait-auth-walkthrough) connects browser sessions with API verification. These are design studies, with their inspected-source limitations recorded alongside them.

## Add tools as requirements appear

Start with Django, DRF, a database and tests. Add Channels for actual live interaction; add a worker for durable asynchronous work. Redis can provide a channel layer or broker, but those are distinct responsibilities. Neither installing Redis nor adding a Python dependency starts the required service.

The framework reference answers every API option. This handbook answers where the tool belongs and how I would verify its use.

## Contracts, safe changes and evidence

Use [API contracts](/guide/api-contracts) to connect server and client expectations, [safe migrations](/guide/safe-database-migrations) to evolve live data, and the [testing strategy](/guide/testing-strategy) to choose meaningful checks. When a check fails, start at the [troubleshooting desk](/guide/troubleshooting-desk).

title: Set up a Django workspace
summary: Create the environment, project configuration and first domain app.
body:
## Begin in your project's backend directory

Use the [full-stack layout](/guide/full-stack-folder-structure), or create a standalone backend repository. The following commands target macOS/Linux and Python 3.12 or another interpreter compatible with Django 5.2. This tutorial deliberately uses Django 5.2; it does not claim that is the newest major release. See the [official Django tutorial](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/5.2/intro/tutorial01/) for the framework's project/app distinction.

```bash
# Terminal — backend/, initially empty.
python3 --version
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -c "import sys; print(sys.executable)"
python -m pip install "Django>=5.2,<5.3"
python -m django --version
python -m django startproject config .
mkdir -p apps/tasks
touch apps/__init__.py
python manage.py startapp tasks apps/tasks
```

On PowerShell activate with `.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1` and create the directories/files with the equivalent shell commands. Confirm the active interpreter in your editor too.

## Register the nested app correctly

Replace the generated app configuration's `name`, then add it to settings. Django's app label remains `tasks`; its import path is `apps.tasks`.

```python
# backend/apps/tasks/apps.py — Register the nested domain package.
from django.apps import AppConfig

class TasksConfig(AppConfig):
    default_auto_field = "django.db.models.BigAutoField"
    name = "apps.tasks"
```

```python
# backend/config/settings.py — Append after the generated INSTALLED_APPS definition.
INSTALLED_APPS += ["apps.tasks.apps.TasksConfig"]
```

Keep the other generated settings intact for this local exercise. If you decide to introduce a custom user model, configure it before your first migrations; changing user models later needs a separate migration plan.

## Check and run

```bash
# Terminal — backend/, virtual environment still active.
python -m pip freeze > requirements.txt
python manage.py check
python manage.py migrate
python manage.py runserver
```

Open `http://127.0.0.1:8000/`. Stop the development server with Ctrl+C before continuing commands. Commit dependency inputs, app code and migrations; ignore the virtual environment and local database. Add DRF in the [first API chapter](/guide/django-first-api), then record its resolved dependencies too.

SQLite is sufficient for this starter. Use PostgreSQL when verifying the production database behavior your application relies on. A development server is for local work; deployment uses a production WSGI or ASGI process.

## Know what was verified

These are runnable reference steps for a separate backend. This frontend handbook does not install Django or execute migrations. Framework checks, API tests and deployment checks must run in the application you create.

title: Containers: images, Dockerfiles, and Compose
summary: Package a Django app the way modern platforms run it: small, non-root, built once and promoted unchanged.

objectives: Explain the difference between an image, a container and a registry
Write a multi-stage, non-root Dockerfile for a Django app
Run Django and PostgreSQL together locally with Compose
Build one image per commit and promote it unchanged from staging to production

body:
## What am I learning?

A **container image** is a packaged filesystem plus metadata: my code, the Python runtime, system libraries and the start command. A **container** is a running process started from that image, with its own view of the filesystem, network and process list. Images follow the [Open Container Initiative](https://opencontainers.org/) standard, so one image runs on Heroku, AWS ECS, Kubernetes or a laptop.

The point: I ship the environment, not just the code. "Works on my machine" becomes "works in this image," and that exact image is what gets tested and deployed.

## Core concepts

| Concept | What it is | Lifetime | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Dockerfile | The build recipe | Versioned in Git | `FROM python:3.12-slim` … |
| Layer | One cached build step | Reused until its inputs change | The `pip install` step |
| Image | The immutable built package | Stored in a registry, tagged | `moneta-api:2f3dec3` |
| Registry | Where images are stored and pulled from | Long-lived | Docker Hub, Amazon ECR, Heroku |
| Container | A running instance of an image | Disposable | One web process |
| Volume | Storage that outlives a container | Managed separately | Local PostgreSQL data |

A container's own filesystem is temporary. Anything written inside it disappears when it's replaced, just like a Heroku dyno. Durable data goes in PostgreSQL or S3.

## Modern patterns

| Pattern | Problem it solves | Use it when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Multi-stage builds** | Build tools bloat the runtime image and widen the attack surface | Always, for compiled dependencies or frontend builds |
| **Slim or distroless base images** | Fewer packages mean fewer vulnerabilities to patch | Always prefer `-slim`; consider [distroless](https://github.com/GoogleContainerTools/distroless) once the app is stable |
| **BuildKit cache mounts** | Reinstalling every dependency on each build is slow | Any build that downloads packages ([cache docs](https://docs.docker.com/build/cache/optimize/)) |
| **Build secrets** | Secrets passed with `ARG` or `COPY` stay in image history | A private package index or token is needed during the build ([build secrets](https://docs.docker.com/build/building/secrets/)) |
| **Non-root user** | A compromised app gets root inside the container | Always |
| **Build once, deploy many** | Rebuilding per environment means production runs an untested image | Every pipeline: tag by commit SHA and promote the same digest |
| **Config from the environment** | Environment-specific images drift apart | Always; the [Twelve-Factor App](https://12factor.net/config) pattern |
| **SBOM and provenance attestations** | No record of what is inside an image or how it was built | Anything shipped to production ([attestations](https://docs.docker.com/build/metadata/attestations/)) |
| **One process per container** | Mixed processes are hard to scale, restart and observe | Separate web, worker and scheduler containers from the same image |
| **Dev containers** | Every laptop has a slightly different toolchain | Teams or multi-machine work ([containers.dev](https://containers.dev/)) |

## Anti-patterns to avoid

- **Deploying `:latest`.** It is a moving pointer, so I can't tell what is running or roll back to it. Deploy by commit SHA or digest.
- **Secrets in the image.** A secret deleted in a later layer still exists in the earlier one.
- **Running as root.** It turns an app bug into control of the container.
- **One image per environment.** Staging tests a different artifact than production runs.
- **State inside the container.** Uploads and sessions on local disk vanish on redeploy.
- **Never rebuilding.** Base images receive security fixes only if I rebuild on them.

## Build it step by step

**Step 1: keep the build context clean.** Create `.dockerignore`:

```text
.git
.env
node_modules
__pycache__
*.sqlite3
```

**Step 2: write a multi-stage Dockerfile.**

```dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM python:3.12-slim AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip \
    pip install --prefix=/install -r requirements.txt

FROM python:3.12-slim
ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /install /usr/local
COPY . .
RUN useradd --create-home --uid 10001 appuser
USER appuser
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["gunicorn", "config.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000"]
```

Requirements are copied before the code because dependencies change rarely. That keeps the slow install layer cached when only code changes.

**Step 3: run the stack locally with Compose.** [Docker Compose](https://docs.docker.com/compose/) starts several containers from one file:

```yaml
services:
  api:
    build: .
    ports: ["8000:8000"]
    env_file: .env
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: local-only
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"]
      interval: 5s
    volumes: [pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data]
volumes:
  pgdata:
```

The health condition makes the API wait until PostgreSQL accepts connections, not just until its container starts.

**Step 4: tag by commit and attach build metadata.**

```text
docker buildx build \
  --tag registry.example.com/moneta-api:$(git rev-parse --short HEAD) \
  --sbom=true --provenance=mode=max --push .
```

Checkpoint: `docker run --rm <image> whoami` prints `appuser`, and `docker history <image>` shows no secrets.

## Where containers run

| Platform | How containers show up |
| --- | --- |
| Heroku | Dynos are containers. Buildpacks build the image, or I push my own through the [Container Registry](https://devcenter.heroku.com/articles/container-registry-and-runtime). |
| AWS ECS on Fargate | I supply the image; AWS schedules containers without servers for me to manage. |
| AWS EC2 | I run a container runtime myself, as one option for Lumen's service instances. |
| Kubernetes | A full orchestrator. Powerful, and usually more than a small team needs. |

Containers share the host's kernel, so they are a weaker isolation boundary than virtual machines. Treat them as packaging, not as a security sandbox.

## Exercise

Containerize one existing Django app.

1. Add `.dockerignore` and the Dockerfile above, adjusted for the project.
2. Add the Compose file and run `docker compose up`.
3. Confirm the health endpoint responds and the container runs as `appuser`.
4. Build with a commit-SHA tag and an SBOM.

**Done means:** the app serves from Compose, runs as non-root, the image tag matches a commit, and `docker history` shows no secrets.

## Check your understanding

- What is the difference between an image and a container?
- Why copy `requirements.txt` before the rest of the code?
- If a later Dockerfile step deletes a secret file, is the image safe?
- Why promote one image from staging to production instead of rebuilding?
- Where should uploaded files go when the app runs in a container?

## Answer key

An image is the immutable package; a container is a running instance of it. Copying requirements first keeps the slow dependency layer cached when only code changes. No: the secret remains in the earlier layer and the image history; use build secrets instead. Rebuilding can produce a different artifact, so production would run something staging never tested. Uploads go to durable storage such as S3, because the container's filesystem is discarded when it's replaced.

## Go deeper

- [Docker build best practices](https://docs.docker.com/build/building/best-practices/)
- [Multi-stage builds](https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-stage/)
- [Open Container Initiative](https://opencontainers.org/)

title: Build your first Django REST API
summary: Install DRF and connect a model, serializer, protected ViewSet and router.
body:
## Continue from the setup guide

Use the Tasks app created in [Django setup](/guide/django-setup). These complete file examples form a local learning API using Django session authentication. They are not an organization-aware production application or an implementation added to this handbook.

```bash
# Terminal — backend/, with its virtual environment active.
python -m pip install djangorestframework
python -m pip freeze > requirements.txt
```

Add `"rest_framework"` to `INSTALLED_APPS`, alongside `"apps.tasks.apps.TasksConfig"`. Freeze records the selected environment; a team can instead use its chosen lockfile tool.

## Define a small model

```python
# backend/apps/tasks/models.py — Store personal task records.
from django.conf import settings
from django.db import models

class Task(models.Model):
    owner = models.ForeignKey(settings.AUTH_USER_MODEL, on_delete=models.CASCADE)
    title = models.CharField(max_length=160)
    completed = models.BooleanField(default=False)
    created_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)
```

## Validate the representation

```python
# backend/apps/tasks/serializers.py — Describe writable and server-owned fields.
from rest_framework import serializers
from .models import Task

class TaskSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):
    class Meta:
        model = Task
        fields = ["id", "title", "completed", "created_at"]
        read_only_fields = ["id", "created_at"]
```

The owner is assigned from the authenticated request, never accepted from browser input.

## Scope every operation

```python
# backend/apps/tasks/views.py — Restrict CRUD operations to the signed-in owner.
from rest_framework.permissions import IsAuthenticated
from rest_framework.viewsets import ModelViewSet
from .models import Task
from .serializers import TaskSerializer

class TaskViewSet(ModelViewSet):
    serializer_class = TaskSerializer
    permission_classes = [IsAuthenticated]

    def get_queryset(self):
        return Task.objects.filter(owner=self.request.user).order_by("-id")

    def perform_create(self, serializer):
        serializer.save(owner=self.request.user)
```

This owner filter also scopes detail lookup, update and deletion. An authenticated stranger's task ID should return 404. Multi-tenant apps need additional membership and role checks: follow [tenant isolation](/guide/tenant-isolation), rather than treating this personal-task pattern as organization authorization.

## Register URLs

```python
# backend/apps/tasks/urls.py — Expose the task resource routes.
from rest_framework.routers import DefaultRouter
from .views import TaskViewSet

router = DefaultRouter()
router.register("tasks", TaskViewSet, basename="task")
urlpatterns = router.urls
```

```python
# backend/config/urls.py — Mount the API and local learning login.
from django.contrib import admin
from django.urls import include, path

urlpatterns = [
    path("admin/", admin.site.urls),
    path("api/", include("apps.tasks.urls")),
    path("api-auth/", include("rest_framework.urls")),
]
```

## Migrate and try it

```bash
# Terminal — backend/, after saving the files above.
python manage.py makemigrations tasks
python manage.py migrate
python manage.py createsuperuser
python manage.py check
python manage.py runserver
```

Visit `/api-auth/login/`, sign in with your local account, then open `/api/tasks/` in DRF's browsable API. Create a task with a title and confirm the returned ID. Log in as a different local user and confirm the original task is absent. Session-authenticated writes require CSRF protection; the browsable API handles its own form flow. Anonymous denials can be 403 under session authentication, so do not assume every missing credential produces 401.

Use the [testing chapter](/guide/django-testing-delivery) to make the ownership checks repeatable. The [DRF quickstart](https://www.django-rest-framework.org/tutorial/quickstart/) provides the upstream walkthrough; our example uses a personal task resource and deliberately scopes its queryset.

title: Function views, APIView, generics and ViewSets
summary: Choose an HTTP interface that makes the operation clear.
body:
## Pick the smallest useful abstraction

| Interface | Good fit | Tradeoff |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Django function view | A small HTML response or framework health endpoint | You handle HTTP behavior directly |
| DRF `@api_view` function | A small JSON operation with explicit methods | Keep serializer and permission policy explicit |
| DRF `APIView` | A command with distinct request handling | More orchestration code is written by hand |
| DRF generic view | Standard list, detail or create behavior | Learn its hooks and queryset behavior |
| DRF ViewSet plus router | Several operations around one resource | Routes and actions become less visible locally |

Function-based does not mean insecure or unmaintainable. Class-based does not automatically mean well-structured. Readability, repeated behavior and the endpoint's contract decide.

## Keep commands recognizable

`POST /reports/{id}/generate/` is a workflow command, not arbitrary model editing. An APIView or a carefully scoped ViewSet action can validate its input and call a service. Use serializer validation for input shape, permission checks for authority and a service for the durable transition.

A ModelViewSet exposes multiple operations by default. If a resource should only be read, use a read-only variant or explicit mixins. Audit the resulting URL and method table, including custom actions.

## Scoping is required with every style

Use a trusted, filtered queryset before looking up an object. List access does not automatically run an object-level permission check on each row. Creation has no existing object on which to run that check. Enforce list scope, create scope and related-object ownership explicitly.

## How I apply it

The [Tasks starter](/guide/django-first-api) uses a ViewSet because its contract is straightforward owner-scoped CRUD. The [Reports API](/guide/reports-api) shows explicit operations around a workflow. Both should delegate shared rules rather than duplicating them across HTTP handlers.

Verify allowed methods, unauthorized requests, foreign IDs, validation failures and the exact routes generated by routers. Consult the [ViewSet reference](https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/viewsets/) for action wiring.

title: Serializers, authentication and permissions
summary: Separate valid input, verified identity and permission to act.
body:
## Follow the request boundaries

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[HTTP request] --> B[Authentication]
    B --> C[Permissions and trusted scope]
    C --> D[Serializer validation]
    D --> E[Service or scoped selector]
    E --> F[Response serializer]
```

This is a conceptual flow; DRF performs authentication and initial permission checks before dispatch, while object checks occur when the view retrieves an object. Your workflow can need additional domain authorization after input validation.

## Serializers describe a contract

Use explicit fields rather than exposing every model column. Mark server-managed identifiers and timestamps read-only. Validate cross-field rules in `validate`, and return field-specific errors where possible. Validate a related record against the authorized organization; accepting a syntactically valid foreign ID is not enough.

Avoid putting a large multi-model financial workflow inside a serializer's `create`. The serializer can pass validated values into an explicit transactional service.

## Authentication is not authorization

Authentication establishes who presented the request. Permissions decide whether that identity may perform the operation. A valid JWT does not prove membership in the requested organization. Middleware selecting an organization does not prove access either.

Start the learning API with session authentication; choose the real application's [authentication method](/guide/authentication-options) deliberately. Session writes need CSRF protection. Cross-origin browser access needs an explicit CORS policy; CORS does not authorize an API caller.

## Keep lists bounded and errors stable

Choose pagination and expose a stable ordering with a tie-breaker. Whitelist filter and ordering fields instead of treating arbitrary request strings as ORM instructions. Use DRF's error handling for expected validation and permission errors; unexpected failures belong in server-side diagnostics with sensitive values excluded.

Request throttles can improve fairness but are not a complete abuse or denial-of-service defense. Apply limits to expensive commands, uploads and provider calls at the appropriate layers.

## Verify the contract

Test anonymous access, another user's record, another organization's related ID, read-only field injection, invalid input and pagination boundaries. Assert both the response and the absence of forbidden writes. See the [DRF permission reference](https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/permissions/) for object-check limitations.

title: Models, migrations and transactional ORM work
summary: Use the database for invariants and make query cost visible.
body:
## Model the durable truth

Use foreign keys for relationships, explicit nullability and database constraints for invariants. Store currency with a suitable decimal representation, not binary floating point. Choose deletion behavior intentionally; historical financial records often need a different policy from disposable personal tasks.

Migrations describe schema evolution and belong in Git. Run `makemigrations`, inspect the migration and apply it against a development database. Editing a model without a migration does not change the deployed schema.

## Make reads deliberate

QuerySets are lazy. Serializing related fields can create N+1 queries. Use `select_related` for single-valued relationships and `prefetch_related` for collections when the representation needs them. Measure with realistic row counts rather than adding every relationship preemptively.

Always scope before lookup. `Task.objects.get(id=...)` is unsafe in an owner-scoped endpoint unless ownership is subsequently enforced correctly. Prefer a filtered queryset that cannot retrieve the forbidden record at all.

## Protect concurrent writes

Use `transaction.atomic` for changes that must commit together. A uniqueness constraint protects against concurrent duplicate inserts; a prior `exists()` check alone does not. Where a workflow needs a row lock, acquire it inside the transaction and verify the behavior against PostgreSQL. SQLite is not evidence of PostgreSQL locking semantics.

An `on_commit` callback runs after a successful commit; it is not a durable delivery guarantee if the process crashes before publishing a job. Use an outbox when losing the event is unacceptable. See [Django transactions](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/5.2/topics/db/transactions/).

## Evolve production safely

For a required field on existing records, consider adding it nullable, backfilling in bounded work, then enforcing the constraint. Check old and new application versions can coexist during deployment. Treat destructive schema changes as a separate release decision with backups and recovery steps.

The [EstateIQ ledger](/guide/ledger-and-read-models) shows why authoritative financial records and derived snapshots have different jobs. Test constraint violations, rollback, query counts and concurrent operations—not only the happy-path serializer.

title: Middleware: establish request context carefully
summary: Use request-wide hooks without turning context into authorization.
body:
## What belongs here

Middleware is useful for request IDs, timing, security headers and resolving shared request context. Keep feature workflows out of it. An ordinary request should not unexpectedly trigger billing mutations or a slow AI call before its view runs.

Django enters middleware in configured order and unwinds responses in reverse. A middleware can also return early. Put dependencies after the middleware that establishes them, and make error/short-circuit behavior explicit. See the [middleware reference](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/5.2/topics/http/middleware/).

## Django authentication and DRF authentication differ

Django's session AuthenticationMiddleware depends on SessionMiddleware. DRF bearer authentication normally occurs later inside the API view. Middleware cannot assume a DRF-authenticated token user is already available on `request.user`. Resolve token-dependent authorization in the API boundary, or deliberately implement and verify a compatible integration.

## Tenant selection is not permission

A header, URL or stored browser preference can select an organization. Validate the selected identifier and then verify the caller's active membership before querying tenant data. Keep request-scoped values on the request; avoid process-global mutable tenant variables that can leak between concurrent requests.

The [EstateIQ tenant boundary](/guide/estateiq-tenant-boundary) separates middleware selection from membership permissions. Missing, malformed, foreign and inactive membership cases all need checks.

## Verify request-wide behavior

Exercise anonymous requests, health checks, exceptions, early responses and concurrent requests for different organizations. Match sync/async support to the deployed stack. Ensure logs do not expose authorization headers, cookies, document contents or secrets.

title: CORS: connect the browser to Django
summary: Configure allowed origins, understand preflight, and separate CORS from cookies, CSRF and API permissions.
body:
## Start with the two URLs

Write down the URL in the browser and the API URL it calls. An origin consists of scheme, hostname and port. `http://localhost:5173` and `http://localhost:8000` have different origins. `localhost` and `127.0.0.1` differ too.

CORS tells a browser whether JavaScript from one origin may access a response from another. It does not authenticate callers, enforce tenant permissions or stop non-browser clients from calling your API. Some cross-origin requests can reach the server even when the browser refuses to expose their response. See [MDN's CORS guide](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS).

## Choose the development connection

| Approach | Browser request | Where configuration belongs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Vite proxy | Relative `/api/tasks/` on the frontend origin | Vite forwards to local Django |
| Direct API | `http://localhost:8000/api/tasks/` | Django allows the exact frontend origin |
| Production reverse proxy | Relative `/api/tasks/` on the public application origin | Hosting routes API traffic to Django |
| Separate production hosts | Frontend calls a different API origin | Django and any upstream proxy must return the correct policy |

The [React connection chapter](/guide/react-api-connection) uses the first approach. A working Vite proxy does not establish the production policy.

## Configure Django for a direct cross-origin API

Install into the separate backend environment and record the resolved dependency:

```bash
# Terminal — backend/, with the project virtual environment active.
python -m pip install django-cors-headers
python -m pip freeze > requirements.txt
```

```python
# backend/config/settings.py — Add the app; keep the existing installed apps.
INSTALLED_APPS += ["corsheaders"]
```

Place `"corsheaders.middleware.CorsMiddleware"` near the beginning of the existing `MIDDLEWARE` list, before CommonMiddleware and any WhiteNoise middleware. Keep the rest of the middleware; replacing the list with only CORS removes unrelated protection.

```python
# backend/config/settings.py — Local direct-origin example, not production settings.
CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS = ["http://localhost:5173"]
CORS_ALLOW_ALL_ORIGINS = False
CORS_URLS_REGEX = r"^/api/.*$"
```

Use the frontend origin, without a path or trailing slash. In production replace the development origin with the exact deployed frontend origin. The [django-cors-headers reference](https://github.com/adamchainz/django-cors-headers) documents these settings and middleware ordering.

Do not allow every Netlify preview or every host on a shared hosting domain by default. Treat access from a preview as an intentional environment decision, particularly when it can reach production data. `ALLOWED_HOSTS` separately validates Django's request host; it is not the frontend origin allowlist.

## Understand preflight

A request with headers such as `Authorization`, or JSON content type in typical API writes, can require an OPTIONS preflight. The browser asks whether the intended method and headers are allowed before sending the actual request. An anonymous OPTIONS request therefore must not be redirected to a login page by a proxy or custom gateway.

Inspect both requests in DevTools. A successful OPTIONS response does not prove the following POST is authorized. Avoid accidental slash redirects by matching Django's actual URL. For a custom request header, extend the package's default allowed-header list rather than accidentally replacing needed headers.

## Bearer authentication versus cookie authentication

With a bearer-token API, explicitly attach the access token through the application's transport policy. The `Authorization` header needs CORS permission, but adding `withCredentials` is not how you create a bearer token.

With session cookies, the browser must be allowed to send credentials and Django must allow the requesting origin. For a direct cookie-based connection:

```typescript
// frontend/src/api/client.ts — Example for an intentionally cookie-authenticated API.
import axios from 'axios';
export const api = axios.create({
  baseURL: 'http://localhost:8000/api/',
  withCredentials: true,
});
```

```python
# backend/config/settings.py — Add only for the chosen cookie-based local flow.
CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS = True
CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS = ["http://localhost:5173"]
```

These settings are not a complete login implementation. The allowed-origin response must name the requesting origin; a wildcard origin is incompatible with credentialed browser access. Cookies still follow their own scope and browser policy.

## CSRF is a separate write protection

For session-authenticated unsafe requests, keep Django's CSRF protection and send the session's current CSRF token in `X-CSRFToken`. Obtain it through your designed login/bootstrap flow; a frontend on another hostname cannot simply read the API hostname's cookie. If returning a token from a bootstrap endpoint, allow only intended origins and send credentials for the same session. Login can rotate the token, so refresh it afterward.

`CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS` permits configured origins in Django's origin checks; it does not waive the token requirement. A same-origin development proxy does not remove CSRF requirements either. Follow [Django's CSRF reference](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/5.2/ref/csrf/).

For genuinely cross-site production cookies, evaluate `SameSite=None` with `Secure` for the relevant cookies and use HTTPS. “Cross-origin” and “cross-site” differ: two ports can be different origins while still being the same site. Browser third-party-cookie restrictions can still prevent the session from working. Prefer an intentional domain/routing design over repeatedly loosening settings.

## Diagnose the actual failure

| Symptom | Inspect next |
| --- | --- |
| OPTIONS redirects or fails | Proxy routing, URL slash, method and header policy |
| Browser reports missing allow-origin header | Exact Origin, middleware ordering, upstream error responses |
| CORS succeeds, request returns 401 or 403 | Credentials, session, permissions and response details |
| Django reports CSRF failure | Trusted origin, session cookie and current token |
| Works in curl, fails in browser | Browser origin rules and cookie policy; curl does not enforce CORS |
| Browser shows only a generic network error | Network panel and server status; a backend failure may lack CORS headers |
| HTTPS frontend calls HTTP API | Mixed-content blocking; use an HTTPS API |

Do not use `mode: "no-cors"` as an API fix: an opaque response is unusable for normal JSON reads. Do not disable CSRF, authentication or tenant checks to quiet a browser error.

## Verify the real deployment

Test an allowed origin and a deliberately unlisted origin in a browser. Check a preflighted authenticated request, an expired session, a session write with and without a valid CSRF token, and an API error response. Confirm no protected write occurs on a rejected request. Verify the actual production URLs, not only the development proxy.

These are proposed application checks. This static handbook does not run a Django API or change any source project's CORS configuration.

title: Signals: useful hooks, visible workflows
summary: Choose between a receiver, an explicit service call and a durable job.
body:
## Use a signal for a small independent reaction

Signals can connect decoupled receivers to framework events. Examples include a lightweight cache invalidation hook or a local integration responding to a model event. A reader should still be able to discover where the receiver is registered and what it does.

If an operation must always occur as part of a business workflow, an explicit service call is usually easier to understand and test. Creating a financial record and updating its authoritative balance should not depend on an easily missed receiver import.

## Know the traps

Model save receivers can run before the enclosing transaction commits. Publishing a task there can expose uncommitted or rolled-back data. Use `on_commit` where appropriate, and a durable outbox when delivery must survive a crash.

`QuerySet.update` and bulk creation do not call each model's `save` and its save signals. A receiver is therefore not a universal invariant enforcement mechanism. Protect durable invariants with database constraints and controlled workflow entry points.

## Register intentionally

Import the receiver module in the app configuration's `ready` method. Do not query the database while loading the app. Use a stable `dispatch_uid` where duplicate registration is possible, keep handlers short and avoid recursive saves. Signals do not turn synchronous work into a background job.

## Decision checklist

| Need | Prefer |
| --- | --- |
| Mandatory multi-model operation | Explicit transactional service |
| Small independent framework-event reaction | Signal with clear registration |
| Slow or retryable external effect | Durable job published after commit |
| Must never lose an event | Transactional outbox and retrying delivery |

Test receiver registration, repeated events, rollback, bulk-operation bypass and handler failure. The [Django signal guide](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/5.2/topics/signals/) explains dispatch and recommends considering explicit calls when code lives in the same project.

title: WebSockets: design the live connection
summary: Choose the transport, define messages, authenticate connections and recover safely after disconnects.
body:
## Choose the transport for the interaction

| Requirement | Starting choice |
| --- | --- |
| Occasional refresh of a dashboard | HTTP polling with a deliberate interval |
| One-way server updates, client commands remain HTTP | Consider server-sent events |
| Frequent two-way game, chat or collaborative interaction | Consider WebSockets |

A WebSocket provides a persistent two-way connection. It does not supply your message contract, application permissions or recovery policy. The [WebSocket API reference](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/WebSockets_API) describes the browser interface. For Django implementation, continue to [Channels](/guide/django-channels).

## Give connection state a visible meaning

Distinguish connecting, connected, reconnecting, disconnected and access denied. Do not present a disabled live connection as an empty game or an empty chat history. A connected transport still needs an authorized subscription and an authoritative snapshot.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Browser
    participant W as WebSocket boundary
    participant D as Domain state
    B->>W: Connect with accepted identity mechanism
    W->>D: Authorize requested room
    D-->>W: Authorized scope
    W-->>B: Current snapshot and version
    B->>W: Command with unique ID
    W->>D: Validate and apply transition
    W-->>B: Acknowledgement and safe state update
    Note over B,W: Connection drops and delivery is uncertain
    B->>W: Reconnect and reauthorize
    W->>D: Read current authoritative state
    W-->>B: Snapshot or supported resume result
```

The diagram describes a recommended contract, not a claim that every inspected game implements replay or resumable events.

## Authenticate and authorize separately

For browser connections, use a deliberate cookie-session or short-lived ticket/token design. The native browser WebSocket constructor cannot attach arbitrary Authorization headers like Axios. Never assume the Axios interceptor authenticates a socket. Avoid long-lived tokens in URLs that may be logged.

Validate the handshake's Origin and authorize the requested room before joining a group. WebSocket origin handling is separate from HTTP CORS response headers; adding `CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS` alone does not secure a socket. Origins can also be forged by non-browser clients, so origin validation is not identity verification. Recheck operation permissions and handle revoked sessions or removed membership while a connection remains open.

The [Channels security guide](https://channels.readthedocs.io/en/stable/topics/security.html) covers origin validators and cookie-based connection risks.

## Define commands, events and acknowledgements

Use explicit message types and validated payloads. A synthetic command envelope might look like:

```json
{
  "type": "game.move",
  "command_id": "demo-command-42",
  "expected_version": 17,
  "payload": { "cell": 4 }
}
```

The server derives the caller and authorized game from trusted connection context. It checks the turn, input and current version before changing state. A command acknowledgement must distinguish accepted, rejected and already applied; a browser `send()` returning does not prove durable completion.

An accepted command can produce different events for different recipients. In poker, another player's hole cards never belong in your payload. Broadcast a safe projection rather than raw internal state.

## Recover without duplicating work

Use capped exponential reconnect delays with jitter. Stop automatic retries for a known authorization denial, and cancel reconnect timers on logout, navigation or unmount. A reconnect creates a new authorization boundary, not a continuation of old permission.

Transport ordering on one connection does not solve gaps between connections or concurrent producers. Use server-defined versions or sequence identifiers, detect gaps and fetch a fresh snapshot. Only offer replay if the backend actually retains and authorizes a replay stream.

After a lost response, a retried command needs a server-side deduplication policy. For commands where duplicates matter, bind the command ID to the actor, target and payload; do not blindly replay every queued action after reconnect.

## Keep the React connection deliberate

Place connection lifecycle in a feature hook or a shared provider where sharing is intentional. UI components render connection state and emit commands. Clean up listeners, timers and the socket when the owner unmounts; development remounts should not leave duplicate subscriptions.

When events affect TanStack Query data, either update a known cache entry from an authoritative event or invalidate the relevant scoped query. Do not mutate unrelated tenant caches or create a second competing source of truth. Keep transient presence separate from durable domain records.

## Heartbeats, load and deployment

Browser JavaScript does not expose protocol ping frames directly. If the application needs a heartbeat, define application messages and timeouts, or use the server's transport-level support appropriately. Tune the policy around the proxy's idle limits. Follow the [browser client guide](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/WebSockets_API/Writing_WebSocket_client_applications) for lifecycle events.

Bound message sizes, rates and queues. The standard browser WebSocket interface has no automatic backpressure; decide whether to coalesce replaceable updates or disconnect a slow consumer rather than buffer indefinitely.

Deploy secure `wss://` connections from HTTPS pages and use a host/proxy that supports long-lived upgraded connections. In Django, an ASGI process serves the socket; a static frontend host does not. A [Channels layer](https://channels.readthedocs.io/en/stable/topics/channel_layers.html) connects instances, while durable business state remains elsewhere. Its existence does not guarantee event persistence or exactly-once delivery.

## Verify the failure cases

Test missing identity, rejected origin, foreign room, revoked membership, malformed payload, duplicate command, stale version, private-data filtering, disconnect during mutation and reconnection on another server instance. Confirm logout closes the connection and clears private state.
