Use the [gaming case study](/guide/gaming-multiplayer-flow) to connect these decisions to real code. These checks remain proposed; this handbook opens no live socket and runs no Channels service.

title: Channels: authenticated real-time systems
summary: Map ASGI, consumers, channel layers and reconnect behavior to the gaming platform.
body:
## Start with the connection contract

Read [WebSockets: design the live connection](/guide/websocket-design) for transport choices, authentication, message contracts, reconnects and React lifecycle. This chapter covers the Django implementation boundaries.

## Add Channels for a real requirement

HTTP fits ordinary request/response work. WebSockets fit live game state, presence and bidirectional commands. A connection is a long-lived transport, not permission to receive every event.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    B[Browser] --> O[Origin validation and authentication]
    O --> R[ASGI route]
    R --> C[Consumer: authorize commands]
    C --> S[Domain service and durable state]
    C --> L[Channel layer]
    L --> P[Per-recipient safe projection]
    P --> B
```

ASGI routes protocols to consumers. A consumer handles connection and message events. A channel layer passes events between instances; a production Redis layer needs an actual reachable Redis service. An in-memory layer cannot connect independent processes.

## Establish identity, then authorize the room

Validate WebSocket origins. Cookie-based credentials can accompany cross-site connection attempts; accepting any origin is unsafe. Channels' `AuthMiddlewareStack` integrates Django session authentication. A JWT design needs a deliberately implemented verifier; do not assume session middleware verifies a bearer token. Avoid putting long-lived credentials into logged URLs. See [Channels security](https://channels.readthedocs.io/en/stable/topics/security.html).

On connect, check access to the game or room. On every command, check current role, turn and game status. Recheck sensitive state as membership or session validity changes. A guessed group name is not an access-control boundary.

## The server owns game state

Validate move inputs and apply transitions on the server. Broadcast only the recipient-safe representation: poker opponents must not receive another player's hole cards. Do not send a complete secret state object and ask the browser to hide it.

The [gaming multiplayer flow](/guide/gaming-multiplayer-flow) and [poker chapter](/guide/gaming-poker-tournaments) show these boundaries. Their inspected process-local timer limitations remain limitations, not a guarantee of distributed scheduling.

## Reconnect from an authoritative snapshot

Treat disconnection as normal. Reauthenticate and reauthorize, retrieve a current snapshot, then resume events with a defined ordering or version policy. Deduplicate commands where retries are possible. Presence is transient and should not decide durable financial or game results.

Use database-safe adapters for synchronous ORM work inside async consumers, or supported async ORM operations with their documented transaction constraints. An `async def` containing blocking calls still blocks useful work.

## Verify more than a connection

Test invalid origin, missing credentials, unauthorized room, forged move, duplicate command, private-data filtering, disconnect/reconnect and multiple server processes. Rate-limit messages and bound payload sizes. A connected socket alone proves none of these properties.

title: Verify a Django API and prepare delivery
summary: Check identity boundaries, migrations and operational readiness before shipping.
body:
## Start with the Tasks API

Create `backend/apps/tasks/tests.py` with this owner-boundary test. Django creates an isolated test database; use synthetic records.

```python
# backend/apps/tasks/tests.py — Prove another user cannot read a task.
from django.contrib.auth import get_user_model
from rest_framework.test import APITestCase
from .models import Task

class TaskIsolationTests(APITestCase):
    def test_other_owner_cannot_read_task(self):
        user_model = get_user_model()
        owner = user_model.objects.create_user(username="owner", password="test-only-password")
        other = user_model.objects.create_user(username="other", password="test-only-password")
        task = Task.objects.create(owner=owner, title="Private task")
        self.client.force_authenticate(user=other)
        self.assertEqual(self.client.get("/api/tasks/").data, [])
        self.assertEqual(self.client.get(f"/api/tasks/{task.pk}/").status_code, 404)
```

This assumes the starter's unpaginated default. If pagination is configured, inspect its `results` field instead. `force_authenticate` tests authorization wiring; it bypasses real login and does not verify credentials, cookies or CSRF. Add separate transport-level authentication tests.

```bash
# Terminal — backend/, with the selected environment active.
python manage.py check
python manage.py makemigrations --check --dry-run
python manage.py test apps.tasks
```

## Broaden by risk

Add validation failures, owner injection, update/delete isolation and anonymous requests. Domain tests should prove constraints, rollback and idempotency. Use the target database for locking and concurrent-write tests. Check query counts for list representations.

For session authentication, use explicit CSRF-enforcing tests. For JWT, verify expiration, issuer/audience where applicable, revoked-session behavior and provider outages. Read the [DRF testing guide](https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/testing/) for the difference between API helpers and full request behavior.

## Prepare deployment as its own step

Run `check --deploy` with production settings; it is a configuration diagnostic, not a complete security audit. Set secrets through the host, configure allowed hosts and trusted origins deliberately, disable debug, apply migrations with a release plan and serve via a production WSGI or ASGI process.

Static frontend hosting does not run Django. Heroku web/worker processes, scheduled work and S3 storage have different responsibilities. Follow the [deployment platforms](/guide/deployment-platforms) and [recovery runbook](/guide/recovery-runbook). Verify backups by restoring them; verify jobs by their recorded outcomes.

The handbook build validates these articles and diagrams. It does not execute this backend or prove that any source project passed the checks listed here.

title: Services write. Selectors read.
summary: Put workflow rules and trusted query scope in explicit domain boundaries.
body:
## Make the operation visible

The reports domain needs a clear distinction between changing durable state and retrieving it. Services own writes and workflow rules. Selectors expose reads with trusted scope. Views resolve identity and authorization, then orchestrate these boundaries.

This pattern is useful when more than one endpoint or job shares an operation. A simple read does not need an elaborate class hierarchy. Start with functions and introduce abstractions when actual repetition appears.

## A scoped read

The example is an excerpt from a separate backend application. It assumes a Report model with organization, creator, status, and created_at fields, plus an already authorized organization object.

**backend/apps/reports/selectors.py · excerpt**

```python
# backend/apps/reports/selectors.py — Retrieve reports within trusted scope.
def report_list(*, organization):
    """Return reports belonging to an authorized organization.

    Args:
        organization: Organization resolved through active membership.

    Returns:
        Queryset of reports ordered from newest to oldest.
    """
    # Step 1: Apply the tenant boundary before returning data.
    return (
        Report.objects.filter(organization=organization)
        .select_related("created_by")
        .order_by("-created_at", "-id")
    )
```

The omitted Report import depends on the application's model package. `select_related` joins single-valued relationships; `prefetch_related` is for collections. Add either because the response needs those relationships, and verify query counts with representative data.

## A transactional write

A create service accepts trusted organization and actor objects plus validated input. It verifies business rules, writes durable state, and returns the authoritative report. The caller must not pass an arbitrary client-supplied organization object without checking membership.

Use database uniqueness constraints for invariants such as an organization-specific external identifier. A Python pre-check alone races: two requests can both observe no existing record and then insert. Handle the constraint violation through the application's error contract.

## Side effects and jobs

Do not send email or publish a job before a transaction commits. `transaction.on_commit` prevents publication for rolled-back writes, but it does not recover from a process crash after commit and before publishing. A durable outbox is appropriate when losing the job is unacceptable.

## Verify isolation and cost

Test two organizations with synthetic reports. A scoped selector for the first organization must never include the second organization's rows. Test related-object assignments as well as the primary report identifier. Use query-count assertions to expose N+1 behavior when serializing several reports.

Test the service directly for invalid workflow transitions, duplicate requests, and rollback on errors. API tests then verify that identity, membership, permission checks, and error responses connect those rules correctly.

title: Networking and load balancers: from domain name to Django
summary: Follow one request through DNS, TLS, a load balancer and a proxy, and design each hop to fail safely.

objectives: Trace a request through DNS, TLS, a load balancer and an app server
Choose between a layer 4 and a layer 7 load balancer
Configure Django correctly behind a proxy
Design health checks, timeouts and retries that fail safely
Explain how blue-green and canary releases use a load balancer

body:
## What am I learning?

Before Django sees a request, it has already passed through several systems. DNS turns the name into an address, TLS encrypts the connection, a load balancer picks a healthy server, and an app server hands the request to Django. Each layer fails in its own way. Knowing the path tells me where to look, and how to design each hop so one failure doesn't become an outage.

## Core concepts

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  B[Browser] -->|DNS lookup| D[DNS]
  B -->|TLS handshake, then HTTPS| L[Load balancer]
  L -->|healthy target| G[Gunicorn or ASGI server]
  G -->|WSGI or ASGI| J[Django]
```

**DNS** maps names to addresses. The records I'll use: A/AAAA (an address), CNAME (another name), ALIAS/ANAME (another name at the zone apex, provider-specific) and TXT (verification). Each has a TTL: how long resolvers may cache it.

**TLS** proves the server's identity with a certificate and encrypts the connection. **TLS termination** is where it gets decrypted, usually the load balancer.

**Load balancers** come in two kinds:

| | Layer 4 (e.g., AWS NLB) | Layer 7 (e.g., AWS ALB) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sees | TCP/UDP connections | HTTP requests: host, path, headers |
| Routes by | Port | Host, path, header, method, weights |
| Use for | Non-HTTP protocols, static IPs, extreme throughput | Web apps and APIs |

An [Application Load Balancer](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/introduction.html) sends requests to **target groups** and only to targets passing **health checks**. A [Network Load Balancer](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/network/introduction.html) forwards connections without reading HTTP. On Heroku, the [router](https://devcenter.heroku.com/articles/http-routing) does the layer 7 job for me.

**Proxy headers** carry what the balancer saw: `X-Forwarded-For` (client IP chain), `X-Forwarded-Proto` (http or https) and `Host`.

## Modern patterns

| Pattern | Problem it solves | How |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Edge first** | Static assets and TLS handshakes waste app capacity and add latency | A CDN serves assets and terminates TLS close to users, with HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 |
| **HTTPS only, with HSTS** | A first plain-HTTP request can be intercepted | Redirect to HTTPS and send [`Strict-Transport-Security`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Strict-Transport-Security) |
| **Liveness versus readiness** | One health check can't tell "restart me" from "don't send me traffic yet" | Liveness: the process responds. Readiness: it can serve, for example migrations finished. |
| **Graceful shutdown and draining** | Deploys cut off in-flight requests | The balancer stops new requests and waits ([deregistration delay](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/edit-target-group-attributes.html)); the app finishes current work on SIGTERM |
| **Timeout budgets** | A slow dependency ties up every worker | Each hop's timeout is shorter than the caller's, and every outbound call has one |
| **Retries with backoff and jitter** | Synchronized retries overload a recovering service | Retry only safe or idempotent calls, with exponential backoff and random jitter ([AWS Builders' Library](https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/timeouts-retries-and-backoff-with-jitter/)) |
| **Blue-green and canary releases** | A bad deploy reaches every user at once | ALB weighted target groups shift traffic gradually (1%, 10%, 100%) or all at once with instant rollback |
| **Private by default** | Databases and app servers exposed to the internet | Only the balancer is public; app and database sit in private subnets, with security groups allowing only the previous hop |

## Anti-patterns to avoid

- **A health check that queries the database.** One database blip fails every target at once and the balancer removes them all.
- **Trusting forwarded headers from anyone.** Clients can send `X-Forwarded-Proto: https` or a fake IP.
- **No timeout on outbound HTTP calls.** One hung provider eventually blocks every worker.
- **Long work inside the request.** It hits a timeout somewhere; it belongs in a [background job](/guide/reliable-job-lifecycle).
- **Sticky sessions as a crutch.** Pinning users to a server hides in-memory state that breaks on deploy. Keep the app stateless instead.
- **Retrying non-idempotent writes blindly.** A retried payment request can charge twice without an idempotency key.

## Build it step by step

**Step 1: trust only your own proxy.** Behind a balancer that sets `X-Forwarded-Proto` and strips client-sent values:

```python
SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER = ("HTTP_X_FORWARDED_PROTO", "https")
SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT = True
SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS = 31536000
ALLOWED_HOSTS = ["app.example.com"]
```

Only set [`SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER`](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/5.2/ref/settings/#secure-proxy-ssl-header) when that proxy guarantee is true. Start HSTS with a short value and raise it once HTTPS is confirmed everywhere.

**Step 2: separate liveness from readiness.**

```python
def live(request):
    return HttpResponse("ok")

def ready(request):
    connection.ensure_connection()
    return HttpResponse("ready")
```

Point the balancer's health check at the cheap liveness endpoint. Use readiness for startup gating and monitoring, so a database problem is alerted on, not "fixed" by removing every server.

**Step 3: set a timeout budget.** Every outbound call gets an explicit timeout shorter than the request's own limit:

```python
response = requests.get(url, timeout=5)
```

**Step 4: plan WebSockets.** [Django Channels](/guide/django-channels) needs an ASGI server. ALBs support WebSockets, but idle connections still close at the idle timeout (60 seconds by default), so send heartbeats.

Checkpoint: Django logs `https` as the scheme and the real client IP for a production request.

## Common failures by layer

| Symptom | Likely layer |
| --- | --- |
| Domain does not resolve | DNS record or TTL |
| Certificate warning | TLS: expired, wrong name, missing chain |
| 502 / 503 from the balancer | No healthy targets, or targets crashing (see [ALB troubleshooting](/guide/troubleshoot-alb)) |
| 504 | App too slow; an upstream timeout fired. Heroku's router ends requests after 30 seconds. |
| Redirect loop to HTTPS | Django doesn't know the request was already HTTPS |
| `DisallowedHost` | `ALLOWED_HOSTS` is missing the domain |

## Exercise

For one deployed app:

1. Run `dig` on the domain and record the record type and TTL.
2. Inspect the certificate: issuer, expiry, and how it renews.
3. Find the balancer or router and its timeout.
4. Add separate liveness and readiness endpoints and point the health check at liveness.
5. Confirm Django logs the correct scheme and client IP.

**Done means:** I can draw every hop with its timeout, and the health check no longer depends on the database.

## Check your understanding

- Why can an ALB route `/api` and `/admin` differently while an NLB cannot?
- What breaks if `SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER` is set without a proxy that strips the header?
- Why add random jitter to retries?
- How does a weighted target group make a canary release possible?
- Which timeout ends a 45-second request on Heroku?

## Answer key

An ALB reads HTTP requests, including paths; an NLB forwards connections without reading HTTP. A client can send the header and make Django treat an insecure request as HTTPS. Without jitter, many clients retry at the same instants and overload the recovering service in waves. The balancer sends a small share of traffic to the new version's targets, so errors show up on a few users before everyone. Heroku's 30-second router timeout, which is why long work belongs in a background job.

## Go deeper

- [ALB target group health checks](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/target-group-health-checks.html)
- [Timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter](https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/timeouts-retries-and-backoff-with-jitter/)
- [MDN: DNS](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/DNS)

title: Build a feature from the inside out
summary: API contracts, query hooks, controllers, and parts with clear responsibilities.
body:
## Start with the contract

A Reports feature starts with an agreed API representation: stable report identifiers, organization scope, status values, and error shape. TypeScript describes the expected contract; it does not validate an arbitrary server response at runtime. Add runtime validation at the boundary when the input needs it.

The handbook runtime has no API calls. Axios and a server-state query library belong in the applications this chapter teaches, not in the static handbook just to mirror an architecture diagram.

## Give each boundary one job

| Boundary | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| API module | URLs, transport, input/output contracts |
| Query hook | Server cache identity, fetch and mutation lifecycle |
| Controller | Combine query state, actions, and local UI behavior |
| Page | Compose the workspace |
| Parts | Render props and emit user intent |
| Barrel | Export the feature's public interface |

Avoid controllers for every small visual component. A controller is useful where several state sources and user actions meet.

## Separate server and local state

Report status belongs to the server. A dialog's open state belongs to the browser. A server-state cache is a snapshot with a refresh policy, not another durable database. Persist only preferences that should survive a reload; do not put access tokens or sensitive report records in reading preferences.

## Organization-aware query keys

Include organization identity in every tenant-specific cache key. When organization changes, requests and views must use the newly authorized scope. On logout, clear user-specific caches so a subsequent session cannot see the previous user's data.

**src/features/reports/api/queryKeys.ts · excerpt**

```typescript
// src/features/reports/api/queryKeys.ts — Partition report cache entries.
export const reportKeys = {
  list: (organizationId: string) =>
    ['organizations', organizationId, 'reports'] as const,
  detail: (organizationId: string, reportId: string) =>
    ['organizations', organizationId, 'reports', reportId] as const,
};
```

These keys express scope; they do not enforce backend authorization.

## Choose a refresh strategy

After creating a report, use the authoritative response to populate its detail entry and invalidate affected list queries. If a mutation changes a field used by a list filter or aggregate, refresh those derived views too. Refetch a specific query when only that snapshot requires a fresh result.

Optimistic updates fit reversible actions with predictable outcomes. Save the previous snapshot, cancel conflicting reads, apply the optimistic change, roll back on failure, and reconcile with the server afterward. For a queued generation job, avoid claiming success optimistically: display the accepted job and observe its actual status.

## Render every state

Loading is not the same as an empty result. Preserve useful existing data during a background refresh. Give failed actions actionable feedback and a retry when safe. Associate form errors with the relevant field, keep focus visible, and return dialog focus to its trigger.

## Verify the behavior

Exercise create success, validation failure, network failure, tenant switching, logout, and job completion. Confirm invalidation targets the correct organization and that parts can render their loading, error, and empty props without an API connection.

## Put the boundaries into folders

Use the [frontend structure](/guide/frontend-folder-structure) for a standalone app or the same layout under `frontend/` in a [full-stack repository](/guide/full-stack-folder-structure). The [Axios and TanStack Query example](/guide/react-api-connection) connects transport, cancellation, cache keys and providers.

title: PostgreSQL performance: indexes, query plans, and connections
summary: Find why a page is slow, fix it at the query, and keep the app inside its connection limit.

objectives: Find and remove N+1 query patterns in Django views and selectors
Read an EXPLAIN ANALYZE plan and choose the right index
Replace OFFSET pagination with keyset pagination for large lists
Prevent lost updates with locks or optimistic concurrency
Keep total database connections under the plan's limit

body:
## What am I learning?

Most slow pages in a Django app are database problems: too many queries, a query with no usable index, or too many connections. The ORM makes queries easy to write and easy to forget about. This lesson is about seeing what the database actually does and fixing problems at the source, before reaching for a cache.

## Core concepts

| Concept | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| Query count | How many round trips one request makes. Many fast queries can be slower than one slow one. |
| Index | A sorted structure that finds rows without scanning the whole table. B-tree is the default. |
| Query plan | How PostgreSQL decides to run a query: which indexes, joins and scans. |
| Transaction | Changes that succeed or fail together. `transaction.atomic()` in Django. |
| Isolation level | What a transaction can see of others' work. PostgreSQL's default is [Read Committed](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html). |
| Connection | A server process with real memory cost. Every plan has a limit. |

## Modern patterns

| Pattern | Problem it solves | Use it when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Eager loading** (`select_related`, `prefetch_related`) | N+1 queries in lists | Any list that shows related data |
| **Composite indexes led by the tenant** | Multi-tenant queries scanning other tenants' rows | Tables filtered by household or organization |
| **Partial indexes** | Indexing rows that are never queried | Queries on a subset, such as `WHERE status = 'pending'` ([docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-partial.html)) |
| **Covering indexes** (`INCLUDE`) | Extra table lookups after the index | Hot queries reading a few extra columns ([index-only scans](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-index-only-scans.html)) |
| **Keyset (cursor) pagination** | `OFFSET 50000` reads and discards 50,000 rows | Long or infinite lists; DRF [CursorPagination](https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/pagination/#cursorpagination) |
| **Optimistic concurrency** | Lost updates without holding locks | Edits by people, using a version column, as in the Moneta budgets feature |
| **Pessimistic locking** (`select_for_update`) | Two writers reading the same old value | Short, critical read-modify-write steps |
| **Expand and contract migrations** | Schema changes that lock tables or break running code | Every production schema change ([safe migrations](/guide/safe-database-migrations)) |
| **Read models** | Expensive aggregations on every page load | Dashboards and ledgers ([read models](/guide/ledger-and-read-models)) |
| **Measure with `pg_stat_statements`** | Guessing which queries matter | Production: rank queries by total time ([docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/pgstatstatements.html)) |

## Anti-patterns to avoid

- **Queries in a loop.** The classic N+1.
- **Deep OFFSET pagination.** Each later page gets slower.
- **Indexing every column.** Each index slows writes and costs storage.
- **Long transactions.** They hold locks and block cleanup.
- **Network calls inside a transaction.** A slow provider now holds database locks.
- **Exact `COUNT(*)` on huge tables for every page.** Show "more results" or an estimate instead.
- **Caching first.** A cache over a slow query hides the problem until the cache misses.

## Build it step by step

**Step 1: count queries.** The most common problem isn't one slow query; it's hundreds of fast ones.

```python
# 1 query for accounts, plus 1 per account for its institution
for account in Account.objects.filter(household=household):
    print(account.institution.name)

# 2 queries total, however many accounts there are
accounts = Account.objects.filter(household=household).select_related("institution")
```

Lock the fix in with a test:

```python
def test_account_list_query_count(self):
    with self.assertNumQueries(2):
        list(account_list(self.household))
```

**Step 2: index the real access pattern.** A multi-tenant app nearly always filters by tenant first:

```python
class Transaction(models.Model):
    household = models.ForeignKey(Household, on_delete=models.CASCADE)
    posted_at = models.DateTimeField()

    class Meta:
        indexes = [models.Index(fields=["household", "-posted_at"])]
```

Column order matters. This serves "this household's transactions, newest first," but not a date filter across all households.

**Step 3: read the plan.**

```python
print(Transaction.objects.filter(household=h).order_by("-posted_at")[:50].explain(analyze=True))
```

Look for a **Seq Scan** on a large table, **estimated rows far from actual rows** (stale statistics; run `ANALYZE`), and the node with the most actual time. [`EXPLAIN ANALYZE`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/using-explain.html) really runs the query, so wrap data changes in a transaction and roll back.

**Step 4: paginate by key, not offset.**

```python
page = (Transaction.objects
        .filter(household=h, posted_at__lt=cursor)
        .order_by("-posted_at")[:50])
```

The index from step 2 finds the next page directly, however deep the user scrolls. Use a unique tiebreaker such as `id` when timestamps can repeat.

**Step 5: prevent lost updates.**

```python
with transaction.atomic():
    budget = Budget.objects.select_for_update().get(pk=budget_id)
    budget.spent += amount
    budget.save()
```

Or update in one statement with `F("spent") + amount`, or check a version column and reject stale edits. Keep the transaction short.

**Step 6: do the connection math.** Total = web processes × workers per process + background workers + one-off scripts. It must stay under the plan's limit.

| Option | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `CONN_MAX_AGE` | Reuses a connection across requests. The default `0` closes after every request. |
| `CONN_HEALTH_CHECKS` | Checks a reused connection before use. |
| Django's PostgreSQL pool | Django 5.1+ with psycopg 3 can keep a [pool](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/5.2/ref/databases/#connection-pool) per process. |
| PgBouncer | A shared pooler for when many processes need more connections than the database allows. |

Checkpoint: the page's query count is fixed by a test and its main query uses an index scan.

## Exercise

Pick the slowest list page in one app.

1. Count its queries and remove any N+1 pattern.
2. Run `explain(analyze=True)` on the main query.
3. Add one index if the plan shows a sequential scan on a large table.
4. Switch the endpoint to cursor pagination if the list can grow large.
5. Record before-and-after timings.

**Done means:** `assertNumQueries` protects the page, the plan uses an index, and timings are recorded.

## Check your understanding

- A list page runs 201 queries for 100 rows. What is the likely cause?
- Why doesn't an index on `(household, posted_at)` help a query filtering only by `posted_at`?
- Why does page 1,000 get slower with OFFSET pagination but not with keyset pagination?
- Two requests add to the same budget at once and one update is lost. What prevents it?
- Why can "too many connections" happen on a database with low CPU usage?

## Answer key

An N+1 pattern; fix it with `select_related` or `prefetch_related`. A B-tree index is ordered by its first column, so it can't efficiently find rows by the second column alone. OFFSET reads and discards every earlier row; a keyset query jumps straight to the position through the index. Locking the row with `select_for_update()`, an `F()` expression update, or a version check. Connections are limited by count, not load: each process holds its connections whether or not it's busy.

## Go deeper

- [PostgreSQL: indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes.html)
- [Django: database access optimization](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/5.2/topics/db/optimization/)

title: Security starts at the boundaries
summary: Trace identity, tenant authority, private files, and operational access through the system.
body:
## Learn the references first

For the vocabulary behind this design, start with [security standards and their publishers](/guide/security-standards-fundamentals), then [NIST](/guide/nist-fundamentals) and [OWASP](/guide/owasp-fundamentals).

## What this design protects

The reports application needs to protect organization-owned records, generated files, session credentials, and operational secrets. Its attacker model includes an anonymous caller, a valid user from another organization, a revoked member with an unexpired token, and a compromised provider or worker credential.

The handbook is public static documentation. Its deployment has no patient records, application session, or project database. Controls described here belong to the application architecture being taught. They have not been tested against a real Gait integration or running reports backend.

## Draw the trust boundaries

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  Untrusted[Untrusted browser - selected tenant and input]
  Identity[Identity verification - issuer and session policy]
  Membership[Project membership - active organization and role]
  Permission[Action and object permission]
  Scope[Scoped query or write service]
  Data[(Organization-owned durable data)]
  Deny[Stop - policy-defined denial]
  Untrusted --> Identity
  Identity -->|Valid identity| Membership
  Identity -->|Invalid credential| Deny
  Membership -->|Active membership| Permission
  Membership -->|Missing or revoked| Deny
  Permission -->|Allowed action| Scope
  Permission -->|Forbidden| Deny
  Scope --> Data
```

**Text alternative:** Every request crosses identity verification, active project membership, action and object permissions, and tenant-scoped data access. Failure at any gate stops the request. A client-selected organization never bypasses these gates.

## Identity does not grant authority

Verify the signature with an allowed algorithm and trusted key source. Validate issuer, intended audience, expiry, and any required token claims. Never accept a token because its payload can be decoded. Cache keys according to the identity provider's actual key-rotation contract and define what happens when an unknown key appears.

The selected identity mechanism owns identity/session behavior; the project owns organization memberships and business roles. Compare [Django auth, Simple JWT, Clerk, and Gait](/guide/authentication-options) before selecting an integration. Local signature verification establishes the signed claims within their validity period. It does not prove that a session remains active. For actions requiring fresh session validation, define a fail-closed policy and use an inspected session contract. Do not invent a Gait session endpoint.

Refresh cookies, browser access tokens, logout, multi-tab refresh, and revocation need explicit integration decisions. Cookie-authenticated writes need a CSRF defense. CORS determines which browser origins can read responses; it does not replace authentication or authorization, and non-browser clients are not constrained by it.

## Deny by default and check every path

Authorize the action and resource at the API boundary and preserve trusted scope through services, selectors, jobs, and downloads. Hiding a React button helps usability but grants no protection. Random identifiers reduce guessing; they do not establish ownership.

| Threat | Control location | Evidence to require |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Foreign report identifier | Scoped API query and related-object validation | Cross-organization read and write denial |
| Revoked member with live token | Project membership check | Denial before token expiry |
| Unauthorized generation | Service action permission | Viewer cannot queue generation |
| Job with forged tenant | Worker lookup and validated durable context | Job cannot load a foreign report |
| Shared private file URL | Download authorization and short lifetime | Unauthorized caller cannot mint URL |
| Leaked secret in bundle | Build/source review | No secret values in public assets |
| Sensitive logs | Redaction at event emission | Synthetic credential does not appear in logs |

OWASP recommends default denial and permission checks on every request. See its [Authorization Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.html) for the underlying principles.

## Private files need a second authorization path

Keep generated reports in private object storage. An authorized download endpoint verifies current membership, report ownership, and the action before issuing a short-lived signed URL. The storage object key is an internal reference, not proof that the requester may download it.

A signed URL is a temporary bearer capability. Anyone holding it can usually use it until expiry; removing a membership does not necessarily invalidate an already issued URL. Keep lifetimes appropriate to the sensitivity and document revocation limits. For immediate revocation requirements, evaluate an authenticated proxy download and its operational cost.

Validate upload size, type, and content according to the workload. User-provided MIME strings and filenames are insufficient. Quarantine and scanning policies depend on the actual file types and threat model; do not assert they exist without implementation evidence.

## Secrets and operator access

Frontend environment values compiled into a bundle are public. Keep provider credentials, database passwords, signing keys, and infrastructure secrets in server-side secret storage. Use separate local, staging, and production credentials and data. Rotate a credential by introducing the replacement, checking consumers, revoking the old value, and verifying that obsolete access fails.

Infrastructure permissions differ from application roles. Workers should access only the queues, objects, and secrets they need. Support access should be time-bounded, scoped, approved according to an explicit policy, and auditable. Logs should contain correlation identifiers and policy outcomes without passwords, refresh tokens, signed download URLs, or sensitive record bodies.

## Harden the public handbook

The static handbook delivers bundled scripts from its own origin. Content Security Policy constrains scripts to that origin and prevents framing. Additional headers disable MIME sniffing and browser features the handbook does not use. Mermaid uses strict rendering with sanitized labels; only repository-controlled Markdown is rendered. Raw HTML is not enabled in the Markdown renderer.

Styles allow inline declarations because the diagram renderer emits SVG styling. The policy permits Google Fonts stylesheet and font origins used by the current design. These are deliberate exceptions, not a claim that every attack class is eliminated. See the [MDN CSP guide](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CSP) for directive behavior.

## Verify with adversarial cases

Create synthetic organizations A and B, users with different roles, and a report owned by each. Attempt every read, mutation, generation, job-status, and download operation using a foreign identifier. Repeat after membership revocation without replacing the access token. Confirm policy-defined denial and absence of unauthorized database changes, queued jobs, or minted URLs.

Exercise unavailable identity validation, expired tokens, unknown signing keys, a retried generation request, and a worker restart. Record observed outcomes separately from proposed controls. A security checklist or architecture diagram alone is not proof of production readiness or regulatory compliance.

## Planned AWS flagship controls

The [Lumen AWS security plan](/guide/lumen-aws-security) applies these boundaries to private EC2 services behind an ALB, Gait identity, clinical permissions, encrypted data, managed secrets and recovery. It is a proposed architecture with explicit [release gates](/guide/lumen-aws-release), not a verified deployment.

title: Caching and rate limiting: speed and protection without new bugs
summary: Cache the right data with tenant-safe keys, avoid stampedes, and rate-limit without mistaking it for security.

objectives: Choose the right cache layer for a piece of data
Build tenant-safe cache keys with a clear invalidation rule
Prevent cache stampedes when a popular entry expires
Pick a rate-limiting algorithm and explain where throttling is not enough

body:
## What am I learning?

A cache stores a result so the next request doesn't recompute it. Rate limiting caps how often a client can do something. Both rely on fast shared storage, often Redis. Both can create serious bugs: a cache can serve stale or wrong data, including another tenant's, and a rate limit can block real users while giving a false sense of security.

## Core concepts

| Layer | What it caches | Controlled by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Browser | Responses, per user | HTTP headers (`Cache-Control`, `ETag`) |
| CDN | Public responses and static assets | HTTP headers and CDN rules |
| TanStack Query | Server data in React | Query keys and stale times |
| Django cache | Computed values, fragments, sessions | Application code |
| PostgreSQL | Data pages in memory | The database itself |

Three questions decide every cache: **what is the key** (everything the value depends on), **how stale may it be**, and **what happens when the cache is down**.

## Modern patterns

| Pattern | Problem it solves | How |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Cache-aside** | Repeated expensive reads | Check the cache, fall back to the source, store the result |
| **Stale-while-revalidate** | Users wait while an expired value is recomputed | Serve the stale value and refresh in the background: the HTTP [`stale-while-revalidate`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Cache-Control) directive, and TanStack Query's [default model](https://tanstack.com/query/latest/docs/framework/react/guides/caching) |
| **Immutable hashed assets** | Users load outdated JavaScript, or caches can't be long | Fingerprinted file names cached for a year; new builds get new names |
| **Scoped, versioned keys** | Cross-tenant leaks and stale shapes after a deploy | `household:{id}:summary:v2` |
| **Invalidate on commit** | Deleting too early lets stale data back in | `transaction.on_commit(lambda: cache.delete(key))` |
| **Stampede protection** | Hundreds of requests recompute the same expired entry at once | A short lock so one request recomputes, plus random TTL jitter |
| **Token bucket or sliding window limits** | Fixed windows allow double bursts at the window edge | Count requests over a rolling window or refill tokens at a steady rate |
| **Edge rate limiting** | Floods reach the app before any throttle runs | Limits at the CDN or load balancer, for example [AWS WAF rate-based rules](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/waf-rule-statement-type-rate-based.html) |
| **Idempotency keys** | Retries repeat side effects | Store the result of a write under a client-sent key and replay it on retry |

## Anti-patterns to avoid

- **A key without tenant scope.** `"dashboard:summary"` serves one household's numbers to all of them. That is a [tenant isolation](/guide/tenant-isolation) bug.
- **No expiry.** Every entry needs a TTL or an explicit invalidation path.
- **Publicly caching private responses.** API responses for a user need `Cache-Control: private` or `no-store`.
- **The cache as the source of truth.** It can be evicted at any time.
- **Caching to hide a slow query.** Fix the [query](/guide/postgres-performance) first.
- **Throttling as the only login protection.** It doesn't stop distributed attacks.
- **Per-process caches in production.** Django's local-memory backend gives each process its own cache and its own throttle counters.

## Build it step by step

**Step 1: configure a shared cache.** Django has a built-in Redis backend since 4.0 ([cache framework](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/5.2/topics/cache/)):

```python
CACHES = {
    "default": {
        "BACKEND": "django.core.cache.backends.redis.RedisCache",
        "LOCATION": os.environ["REDIS_URL"],
    }
}
```

**Step 2: cache-aside with a scoped key and jittered TTL.**

```python
import random
from django.core.cache import cache

def household_summary(household_id: int) -> dict:
    key = f"household:{household_id}:summary:v1"
    summary = cache.get(key)
    if summary is None:
        summary = compute_summary(household_id)
        cache.set(key, summary, timeout=300 + random.randint(0, 60))
    return summary
```

The jitter spreads expiry so many keys don't expire at the same moment.

**Step 3: invalidate after commit.**

```python
def record_transaction(household, data):
    with transaction.atomic():
        create_transaction(household, data)
        transaction.on_commit(
            lambda: cache.delete(f"household:{household.id}:summary:v1")
        )
```

**Step 4: protect a hot entry from a stampede.** Let only one request recompute:

```python
if summary is None and cache.add(f"{key}:lock", 1, timeout=30):
    summary = compute_summary(household_id)
    cache.set(key, summary, timeout=300)
    cache.delete(f"{key}:lock")
```

`cache.add` only succeeds if the lock key doesn't exist yet. Other requests serve a stale copy or wait briefly.

**Step 5: throttle expensive endpoints.** Django REST framework provides [throttles](https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/throttling/):

```python
REST_FRAMEWORK = {
    "DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES": ["rest_framework.throttling.UserRateThrottle"],
    "DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES": {"user": "1000/day", "ai": "30/hour"},
}
```

Give a view its own limit with `ScopedRateThrottle` and `throttle_scope = "ai"`. DRF's documentation is explicit that throttling is not a security measure against brute force or denial of service. Real login protection combines edge limits, backoff or lockout, MFA and [security monitoring](/guide/observability-and-security-monitoring). Client IPs for limits must come from trusted [proxy headers](/guide/networking-and-load-balancers).

**Step 6: choose failure modes.** A speed-only cache falls back to the database when Redis is down. A login throttle may fail closed. Decide and document which is which.

Checkpoint: a test proves two households never share a cached summary.

## Exercise

In one app:

1. Cache a slow, read-heavy summary with a tenant-scoped, versioned key and jittered TTL.
2. Invalidate it on commit when the underlying data changes.
3. Add a scoped throttle to the most expensive endpoint.
4. Set `Cache-Control: private` on user-specific API responses.

**Done means:** tests prove tenant separation, invalidation after a write, and a 429 response after the limit.

## Check your understanding

- What is wrong with the key `"dashboard:summary"` in a multi-tenant app?
- Why delete a cache key in `on_commit` instead of right after `save()`?
- What is a cache stampede, and what stops it?
- Why does the local-memory backend break throttling with three web processes?
- Is a DRF throttle enough to stop credential stuffing?

## Answer key

It has no tenant scope, so every tenant reads the first tenant's summary. If the transaction rolls back, or another request reads before commit, the cache refills with stale data. A stampede is many requests recomputing one expired entry at once; a short recompute lock and TTL jitter prevent it. Each process keeps its own counters, so clients get three times the limit. No: attacks spread across IPs and accounts, so it takes edge limits, backoff or lockout, MFA and pattern monitoring together.

## Go deeper

- [MDN: HTTP caching](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Caching)
- [Redis documentation](https://redis.io/docs/latest/)

title: Security standards: who publishes what?
summary: Understand NIST, OWASP, standards, frameworks, requirements, and evidence before trying to follow a checklist.
body:
## What am I learning?

When someone says “follow security standards,” my first question should be: **which publication, for which system, and what evidence would show it is followed?** NIST and OWASP are important names, but they produce different kinds of material. They are not one global authority approving every application.

## Who are these organizations?

| Organization | What it is | Why I encounter it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| NIST | The U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology, part of the Department of Commerce | Cybersecurity frameworks, technical standards, and guidance |
| OWASP | The Open Worldwide Application Security Project, a nonprofit foundation supporting community projects | Application-security awareness, verification requirements, and practical guidance |
| ISO and IEC | International standards organizations | Standards such as ISO/IEC 27001 for information security management systems |

These roles are described by [NIST](https://www.nist.gov/about-nist), [OWASP](https://owasp.org/about), and [ISO's ISO/IEC 27001 overview](https://www.iso.org/standard/27001). A publisher's name alone does not tell me the scope or status of a particular document.

## Separate the vocabulary

My learning vocabulary:

| Term | Question I ask |
| --- | --- |
| Framework | How do I organize outcomes, responsibilities, and gaps? |
| Standard or requirement set | What specific expectations am I using? |
| Control | What measure reduces a particular risk? |
| Guidance | What practices help me implement the idea? |
| Evidence | What observed result supports my claim? |
| Assessment | Who evaluated which scope against which criteria? |

For example, “protect private reports” is an outcome. “Enforce organization scope on every report lookup” is a control choice. A negative API test is one piece of evidence. These are related, but they are not interchangeable.

## Read the scope before the checklist

The NIST Cybersecurity Framework organizes cybersecurity outcomes. OWASP's Top 10 builds awareness of application risks, while ASVS supplies application-security verification requirements. ISO/IEC 27001 concerns an information security management system, not a seal proving every line of code is safe. See the [CSF FAQ](https://www.nist.gov/cyberframework/faqs), [OWASP's comparison](https://top10.owasp.org/2025/0x03_2025-Establishing_a_Modern_Application_Security_Program/), and [ISO's scope](https://www.iso.org/standard/27001).

A framework can inform a policy without itself being a law. A requirement can also be adopted through an organization's obligations or agreements. For engineering work, record which requirements actually apply rather than assuming that every published document is mandatory for every app.

## Turn a concern into something testable

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Risk[Private report exposure] --> Outcome[Only authorized readers]
  Outcome --> Requirement[Check scope on every path]
  Requirement --> Control[Scoped lookup and permission gate]
  Control --> Evidence[Allowed and denied request results]
  Evidence --> Review[Review scope and remaining gaps]
```

This is my own teaching example. A practical evidence record could name the endpoint, test fixture, candidate revision, expected denial, actual result, and unresolved paths. A screenshot of a shield icon would not demonstrate authorization.

## How I would use these references together

Start with [NIST concepts](/guide/nist-fundamentals) to connect security work to outcomes and responsibilities. Read [OWASP concepts](/guide/owasp-fundamentals) to move from application risks toward verifiable requirements. Then apply the ideas to [the handbook's security boundaries](/guide/security-boundaries).

Reading these lessons does not assess an application or certify an organization. The useful learning outcome is being able to explain a risk, choose an appropriate requirement, and ask for meaningful evidence.

## Check your understanding

- Is OWASP a government regulator?
- Is a framework outcome the same as an implemented control?
- Does citing a standard establish that my application meets it?

## Answer key

OWASP is a nonprofit foundation. An outcome describes what I want; a control is a measure intended to achieve it. A citation identifies a reference, while an assessment needs defined scope and evidence.

title: NIST: outcomes, frameworks, and secure development
summary: Learn the six CSF functions and the role of the SSDF through a private-document example.
body:
## What am I learning?

**NIST** is the National Institute of Standards and Technology. In this lesson, I am learning how two of its publications help organize security thinking: the Cybersecurity Framework, or CSF, and the Secure Software Development Framework, or SSDF. The organization publishes many documents; “NIST” is not the name of one checklist. [About NIST](https://www.nist.gov/about-nist).

## Why a framework helps

Suppose I have login, encrypted traffic, and backups. Those features do not tell me who owns security decisions, what data I hold, how I notice misuse, or whether restoration works. A framework helps make those missing questions visible. CSF 2.0 describes outcomes that organizations can use to understand and communicate cybersecurity risk. [CSF overview](https://www.nist.gov/cyberframework).

## The six CSF functions

CSF 2.0 uses **Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover**. These are connected areas of work, not six deployment commands to run once. [NIST's CSF 2.0 explanation](https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2024/02/nist-releases-version-20-landmark-cybersecurity-framework).

The drawing keeps governance connected to the other functions rather than presenting security as a one-time sequence.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  Govern[Govern - ownership and decisions]
  Govern --> Identify[Identify - understand assets]
  Govern --> Protect[Protect - reduce exposure]
  Govern --> Detect[Detect - notice events]
  Govern --> Respond[Respond - act on incidents]
  Govern --> Recover[Recover - restore service]
```

My own example: a Django application holding private customer documents.

| Function | The question I ask | Example evidence to seek |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Govern | Who owns the risk and the release decision? | Named owner and reviewed access policy |
| Identify | What assets, data, and dependencies exist? | Inventory of file stores, APIs, and readers |
| Protect | How do I reduce unauthorized access? | Scoped authorization and protected storage |
| Detect | How would I notice unexpected access? | A tested signal for suspicious download patterns |
| Respond | What happens after a suspected exposure? | An incident procedure with named responsibilities |
| Recover | How do I restore a useful service? | A recorded restoration exercise |

The examples illustrate my interpretation; they are not a complete CSF mapping or evidence that these controls are deployed.

## Current state versus target state

CSF Organizational Profiles can describe current and target outcomes. That makes a gap more useful than a vague claim of being “secure.” [CSF FAQ](https://www.nist.gov/cyberframework/faqs).

For my example: **current** — backups exist, but I have never restored them. **Target** — a responsible person can restore an isolated copy and check that the application's essential records are usable. The gap becomes an owned exercise with observable results. An inventory entry saying “backups enabled” does not close it.

## Where the SSDF fits

The SSDF addresses secure software development. The final SP 800-218 v1.1 organizes practices into preparing the organization, protecting software, producing well-secured software, and responding to vulnerabilities. It is intended to be integrated into development lifecycles rather than replace them. [Final SSDF publication](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/218/final).

My learning translation: decide expectations before coding, protect source and release material, build with security checks, and have a process when a vulnerability is found. [CI/CD](/guide/ci-cd-fundamentals) can automate some evidence collection; it cannot decide every risk question for me.

## Read editions and status carefully

A publication number, edition, and status belong in a reference. A draft describes work under consideration; it is not automatically the final version I should claim to follow. The [SSDF project page](https://csrc.nist.gov/Projects/ssdf) distinguishes published material and revision activity. When revisiting this lesson, inspect the publication's current status before reusing a requirement identifier.

## Check your understanding

- Where would naming a security owner fit?
- What is missing if backups run but no restore has been attempted?
- Does a green pipeline establish that every CSF outcome is achieved?

## Answer key

Ownership belongs in Govern. Restoration evidence is still missing for the recovery goal. A pipeline establishes results for its configured checks; it does not establish a complete cybersecurity program.

title: OWASP: from risk awareness to verifiable requirements
summary: Understand the Top 10, ASVS, and cheat sheets, then trace a tenant-isolation concern into a testable expectation.
body:
## What am I learning?

**OWASP** means the Open Worldwide Application Security Project. Its nonprofit foundation supports community work on software security. I should think of OWASP as a family of projects, not one product, regulator, or automatic certificate. [About OWASP](https://owasp.org/about).

For learning application security, three resources do different jobs.

## The Top 10: know what can go wrong

The OWASP Top 10 is an awareness document about significant web-application security risks. It gives developers shared language for discussing recurring problems. The reviewed edition is **Top 10:2025**; older articles may refer to different categories or rankings. [Official Top 10 project](https://owasp.org/projects/top-ten).

Read a category as a prompt for investigation. A list of ten risks cannot describe every requirement for every application, and copying the names into a README does not demonstrate that a system handles them.

## ASVS: decide what to verify

The **Application Security Verification Standard**, or ASVS, provides application-security requirements that can guide design and testing. Its purpose is more directly verifiable than the Top 10's awareness role. [ASVS project](https://owasp.org/projects/asvs).

The reviewed stable release is **ASVS 5.0.0**. ASVS uses requirement identifiers and verification levels; record the edition and the requirements in scope when referring to them. A level is not a score automatically awarded by a scanner. Use the actual release text when selecting requirements rather than borrowing an identifier from a different version. [ASVS 5.0.0 release](https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/tree/v5.0.0).

## Cheat sheets: understand implementation choices

Cheat sheets explain focused topics. For example, OWASP's Authorization Cheat Sheet discusses denying by default and checking permissions on every request. It also distinguishes authentication from authorization. [Authorization Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.html).

My translation: a valid login identifies a user. It does not prove the user may read another organization's report. Hiding a button in React does not enforce the API's permission rule.

## Work through one concern

Teaching scenario: a user from Organization A changes a document identifier to one belonging to Organization B.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Concern[Cross-tenant document access] --> Expectation[Authorize the requested object]
  Expectation --> Design[Scope lookup and download path]
  Design --> Test[Exercise allowed and denied access]
  Test --> Evidence[Record actual results and gaps]
```

I would ask:

1. Which server path resolves the document?
2. Where does trusted organization membership come from?
3. Does the download path enforce the same boundary?
4. Can an old signed URL remain usable after permission changes?
5. Which result would prove a denied request revealed no document bytes?

These are original learning questions, not a claim that this scenario exhausts an ASVS requirement. See [tenant-boundary design](/guide/estateiq-tenant-boundary) for the application's concrete paths.

## Keep the three resources in their roles

| I need to… | Start with… | Then do… |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Recognize a risk category | Top 10 | Inspect whether that failure could occur here |
| Define application verification scope | ASVS | Select versioned requirements and evidence |
| Understand a focused practice | Cheat sheets | Apply it to the actual framework and paths |

OWASP explicitly recommends ASVS when adopting a verifiable application-security standard rather than treating the Top 10 as that standard. [OWASP's application-security program guidance](https://top10.owasp.org/2025/0x03_2025-Establishing_a_Modern_Application_Security_Program/).

## Check your understanding

- Is learning the Top 10 the same as verifying the whole application?
- Can successful authentication replace object-level authorization?
- Why record an ASVS edition alongside a requirement identifier?

## Answer key

Awareness is not a complete verification exercise. A known user can still lack permission for a particular object. Editions matter because requirement organization and wording can change; evidence must refer to a definite expectation.

title: Tenant isolation, from request to file
summary: Carry trusted organization scope through reads, writes, queued jobs, caches, and downloads.
body:
## Resolve scope once, preserve it everywhere

An organization is the tenant boundary for the synthetic reports domain. Membership connects a user to an organization with an active status and role. A facility may narrow access inside an organization; it does not substitute for the organization boundary.

A client sends a selected organization identifier. The API resolves that selection through the authenticated user's active memberships. Views pass the resulting trusted scope into selectors and services. Never accept an organization field from the request body as authority.

## Establish an explicit permission matrix

This matrix is a proposed teaching policy, not an inspected production contract. Application owners must approve the actual role model.

| Action | Viewer | Editor | Organization administrator |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| List and read in-scope reports | Allow | Allow | Allow |
| Create or edit in-scope reports | Deny | Allow | Allow |
| Request generation | Deny | Allow | Allow |
| Download an in-scope completed file | Allow | Allow | Allow |
| Manage memberships | Deny | Deny | Allow |
| Any cross-organization operation | Deny | Deny | Deny |

Check both the role's action permission and the object's scope. A global administrator capability, if needed, must be a separate audited policy; do not quietly make an organization administrator global.

## Reads and related-object writes

Start every report query with organization scope. Pagination, counts, search, and exports must apply that same scope before computing results. An unscoped aggregate can leak business information even when the displayed list is correct.

For a report referencing a facility or template, resolve those related objects within the trusted organization too. A scoped report write that accepts a foreign facility still creates a cross-tenant relationship. Use database constraints where the schema can express an invariant; retain service checks for rules spanning workflow or membership state.

**backend/apps/reports/selectors.py · excerpt; Report import omitted**

```python
# backend/apps/reports/selectors.py — Retrieve a report only in trusted scope.
def report_get(*, organization, report_id):
    """Find a report belonging to the authorized organization.

    Args:
        organization: Scope resolved from active membership.
        report_id: Requested stable report identifier.

    Returns:
        Matching report, or None when it is outside the scope.
    """
    # Step 1: Combine identity and tenant predicates in the same lookup.
    return Report.objects.filter(
        organization=organization,
        id=report_id,
    ).first()
```

The API maps no scoped match to a consistent denial or not-found response according to its information-disclosure policy. Do not fetch globally first and accidentally serialize before the ownership check.

## Jobs carry durable context

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant A as Authorized API
  participant D as Project database
  participant W as Worker
  participant S as Private storage
  A->>D: Record report, organization, actor and generation intent
  D-->>A: Commit job and durable outbox
  D-->>W: Broker delivers durable job identifier via dispatcher
  W->>D: Load job and report within recorded organization
  W->>W: Check execution policy and idempotent state transition
  W->>S: Write private file for authorized report
  W->>D: Record object reference and terminal status
```

**Text alternative:** The API records trusted organization and actor context with durable generation intent. An outbox dispatcher publishes a job identifier through the broker. The worker loads the job and report within the recorded organization, applies its execution policy, writes a private file, and records the outcome.

Decide whether authorization is checked only when work is accepted or again at execution. For sensitive user-driven exports, rechecking active membership before execution may be required. Record cancellation or denial when that policy fails. Membership revocation after acceptance must have a documented outcome.

## Downloads and frontend caches

Job-status and download endpoints need the same tenant boundary as report detail. Resolve the file through an authorized report, then mint access. Do not let callers nominate an arbitrary storage key.

Partition frontend query keys by organization and clear user-specific state on logout. Cancel obsolete requests when switching scope and avoid showing an old response as current data. Cache partitioning prevents accidental UI leakage; backend scope checks remain the enforcement boundary.

## Test negative paths, not only success

| Exercise | Expected outcome |
| --- | --- |
| User A requests report B | No report representation |
| Editor A assigns facility B | Rejected without mutation |
| Viewer A queues generation | Denied without job or outbox entry |
| Revoked A polls old job | Denied according to current membership policy |
| Worker job pairs organization A with report B | Fails without creating a file |
| User A requests file B | No signed URL |
| Switch frontend from A to B | No A data rendered as B's current view |

Include list, detail, update, delete, aggregate, export, queued job, and download paths in the coverage. Test database outcomes as well as response codes. These exercises are acceptance requirements; they have not been executed against a backend in this frontend-only repository.

Use [OWASP's authorization testing guidance](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authorization_Testing_Automation_Cheat_Sheet.html) to turn the permission matrix into repeatable tests.

title: Infrastructure as code: reviewable, repeatable cloud resources
summary: Describe cloud resources in versioned files, review every plan, and apply from CI without long-lived keys.

objectives: Explain declarative infrastructure, state and drift
Run a plan, review it, and apply it from CI
Store state remotely, locked and protected
Authenticate CI to AWS with OIDC instead of stored access keys
Separate environments so staging mistakes cannot reach production

body:
## What am I learning?

Infrastructure as code (IaC) means describing servers, networks, databases and permissions in files, then letting a tool create or change them to match. Infrastructure gets the same treatment as application code: version control, review, repeatability and history.

Without it, a cloud account is configured by hand in a console ("ClickOps"). Nobody can review those changes, rebuild the environment, or see what changed before an outage. Lumen's [AWS design](/guide/lumen-aws-architecture) spans subnets, security groups, an ALB, EC2, RDS and S3 policies. That is too much to keep correct by hand.

## Core concepts

| Concept | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| Declarative | I describe the end state; the tool works out the steps |
| Provider | The plugin that talks to a cloud API, such as AWS |
| State | The tool's record mapping code to real resources |
| Plan | A preview of what will be created, changed or destroyed |
| Drift | Real infrastructure that no longer matches the code |
| Module | A reusable group of resources with inputs and outputs |

The main tools:

| Tool | Language | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Terraform](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/intro) | HCL | Most widely used; Business Source License since 2023 |
| [OpenTofu](https://opentofu.org/docs/) | HCL | Open-source fork under the Linux Foundation; largely compatible |
| AWS CloudFormation | YAML / JSON | AWS-native; AWS manages the state |
| [AWS CDK](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cdk/v2/guide/home.html) | TypeScript, Python, … | Real programming languages that generate CloudFormation |

The concepts carry over. Pick one per project and stay consistent.

## Modern patterns

| Pattern | Problem it solves | How |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Plan in the pull request** | Infrastructure changes merged without anyone seeing their effect | CI posts the plan on every PR; reviewers approve the plan, not just the diff |
| **Apply only from CI** | Laptop applies with stale code and personal credentials | Merging to main triggers the apply of the reviewed plan |
| **OIDC federation for CI** | Long-lived cloud keys stored as CI secrets can leak | CI exchanges a short-lived identity token for a scoped role ([GitHub OIDC with AWS](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/security-for-github-actions/security-hardening-your-deployments/configuring-openid-connect-in-amazon-web-services)) |
| **Remote, locked, encrypted state** | Lost state, concurrent applies, leaked secrets | An S3 backend with locking, encryption and narrow access |
| **Account per environment** | A staging mistake destroys production | Separate AWS accounts for staging and production ([AWS guidance](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/organizing-your-aws-environment/organizing-your-aws-environment.html)) |
| **Versioned modules** | Copy-pasted resources drift between environments | One module, pinned versions, different inputs per environment |
| **Policy as code** | Unsafe settings, such as public buckets, pass review | Automated checks on the plan with [Open Policy Agent](https://www.openpolicyagent.org/docs/latest/) or [Checkov](https://www.checkov.io/) |
| **Scheduled drift detection** | Manual console changes go unnoticed | A nightly plan that alerts when it isn't empty |
| **Immutable infrastructure** | Hand-patched servers become unique and unrebuildable | Replace servers from a new image instead of changing them in place |
| **Ephemeral preview environments** | Testing infrastructure changes only in shared staging | Short-lived environments per branch, destroyed after merge |

## Anti-patterns to avoid

- **ClickOps in production.** Every console change is invisible to review and is drift.
- **Applying from a laptop.** Unreviewed, unlogged, and with whatever credentials that laptop has.
- **Long-lived access keys in CI.** Use OIDC.
- **Secrets in `.tfvars` committed to Git.** Reference a secrets manager.
- **One giant state for everything.** Every apply risks everything; split by lifecycle and blast radius.
- **Editing state by hand.** Use the tool's state commands.
- **Copy-pasted environments.** Staging stops rehearsing production.

## Build it step by step

**Step 1: describe a resource declaratively.**

```hcl
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "documents" {
  bucket = "lumen-documents-staging"
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block" "documents" {
  bucket                  = aws_s3_bucket.documents.id
  block_public_acls       = true
  block_public_policy     = true
  ignore_public_acls      = true
  restrict_public_buckets = true
}
```

If the bucket exists and matches, nothing happens. If someone made it public by hand, the next plan shows the drift.

**Step 2: configure remote state.**

```hcl
terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket  = "lumen-terraform-state"
    key     = "staging/storage.tfstate"
    region  = "us-east-1"
    encrypt = true
  }
}
```

Enable locking for the backend so two applies can't run at once. State can contain [sensitive values in plain text](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/state/sensitive-data), such as generated passwords, so restrict who can read it.

**Step 3: plan, review, apply.**

1. Change the files on a branch.
2. CI runs `terraform plan` and posts the result on the pull request.
3. A reviewer reads the plan, watching especially for `destroy` and `replace` on stateful resources such as databases.
4. After merge, CI applies the reviewed plan using an OIDC role.

This is the same evidence-then-release flow as the [CI/CD release workflow](/guide/ci-cd-release-workflow).

**Step 4: add a policy check.** Run a policy tool against the plan in CI and fail the build on rules such as "no public S3 buckets" or "databases must be encrypted."

Checkpoint: a pull request shows the plan, and no AWS access key exists in CI secrets.

## What stays out of IaC

- Secret values themselves. Reference them from a secrets manager.
- Application data. IaC creates the database, not the rows.
- One-off experiments. Use a sandbox account and delete it.

## Exercise

In a sandbox AWS account:

1. Write IaC for a private S3 bucket with public access blocked, encryption and a lifecycle rule.
2. Store state remotely with locking.
3. Plan and apply.
4. Change a setting by hand in the console and confirm the next plan detects it.
5. Run `destroy` and confirm nothing remains.

**Done means:** the bucket is created from code, drift shows up in the plan, and cleanup is complete. Stretch goal: run the plan from GitHub Actions with OIDC.

## Check your understanding

- Why review the plan instead of only the code diff?
- What goes wrong when two people apply with local state files?
- Why is the state file sensitive even when no secrets appear in the code?
- What does OIDC federation replace, and why is that safer?
- How does IaC help after someone changes a security group by hand?

## Answer key

The plan shows the real effect, including destroys and replacements the diff doesn't make obvious. Each person's state misses the other's changes, so applies can overwrite or duplicate resources; remote locked state prevents it. Providers write resource attributes, including generated passwords, into state. It replaces long-lived access keys stored in CI with short-lived credentials issued per run, so there is no permanent key to leak. The next plan reports the drift, and applying restores the reviewed configuration.

## Go deeper

- [Terraform: introduction](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/intro)
- [OpenTofu documentation](https://opentofu.org/docs/)

title: Django auth, Simple JWT, Clerk, and Gait
summary: Choose and verify an identity mechanism while keeping application permission rules explicit.
body:
## One authorization boundary, several identity approaches

I have used Django authentication, Simple JWT, Clerk, and Gait across projects. They are options selected per application, not four services that every request must pass through. The runtime map uses an identity boundary that can be implemented differently in each project.

Security extends beyond identity: tenant ownership, database invariants, private storage, secret handling, operator access, backup protection, and dependency policy still need their own controls.

## Compare ownership and verification

| Approach | Credential and identity ownership | Backend verification | Remaining application duty |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Django auth and sessions | Project user accounts and server-managed session state | Session middleware and authentication backend | Tenant membership, action and object rules |
| Simple JWT with Django/DRF | Project user accounts with JWT issue/refresh policy | Configured DRF token authentication | Revocation policy, tenancy, roles and protected actions |
| Clerk | Managed identity and session service | Supported backend verification of Clerk session credentials | Map stable subject to local membership and enforce domain policy |
| Gait | Application identity/session platform | Inspected SDK and credential/session contract | Project membership and business authorization |

Inspect each application's actual settings and code before claiming that a mechanism, token rotation, or logout behavior is verified.

## Django session authentication

Django's authentication framework connects accounts, permissions, and sessions through middleware. A browser presents a session cookie; the server resolves the associated session and user. Use HTTPS and appropriate secure cookie settings. Cookie-authenticated writes need CSRF protection; do not disable it merely to make a cross-origin frontend request succeed.

Django model permissions can express actions such as viewing or changing a model. Organization-specific object access still needs an explicit scope policy. An authenticated user with a model-level permission should not automatically read every tenant's reports.

See [Django's authentication system](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/5.2/topics/auth/default/). Verify anonymous denial, authenticated access, CSRF rejection, logout, and membership revocation in the actual deployment topology.

## Simple JWT for a Django API

JWT access credentials let the API verify signed claims under the configured token policy. Define access lifetime, refresh lifetime, signing/verification keys, allowed algorithms, issuer/audience expectations, and user resolution. Keep the frontend transport contract separate from the domain permission checks.

Simple JWT's optional blacklist app tracks outstanding and blacklisted refresh or sliding tokens. Install its app and migrations before expecting that policy to work. Do not assume blacklisting a refresh token immediately revokes a previously issued ordinary access token. Document the remaining access window and whether sensitive actions require additional state checks.

See [Simple JWT's blacklist documentation](https://django-rest-framework-simplejwt.readthedocs.io/en/stable/blacklist_app.html). Exercise refresh replay, logout, expired credentials, disabled users, and a revoked membership with an access token that has not yet expired. The observed outcome must match the configured version and policy.

## Clerk as managed identity

Clerk provides session credentials for authenticating backend requests. Use a supported verification path appropriate to the backend and validate the expected issuer and other required claims. A same-origin cookie path differs from an API hosted at another origin; inspect the transport instead of assuming an authorization header is always present.

Map a verified provider subject to a project-owned user or membership record. Avoid using mutable email as the only durable link. Even where provider organization features are used, define which data source controls business roles and how revocation reaches API decisions.

See [Clerk session tokens](https://clerk.com/docs/guides/sessions/session-tokens) and [request transport](https://clerk.com/docs/guides/development/making-requests). Verify wrong-issuer tokens, expired tokens, missing membership, and provider outages. No Clerk integration is installed in the handbook.

## Gait when the project uses it

Gait is another identity/session option in my ecosystem. Before implementing its adapter, inspect the real SDK, token fields, key discovery, refresh behavior, and session validation contract. The handbook has not audited those contracts.

Keep its identity/session truth separate from project-owned reports and memberships. Explicitly document how active-session requirements, logout, and membership revocation interact. A diagram should say “identity provider” when the application has not selected Gait specifically.

## Put a stable seam in the application

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Session[Django session] --> Verify[Selected identity adapter]
  JWT[Simple JWT] --> Verify
  Clerk[Clerk credentials] --> Verify
  Gait[Gait credentials] --> Verify
  Verify --> Subject[Verified project user or external subject]
  Subject --> Membership[Active local membership]
  Membership --> Rules[Action and object policy]
  Rules --> Scope[Tenant-scoped operation]
```

**Text alternative:** A project selects an identity adapter for its configured credential type. Verified identity resolves to active membership and then action/object policy before a tenant-scoped operation. The arrows illustrate alternative integrations, not automatic fallback between providers.
