Do not try several issuers until one accepts a credential. Select a deliberate trust configuration and reject ambiguous or unsupported credentials. If multiple issuers are intentionally supported, define disjoint verification and account-linking rules.

## Record the per-project decision

For each application, record the chosen mechanism, account owner, trusted issuers, credential transport, session/revocation policy, local membership mapping, sensitive-action requirements, outage behavior, and negative tests. That adoption record is more useful than labeling the whole stack “JWT security.”

title: Heroku, frontend hosting, and S3
summary: Connect Heroku application processes, Vercel or Netlify frontend delivery, and private S3 files.
body:
## Start with the platforms I actually use

Heroku is my main application hosting platform. I have also used Vercel for frontend delivery and AWS S3 for object storage. This handbook is currently delivered by Netlify. AWS experience described here is S3; ECS, RDS, VPC, and broader AWS designs are future reference topics rather than a claim of deployed experience.

The diagram is a representative composition of these tools, not an assertion that all of my projects have this exact topology.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  Foundry[Foundry - tasks and candidate evidence] --> Revision[Reviewed application revision]
  Revision --> Frontend[Vercel or Netlify - frontend build and delivery]
  Revision --> Release[Heroku build and release]
  Frontend --> Browser[React browser]
  Browser -->|HTTPS API requests| Web[Heroku web process - Django]
  Browser --> Identity[Selected auth - Django, Simple JWT, Clerk, or Gait]
  Release --> Web
  Release --> Worker[Heroku worker process when needed]
  Web --> DB[(Heroku PostgreSQL)]
  Web --> Broker[Configured broker when needed]
  Broker --> Worker
  Worker --> DB
  Worker --> S3[Private AWS S3 objects]
  Web -->|Authorize and mint temporary access| S3
  Scheduler[Scheduled task trigger] --> Broker
  DB -. Scheduled logical backup .-> Backup[Protected backup artifact]
```

**Text alternative:** Foundry supports candidate review before separate frontend and Heroku delivery. React calls a Django web process. The selected identity mechanism supplies authentication. PostgreSQL holds durable business data. Optional broker/worker processes execute jobs and store files in S3. Scheduling triggers work, while database backup is a separate protected operation.

## Heroku process responsibilities

The web process handles HTTP requests; a worker consumes background jobs; release-time commands prepare the deployment according to an explicit migration plan. They use the same application revision but have different responsibilities and scaling needs. A scheduler is a trigger, not a continuously running web request.

**Procfile · reference excerpt, adapt module and queue settings**

```text
# Procfile — Define independent application process responsibilities.
web: gunicorn config.wsgi:application
worker: celery -A config worker --loglevel=info
release: python manage.py migrate --noinput
```

This excerpt assumes configured Gunicorn, Celery, Django, database credentials, and a supported broker. It is not installed in this frontend repository. Add a worker only when the application needs one. Avoid publishing operational commands without their dependencies and environment assumptions.

A release migration must remain compatible with the running and rollback revisions. Rolling back application code does not undo data migrations. Check release logs, smoke-test a real request, and observe error rates and worker health rather than considering a build success sufficient.

## Frontend delivery with Vercel or Netlify

A Vite handbook produces static `dist/` assets. History-based routes need the host's SPA fallback so a direct article URL loads. This project has that configuration in `netlify.toml`; a separate Vercel deployment would need the equivalent platform setup. See [Vercel's Vite guide](https://vercel.com/docs/frameworks/frontend/vite).

Frontend and API origins may differ. Record frontend/API/auth origins per environment and configure CORS, credential transport, CSRF, and callback URLs accordingly. A variable compiled into a frontend bundle is public even when entered through a host's environment settings. Never put a database password or private provider key there.

## AWS S3 is durable file storage

Store object references in the database and file bytes in private S3 objects. A container or dyno's filesystem is suitable for temporary processing, not the durable home of generated reports. Keep upload, validation, generation, publication, and cleanup states explicit.

Authorize report access before issuing a short-lived download URL. A presigned URL carries temporary access granted by the signing credentials and can be shared by its holder. Its effective lifetime can be limited by the underlying credentials. Avoid recording the URL in general application logs. See [AWS presigned URL behavior](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html).

Use least-privilege S3 access, appropriate encryption and retention, and a cleanup policy for abandoned uploads or failed generation. Object versioning and lifecycle rules should be recorded as configured facts, not assumed protections.

## Verify the deployment as one request flow

Load a direct frontend route. Make an authenticated API request using the project's selected identity mechanism. Read a scoped report, queue a job if supported, observe durable completion, and download only through the authorized path. Repeat with a foreign organization identifier and expect denial.

Then inspect web/worker logs using the same request/job identifiers. Confirm secrets are absent from frontend assets and signed file URLs are absent from telemetry. Use separate staging data and credentials for these exercises.

## Planned AWS flagship deployment

[Lumen](/guide/lumen-platform-design) is the flagship planned for dedicated EC2 service instances behind an ALB. Follow its [AWS topology](/guide/lumen-aws-architecture), [security plan](/guide/lumen-aws-security), and [release gates](/guide/lumen-aws-release). This extends the intended platform coverage; it does not turn earlier S3 experience into a claim of completed EC2 deployment.

title: Observability and security monitoring: ownership, evidence, and alerts
summary: Decide what the application watches, what the security system evaluates, and who answers each alert.
body:
## Three questions, three owners

Observability is the broad practice of understanding what a system is doing. Security monitoring reuses some of that evidence to detect threats. They overlap, but they answer different questions and belong to different owners.

| Area | Question it answers | Moneta example | Responsible system |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Application operations | Is the app working correctly? | A Plaid sync failed; an API is returning errors | Moneta's operational monitoring |
| Product and data health | Is the app delivering useful, accurate results? | Balances are stale; an account is missing transactions | Moneta |
| Security monitoring | Is access legitimate, and are protections working? | Unauthorized access attempts; MFA enforcement disabled | Gait, using evidence Moneta supplies |

Moneta is the worked example. The same split applies to any application that uses a separate security system.

## The rule that matters most: enforce here, observe there

**The application enforces security. The security system observes and evaluates it.**

Moneta decides on every request whether the identity, session, MFA requirement and household membership allow the action. Gait never sits in that decision path as a monitor. If Gait is slow, unreachable or rejecting signals, Moneta still denies what it should deny and still protects financial data. Reporting can fail without affecting enforcement. Enforcement never waits for reporting.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  U[Request] --> M[Moneta enforces identity, MFA, membership]
  M -->|allowed or denied| R[Response]
  M --> L[Logs, metrics, traces]
  L --> O[Operational monitoring]
  O --> OA[Owner: reliability alert]
  M -.->|approved security events only| G[Gait]
  G --> GA[Owner: security finding or alert]
```

The dashed line is optional and one-way. Removing it must not change any response Moneta returns.

Identity checks that Moneta makes *to* Gait (token and session verification) are a separate matter. They are enforcement dependencies, and they fail closed: see [authentication options](/guide/authentication-options). This guide covers only the reporting path.

## Shared building blocks: logs, metrics, traces

An application produces three kinds of evidence:

- **Logs** record individual events: "Plaid sync failed for connection 41."
- **Metrics** record counts and measurements: "20% of syncs failed this hour."
- **Traces** record the path of one request: "the dashboard was slow because its database query took three seconds."

These are shared building blocks, not destinations. Operational tools get the evidence needed to diagnose reliability. Gait gets only the narrow subset needed to assess security. Nothing should go to both systems unchanged by default.

## What the application must instrument

Moneta owns its own reliability and data health. Instrument at least these:

| Concern | Evidence | Healthy signal |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Availability and errors | Request logs, error rate, health endpoint | Health returns 200; error rate within the agreed threshold |
| Latency and resources | Request duration, slow query traces, dyno memory | Key pages within budget; no sustained memory pressure |
| Plaid connections | Per-connection status, sync attempts, retries, last success time | Every active connection synced inside its freshness window |
| Data freshness | Age of the newest balance and transaction per account | No account silently older than its window |
| Scheduled jobs | Start, finish, outcome and duration per run | Every expected run recorded; failures alert |
| Backups | Backup completion and periodic restore checks | Recent backup exists; a restore has been exercised |
| AI features | Request failures, latency, token cost | Failures fall back cleanly; spend within budget |

Data freshness needs its own check. A sync job can "succeed" while an account quietly stops receiving transactions. Measure the age of the data itself, not just whether the job finished. [Scheduled task reliability](/guide/backup-and-scheduled-tasks) covers the job side.

## What goes to the security system

Gait's scope stays narrow and deliberate:

- Authentication, MFA, sessions and access-control violations.
- Changes to credentials, privileges and security configuration.
- Security-relevant suspicious behavior, such as one session probing many households.
- Security self-checks, findings, evidence freshness and security alerts.

The Gait SDK submits these through one write-only call. These properties come from its contract:

| Property | What it means for the application |
| --- | --- |
| Approved `signal_type` only | Gait keeps the registry. An unapproved type is rejected, not stored. |
| Gait derives the scope | Organization, environment, application and control mapping come from the application credential, never from the payload. |
| Customer-reported evidence | Gait records the signal as the application's own claim, never as independent verification. |
| Required `source_reference` | A stable key per logical event, such as a job run ID. Retries with the same key do not create duplicates. |
| Bounded payload | Minimal, non-sensitive context. Gait treats it as opaque data, not authority. |
| Every failure raises | Catch the error, log it locally, and continue. Never turn a reporting failure into an enforcement failure. |

## What never goes to the security system

Gait is not a log sink or a debugging platform. Do not send:

- Ordinary application logs, stack traces or request bodies.
- Financial data: balances, transactions, account numbers, Plaid tokens.
- Passwords, tokens, session cookies, MFA secrets or connection keys.
- Raw AI prompts or responses.
- Reliability metrics such as latency, sync volume or cost.

If a security event needs context, send a reference Moneta can resolve internally, such as an audit event ID. Do not copy the record itself.

## One event, two readers

The same underlying event can matter to both owners.

A single failed login is probably a mistyped password. Moneta records it safely in its own logs: user reference, outcome, time, correlation ID, and never the attempted password. A burst of failures across many accounts may be credential stuffing. That pattern is a security question, so Gait assesses it from the defined security events Moneta reports.

AI splits the same way. A model call that times out, runs slowly or costs too much is an operations concern. A prompt or tool call that tries to read another household's data is a security event. Moneta still blocks it, and the attempt is reported.

## Who receives each alert

Every alert needs a named receiver and a first response. An alert with no owner turns into noise.

| Alert | Raised by | Received by | First response |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| API error rate or health check failing | Operational monitoring | Moneta owner | [Operational runbook](/guide/operational-runbooks): check the deploy, then roll back or fix |
| Plaid sync failing or data stale | Moneta | Moneta owner | Check connection status; ask the user to re-link if the provider requires it |
| Scheduled job or backup missed | Moneta | Moneta owner | Re-run safely; confirm the next run; check a restore if backups are affected |
| AI failures or cost over budget | Moneta | Moneta owner | Confirm the fallback is working; throttle or disable the feature |
| Unusual failed-login or access-denial pattern | Gait | Security owner | Review the pattern; lock affected accounts or rotate credentials if confirmed |
| MFA or security configuration disabled | Gait, from a Moneta self-check | Security owner | Restore the setting; find out how it changed |
| Security evidence stale (no recent self-check) | Gait | Security owner | Check Moneta's reporting job before trusting the posture |
| Gait reporting failing | Moneta | Moneta owner | Fix reporting; enforcement is unaffected but security evidence is going stale |

In a one-person project, the Moneta owner and the security owner are the same person. Keep them as separate rows anyway. The responsibilities differ, and they separate once the team grows.

## Standards this follows

There is no single regulator for application observability. Several standards bodies publish what practitioners follow. This design takes each one for the part it actually governs.

| Body | Standard | What it governs here | How this design applies it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| OWASP | [Top 10:2025 A09 Security Logging and Alerting Failures](https://owasp.org/Top10/2025/A09_2025-Security_Logging_and_Alerting_Failures) | The risk of missing, unsafe or unread security logs. Its CWEs: log injection (CWE-117), sensitive data in logs (CWE-532), insufficient logging (CWE-778). | Encode untrusted values before logging, keep secrets and financial data out, and give every security event an alert owner. |
| OWASP | [ASVS 5.0.0 V16 Security Logging and Error Handling](https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/tree/v5.0.0) | Verifiable requirements: logging documentation (V16.1), general logging (V16.2), security events (V16.3), log protection (V16.4), error handling (V16.5). | Keep a written log inventory, log the defined security events, protect logs, and return safe errors. Pick the exact requirement IDs and level from the release text. |
| OWASP | [Logging Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Logging_Cheat_Sheet.html) and [Logging Vocabulary Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Logging_Vocabulary_Cheat_Sheet.html) | Practical guidance on what to log, and shared names for security events. | Name security events consistently, for example `authn_login_fail` and `authz_fail`, before mapping them to Gait's `signal_type` registry. |
| NIST | [Cybersecurity Framework 2.0](https://www.nist.gov/cyberframework) | Outcomes. Detect covers Continuous Monitoring (DE.CM) and Adverse Event Analysis (DE.AE); Respond covers incident handling. | Operational and security monitoring are DE.CM. Gait's pattern assessment is DE.AE. The alert table is the Respond hand-off. |
| NIST | [SP 800-61 Rev. 3](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/61/r3/final) (April 2025) | Incident response aligned to CSF 2.0. | Each security alert has a named receiver and a first response. Lessons from incidents feed back into the event list. |
| NIST | [SP 800-92](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/92/final) (2006); [Rev. 1](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/92/r1/ipd) is still a draft | Log management planning: generation, transmission, storage, retention and disposal. | Decide retention and access for each log store in the inventory. Cite Rev. 1 as a draft until NIST finalizes it. |
| NIST | [SP 800-53 Rev. 5](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/53/r5/upd1/final), AU family and SI-4 | A control catalog for audit records and system monitoring. | A reference vocabulary only. Moneta is not claiming an 800-53 baseline. |
| CNCF | [OpenTelemetry](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/) (graduated May 2026) | A vendor-neutral API, SDK and protocol for traces, metrics and logs, plus semantic conventions for naming. | Instrument through OpenTelemetry so the operational backend can change without re-instrumenting. Check each semantic convention's stability before relying on it. |
| W3C | [Trace Context](https://www.w3.org/TR/trace-context/) (Recommendation) | The `traceparent` and `tracestate` headers that carry a trace across services. | Use the trace ID as the correlation ID from browser to API to job. Do not invent a separate format. |

Laws and industry rules, such as PCI DSS for cardholder data or financial-privacy regulations, depend on what data the application holds and who operates it. This guide has not assessed them for Moneta. Get that decision explicitly before claiming compliance with any of them.

## Instrument safely

- **Log identifiers and outcomes, not contents.** Redact secrets and financial values before the log call, not afterward (CWE-532).
- **Neutralize untrusted input.** Encode newlines and control characters in user-supplied values, or use structured JSON fields, so nobody can forge a log line (CWE-117).
- **Correlate with W3C Trace Context.** Carry the `traceparent` trace ID from each request into jobs and audit events, so a log line, a trace and an audit event can be joined.
- **Write the log inventory down (ASVS V16.1).** For each store, record what is logged, where it goes, who can read it, how long it is kept, and which events are security events.
- **Protect the logs (ASVS V16.4).** Restrict read access, keep security audit records separate from debug output and harder to tamper with, and use UTC timestamps from a synchronized clock.
- **Return safe errors (ASVS V16.5).** Users get a generic message with a reference ID. Details stay in the protected log.
- **Keep the security-event schema small and explicit.** Adding a new kind of event is a reviewed change on both sides.
- **Make reporting idempotent and retryable.** A stable `source_reference` lets a retry report the same event without creating a duplicate.
- **Separate "the check ran and passed" from "the check did not run."** Missing evidence is its own alert.

## Verify the boundary

These are proposed checks. Run them in the real integration with synthetic data:

| Scenario | Expected result |
| --- | --- |
| Gait unreachable during a protected request | Moneta's permission decision is unchanged; no data is exposed |
| Gait rejects a security signal | Error is logged locally; the user-facing request is unaffected |
| Same self-check retried with the same `source_reference` | One signal recorded, same receipt returned |
| Payload contains a financial value or secret | Caught by review or tests before sending; Gait-side redaction is a backstop, not the control |
| Sync job finishes but one account stops updating | Freshness alert fires for that account |
| AI request for another household's data | Request denied and a security event reported; no data returned |
| User input containing a newline or fake log prefix | Stored as one encoded field; no forged log entry |
| Unhandled server error | Generic message with a reference ID; stack trace only in the protected log |
| Trace across browser, API and job | The same `traceparent` trace ID appears in all three |

## Current state

This is a proposed design, not a verified deployment. Moneta has a Gait configuration self-check reporter that runs dry-run by default, with sending disabled until credentials are confirmed. No live Gait evidence or continuous security monitoring is claimed. The Gait SDK's signal API is write-only: it does not instrument anything automatically and does not retrieve findings. Moneta's operational alerting tools and thresholds have not been selected or audited here. Aligning with the standards above is a design intent. No ASVS level or NIST control baseline has been assessed.

title: Automatic backups and scheduled tasks
summary: Separate backup capture from proven recovery, and scheduled triggers from reliable job completion.
body:
## Two kinds of automation

Automatic backups protect recoverability; scheduled tasks initiate recurring application work. Both need monitoring and an owner. A configured schedule is not evidence that its latest execution succeeded, and a captured backup is not proof that it restores correctly.

These guides reflect my use of backups and scheduled tasks, but no live account settings or restore history have been inspected for this handbook.

## Schedule and inspect PostgreSQL backups

Heroku PGBackups supports scheduled logical backups for applicable database offerings. Verify the current database product and plan first; do not assume every Heroku database has identical backup capabilities. The [PGBackups documentation](https://devcenter.heroku.com/articles/heroku-postgres-backups) covers scheduling and backup inspection.

**Terminal · reference commands, synthetic application name**

```bash
# Step 1: Review existing schedules before making a change.
heroku pg:backups:schedules --app example-app
# Step 2: Configure a daily backup for the selected attachment.
heroku pg:backups:schedule DATABASE_URL --at '02:00 America/New_York' --app example-app
# Step 3: Inspect captured backups and their outcomes.
heroku pg:backups --app example-app
```

These commands are examples; they were not run against your applications. Scheduling changes remote configuration. Confirm the attachment, timezone, retention policy, and product support in the target environment.

Protect backup artifacts with restricted access and encryption. A backup download link is sensitive. Do not expose it in a public handbook, build log, or issue comment. Database backup does not automatically back up S3 file contents or guarantee that restored database references match the files still available.

## Prove recovery with a separate restore

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  DB[(Live PostgreSQL)] --> Capture[Scheduled backup capture]
  Capture --> Artifact[Protected backup artifact]
  Artifact --> Restore[(Separate restore database)]
  Restore --> Checks[Schema, row counts, tenant checks and application reads]
  Checks --> Evidence[Measured recovery evidence]
  S3[Retained S3 file objects] --> Checks
```

**Text alternative:** Capture a protected database backup, restore into a separate disposable database, and verify schema, representative data, tenant boundaries, application reads, and referenced S3 files. Record timing and findings as recovery evidence. The exercise must not overwrite production.

Choose a backup with a recorded completion time. Restore into an isolated environment with separate credentials. Check migrations/schema, representative synthetic rows, tenant relationships, and an application read. Validate file references against retained storage objects, then remove the disposable environment through the approved cleanup process.

RPO describes acceptable data loss; RTO describes acceptable restoration time. As a proposed example, a daily backup can leave close to a day of changes outside the latest capture if no other recovery mechanism exists. Measure the actual recovery process and data gap; do not convert a desired target into a guarantee.

## Scheduled tasks need a durable outcome

A scheduler initiates work at a configured interval. Use it to enqueue heavier work when a worker system exists, rather than running long processing inside the trigger. For small management commands, keep the execution bounded and record durable success/failure.

Heroku Scheduler is best-effort and recurring jobs must tolerate missed or duplicate triggers. A dedicated clock process is another option when the application needs stronger scheduling control. See [Heroku Scheduler](https://devcenter.heroku.com/articles/scheduler) and [custom clock processes](https://devcenter.heroku.com/articles/scheduled-jobs-custom-clock-processes).

For each recurring job, record its purpose, timezone, interval, tenant scope, expected duration, timeout, last-success threshold, retry rules, and owner. Examples include expired-token cleanup, report retention, outbox dispatch, and reconciliation. These have different consequences when a run is missed; they should not share an unexplained universal retry policy.

## Idempotency and overlap

Give recurring work a durable run identity such as `(job type, organization, period)`. Enforce uniqueness where appropriate and make each step safe to retry. If processing stops halfway, record a cursor or item-level progress so recovery does not repeat an irreversible side effect.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  Tick[Scheduled trigger] --> Claim[Claim durable run for tenant and period]
  Claim -->|Already complete| Skip[Skip duplicate]
  Claim -->|New or recoverable| Queue[Queue bounded work]
  Queue --> Worker[Worker with timeout and retry policy]
  Worker --> Result[Persist success, failure and progress]
  Result --> Monitor[Alert on missed success or repeated failure]
```

**Text alternative:** A scheduled trigger claims a durable tenant/period run, skips completed duplicates, queues bounded work, records the worker result and progress, and alerts on missed success or repeated failure.

A lock can prevent overlap, but abandoned locks need expiry or ownership recovery. Do not claim exactly-once execution. Verify that duplicate triggers, retries, and worker crashes produce the intended durable result without duplicate emails, exports, or destructive cleanup.

## Security and verification

A scheduled command runs with service authority; it does not inherit a safe tenant scope from a browser. Resolve and validate the organizations/items it may process. Protect scheduler credentials and restrict destructive maintenance separately from routine reads.

Test a missed trigger, two simultaneous triggers, a crash after an item completes, an unavailable broker, a failed backup, and a failed restore. Confirm the expected record, alert, retry, and recovery action for each. Preserve the results with revision/configuration context in the project's evidence; Foundry can coordinate this engineering work, but cannot make an untested restore successful by recording a checklist.

title: EstateIQ: the domain map
summary: Understand who owns each fact before adding APIs, AI, or automation.
body:
## A modular monolith with explicit ownership

EstateIQ deploys a Django application organized into domain packages, with a React/TypeScript client organized into features. A domain boundary is a responsibility inside the codebase; it does not imply a separate service or database. That distinction keeps transactional workflows practical without turning every feature into infrastructure.

The source review inspected architecture documents and representative implementation files. It did not execute the backend suite or audit production. “Present in source” and “verified in production” remain different claims.

## The complete ownership map

| Domain | Owns | Consumers and boundaries |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Identity and tenancy | Accounts, organizations, active membership, selected scope | Every scoped API; no financial calculations |
| Buildings and units | Property structure and unit identity | Leasing, expenses, property finance |
| Leasing | Tenant relationships, effective lease lifecycle, occupancy | Billing and reporting; no payment allocation |
| Billing | Lease charges, payments, allocations | Revenue and portfolio reporting |
| Revenue | Deterministic read models over Billing | Frontend and AI tools; no revenue writes |
| Expenses | Confirmed spend, categories, vendors, evidence links | Reporting and tax preparation |
| Property finance | Owner-side financing and obligations | Reporting; separate from tenant receivables |
| Documents | Private files, metadata, preview, extracted text | Evidence and document Q&A |
| Document intake | Incoming artifacts, extraction and review drafts | Confirmation workflow; no automatic accounting truth |
| Financial workflows | Cross-domain orchestration | Delegate actual writes to owning services |
| Reporting | Aggregate read contracts | Dashboard; no replacement financial ledger |
| Tax documents | Accountant-preparation composition | Review issues and links; planned packet features stay labeled |
| Onboarding | Derived setup status and next steps | Client and Copilot; no duplicate completion truth |
| Subscriptions | Owner-to-platform entitlement and provider synchronization | Feature gates; separate from lease billing |
| AI Copilot | Intent, tool routing, context, structured presentation | Selector-backed facts; read-only financial behavior |
| Operations | Delivery, schedules, logs, backup and recovery practices | Require configuration and execution evidence |

## Follow the ownership chain

## Project architecture

```mermaid
%% handbook-project:estateiq
flowchart TB
  N0[Property and lease] --> N1[Billing ownership] --> N2[Revenue and reports]
  N3[Private documents] --> N4[Reviewed draft] --> N5[Confirmed expense]
  N6[Scoped question] --> N7[Deterministic reads] --> N8[Structured answer]
```

**Text alternative:** Property and lease → Billing ownership → Revenue and reports. Private documents → Reviewed draft → Confirmed expense. Scoped question → Deterministic reads → Structured answer. These are responsibility lanes; the detailed diagram below describes the connected workflow.

## Detailed flow

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  Property[Buildings and units] --> Lease[Leases and occupancy]
  Lease --> Ledger[Charges and allocations]
  Ledger --> Revenue[Revenue read models]
  Revenue --> Reports[Reporting and AI tools]
  Evidence[Private documents] --> Review[Reviewed intake draft]
  Review --> Workflow[Financial workflow]
  Workflow --> Expense[Confirmed expense]
  Expense --> Reports
```

**Text alternative:** Property structure supports leases; leases own their ledger history; Revenue reads charge/allocation facts for reporting and AI. Private documents produce reviewed drafts, and a workflow delegates confirmed expense creation to the expense domain.

## Locate the boundaries in the repository

Backend owners live under `backend/apps/`; shared tenancy and permission mechanisms live under `backend/shared/`. Frontend features live under `frontend/src/features/`. Domain architecture pages live under `docs/architecture/domains/`. Tests belong near the domain whose behavior they protect.

For a new feature, identify the owning records and services first. Then identify read-model consumers, cache invalidation, authorization, and evidence links. A dashboard card is a view of domain truth, not a new owner of that truth.

## Verify a vertical slice

Choose a synthetic organization and one lease. Trace a write through authentication, active membership, input contract, service transaction, models, selector response, and frontend cache refresh. Repeat with a foreign organization and confirm no mutation. Then compare dashboard and AI answers with the same selector results.

## Errors this map helps prevent

A document extraction should not silently create an expense. Revenue should not post charges. Subscription billing should not be merged into lease receivables. An AI response should not calculate a balance independently. Correct those failures at the owning boundary rather than patching the presentation to hide disagreement.

title: Tenant isolation in the actual request path
summary: Connect X-Org-Slug, membership permissions, scoped lookups, and frontend recovery.
body:
## Selection is not authority

EstateIQ's browser sends JWT authorization and `X-Org-Slug`. The slug nominates an organization. Backend code must establish active membership and then filter the requested records within that scope. A remembered workspace selection is a convenience, not a credential.

The inspected `backend/shared/tenancy/middleware.py` resolves organization context and attaches `request.org`, `request.organization`, and `request.org_member`. It also records whether resolution came from a valid membership, a header-only organization, a missing header, or another failure.

## The important middleware caveat

The middleware can resolve an organization when the user is not yet authenticated at that layer. Django middleware and DRF JWT authentication do not necessarily see the same established user at the same point in the request. Therefore the presence of `request.org` alone is not sufficient proof of membership.

The inspected `backend/shared/auth/permissions.py` implements `IsOrgMember`. It requires a resolved organization, an authenticated user, and a membership matching both `is_active=True` and active status. Endpoint-specific action/role permissions and object scoping still follow that check.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  Header[JWT and X-Org-Slug] --> Context[Resolve organization context]
  Context --> Auth[DRF authenticated user]
  Auth --> Member[Explicit active membership check]
  Member --> Policy[Action and object policy]
  Policy --> Query[Organization-scoped lookup]
```

**Text alternative:** Request headers resolve context. DRF establishes the authenticated user. Explicit membership permission verifies current authority before action/object policy and organization-filtered lookup.

## Keep the tenant predicate in the query

Use organization-filtered selectors for list, detail, aggregation, and related-object resolution. A globally fetched record followed by an informal ownership check is easier to misuse. For writes that lock a record, retain the organization predicate in the locked lookup too.

**backend/apps/example/selectors.py · synthetic excerpt, model import omitted**

```python
# backend/apps/example/selectors.py — Scope a lookup before returning a record.
def get_scoped_record(*, organization, record_id):
    """Return an authorized organization's record or no match.

    Args:
        organization: Scope established by membership and permission checks.
        record_id: Requested identifier.

    Returns:
        Scoped record, or None.
    """
    # Step 1: Preserve organization scope in the database predicate.
    return Record.objects.filter(
        organization=organization, id=record_id
    ).first()
```

This is a teaching excerpt, not copied runnable EstateIQ code. The selected service still owns workflow constraints and related-object validation.

## Frontend workspace recovery

The inspected OrgProvider loads permitted organizations from an organization-list endpoint, prioritizes URL selection over stored selection, and synchronizes the selected slug. It invalidates query keys beginning with `org` when switching. It clears invalid context or selects the only remaining valid organization when recovering.

The implementation also auto-selects the earliest organization when no context exists, even though an introductory comment describes exactly-one behavior. Teach the implementation as observed and keep documentation reconciled; stale comments are not acceptance evidence.

## Test the complete boundary

Exercise missing headers, unknown organizations, foreign organization slugs, inactive membership, revoked membership with a still-valid token, foreign object IDs, and related-object assignments. Confirm the view uses a membership permission rather than merely checking that middleware attached context.

On the client, switch organizations while a request is in flight and log out before another user signs in. Inspect displayed data, request scope, and cache identity together. These are recommended verification cases; the source review did not run EstateIQ's backend tests.

title: AI grounded in structured truth
summary: Route questions to scoped tools and keep financial facts out of model-generated calculations.
body:
## Learn the connection model

For the concepts behind connecting an AI host to external capabilities, read [MCP: tools and context](/guide/mcp-fundamentals). MCP supplies an integration contract; the scoped business facts still come from the application.

## Start with a fact-producing system

EstateIQ's portfolio Copilot is a read-only interpretation layer. It does not own charges, payments, leases, expenses, or balances. Domain selectors produce the facts, and registered tools decide how to answer a supported question.

The inspected message view, conversation orchestrator, and analyst router support that division. Architecture documentation describes optional LLM presentation for portfolio Copilot as planned; a product label saying AI does not establish that every answer calls a language model.

## Follow one message

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  Question[User question and page context] --> Gates[Auth, organization and access gates]
  Gates --> Intent[Intent and scope resolution]
  Intent --> Clarify[Clarify ambiguous scope]
  Intent --> Help[Product Guide]
  Intent --> Tool[Registered analyst tool]
  Tool --> Selector[Scoped deterministic selectors]
  Selector --> Answer[Structured facts and formatted answer]
  Help --> Answer
```

**Text alternative:** Authenticate and gate the request before resolving intent and scope. Ambiguity produces clarification. Help routes to Product Guide; analytical questions route to registered selector-backed tools. Both produce structured responses.

## Request and response contracts

`backend/apps/ai_copilot/views/message_views.py` resolves the organization, checks subscription standing and daily usage when applicable, validates input, delegates response building, and validates output before returning. The inspected quota lookup is user-based; do not casually relabel it an organization-wide counter.

Response fields, tool identifiers, route names, and page context are contracts. A frontend renderer should not need to parse prose to discover the selected period or destination. Store structured source and scope information alongside the explanation where supported.

## Tool selection is deterministic behavior

`routing/analyst_router.py` selects from a priority-ordered registry, supports safe contextual follow-ups, and prevents direct domain requests from being hijacked by prior context. A tool still rebuilds fresh data after selection. The router should not calculate financial metrics itself.

Product help such as “how do I post rent?” must route to the owning lease-ledger action. Portfolio analysis such as “what remains outstanding?” must resolve the intended period/entities and query the appropriate scoped selector. A vague prompt should not silently borrow stale amounts from the last answer.

## Keep the LLM seam narrow

If a provider is introduced for presentation, pass only permitted structured facts and require the response to preserve their meaning. The provider must not invent missing totals, compute balances, issue financial mutations, or enlarge the selected scope. Handle timeout and unavailable-provider cases with a deterministic fallback or explicit unavailable state according to policy.

Treat user text and document text as untrusted input. Prompt instructions cannot confer authority to query another tenant or call a mutation. The tool registry and API/service policy must enforce that boundary independently of the model's willingness to follow it.

## Verify with fixtures and routing cases

For synthetic charges and allocations, assert the selector's numbers and the structured answer agree. Check Product Guide precedence, direct intent versus historical context, unsupported scope, missing membership, quota denial, and a foreign entity ID.

Existing EstateIQ test files were located for routing, scope, analyst tools, API contracts, and product-guide matching. Their existence is not a passing test result; rerun the relevant suite when adapting the pattern. Record any provider path separately from deterministic tool coverage.

title: MCP: how AI connects to tools and context
summary: Understand the host, client, server, and tool-call loop before connecting an AI application to anything.
body:
## What am I learning?

MCP means **Model Context Protocol**. It gives AI applications a common way to discover and use capabilities supplied by other programs. Think of a shared connection contract: the model can propose using a capability, while software performs the request and returns the result.

The protocol does not choose your model or decide whether its answer is correct. Its value is making connections less bespoke. A different AI host can understand the same server when both support compatible protocol versions and capabilities. [Official architecture overview](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/2026-07-28/learn/architecture).

## Who does what?

| Participant | Explain it to myself |
| --- | --- |
| Host | The AI application I interact with; it manages the conversation and available connections. |
| Client | The component inside the host that speaks MCP to a particular server. |
| Server | The program exposing a defined set of capabilities; it can run locally or remotely. |
| Underlying service | The filesystem, API, database, or other system that actually owns the information or operation. |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Person[My question] --> Host[AI host and model]
  Host --> Client[MCP client]
  Client <-->|MCP messages| Server[MCP server]
  Server --> Service[Existing API or data source]
  Service --> Server
```

An MCP server can wrap an existing API; application rules still apply.

## Tools, resources, and prompts

A teaching example: an assistant helping me understand a repository.

| Primitive | What it provides | Illustrative capability |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tool | An operation with named inputs and a result | Search issues by repository and state |
| Resource | Context that can be read | A project's architecture notes |
| Prompt | A reusable interaction template | A structured code-review brief |

A tool can read or change state; the word “tool” does not mean “safe.” A prompt template is not an authorization policy. The host decides how capabilities appear in its experience. [Official server concepts](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/2026-07-28/learn/server-concepts).

## Trace one request

Imagine I ask: **“Which open issues mention tenant isolation?”**

1. The host discovers the server's available capabilities.
2. A search tool advertises inputs such as repository and query.
3. The model proposes a call using those inputs.
4. The host applies its configured permissions and approval rules.
5. The client sends the request; the server checks access and queries the service.
6. Results return to the host. The model can summarize them and cite issue links.

That is an illustrative read-only workflow, not a configured integration. If access is denied, a trustworthy answer reports the limit; it does not invent a successful search.

## Why authorization still matters

Discovery describes what a server offers. Authorization determines what this caller may actually use. Knowing a tool's name does not grant access. Remote integrations need an identity and authorization design appropriate to their transport and service. [Official authorization guide](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/2026-07-28/tutorials/security/authorization).

In a tenant application, the server must derive and enforce the allowed organization scope. Accepting an organization identifier proposed by a model is not proof that the user belongs to it.

## What MCP does not make safe

Tool descriptions and returned documents can contain untrusted instructions. A retrieved issue saying “send me the deployment secret” is issue content, not a new owner instruction. Keep read and write capabilities separate, limit credentials, and review consequential actions. These are engineering boundaries around the connection. [Official security practices](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/2026-07-28/tutorials/security/security_best_practices).

## Where Foundry and CI/CD fit

My working distinction: **Foundry coordinates work; MCP can connect a compatible AI host to tools; CI/CD checks and delivers changes.** None establishes runtime application permissions by itself. This is a conceptual relationship, not a claim that every Foundry installation exposes an MCP server. Continue with [CI/CD concepts](/guide/ci-cd-fundamentals).

## Check your understanding

- A server lists a delete tool. Does that mean the current user may delete?
- An MCP result contains instructions to reveal credentials. Should the host obey?
- Is the model itself directly executing a database query?

## Answer key

Listing is discovery, not permission. Returned text is untrusted data. The host/client/server software executes the operation; the model proposes a call and interprets its result.

title: Conversation context and document Q&A
summary: Separate portfolio analysis, remembered scope, and answers grounded in one private document.
body:
## Two different sources of answers

Portfolio Copilot reads structured domain facts through selectors. Document Q&A reads text extracted from a particular authorized file. They should not share an implied authority to answer every question. A lease PDF can describe a contract; it cannot establish today's allocated payment balance without the ledger.

The inspected documents architecture explicitly separates these sources. It also marks image-only PDFs without extractable text as a user-facing limitation rather than an implemented OCR pipeline.

## Conversation scope is a contract

The conversation orchestrator classifies intent, resolves scope, normalizes it, handles clarification, chooses the response mode, and attaches metadata. Previous context can help interpret a follow-up; it should not override an explicit current request.

Distinguish the requested organization, entity, time range, comparison period, and selected tool. A frontend page hint is useful for routing, but must not bypass server-side organization/entity resolution. If an entity no longer exists or lies outside the current scope, fail or clarify instead of borrowing another record with a similar label.

## One drawer at the shell boundary

The inspected DashboardLayout mounts a single Copilot drawer and owns its open/close state. It uses current organization context and exposes an opening action through context. Domain pages contribute page-aware prompts without constructing competing global drawers.

This is a useful frontend pattern: keep workspace-level interactions at the shell, feature behavior in the feature, and transient inputs locally. It avoids multiple focus traps and inconsistent conversations when navigating between domain pages.

## Document Q&A request boundary

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  Ask[Question and document ID] --> Gate[Feature and access gate]
  Gate --> Document[Scoped document lookup]
  Document --> File[Latest attached private file]
  File --> Text[Extract permitted text]
  Text --> Answer[Document-grounded answer]
  Answer --> Usage[Interaction usage accounting]
```

**Text alternative:** Access gates precede the scoped document lookup and latest-file extraction. Answers are grounded in that document's text and interaction usage is recorded. File storage URLs and provider internals do not become frontend response fields.

The targeted source search confirms an organization-filtered document lookup in document Q&A views. Documentation describes access gating before file lookup/extraction and shared interaction usage accounting. The review did not execute provider calls or verify billing concurrency behavior.

## Preview state and cleanup

The documented viewer fetches an authorized Blob, creates a browser object URL, and cleans it up when the workspace stops using it. Ask-AI mode presents preview and chat together. Chat history is session-only and resets when the preview closes.

A Blob URL is a local presentation handle, not backend authorization. Recheck access when fetching the file. Clean up object URLs, abort obsolete fetches, preserve focus when opening/closing the modal, and show explicit unsupported-file errors.

## Verify leakage and context errors

Ask about a different document, send a foreign document identifier, change organizations during a preview request, close/reopen the chat, and supply an image-only PDF. Confirm no unauthorized file/text reaches the response and that unsupported inputs produce an honest limitation.

For portfolio follow-ups, change the time period and issue an explicit different-domain question. Verify routing rebuilds current scoped facts rather than using stale conversation numbers. Provider errors should not fabricate a confident answer.

title: Ledger truth and derived read models
summary: Use charges and allocations as durable facts, then build Revenue and reporting from them.
body:
## The lease owns its financial history

EstateIQ's Billing domain is a lease receivables subledger. A unit has a timeline of leases; each lease preserves its own charges, payments, allocations, and derived balance. Replacing a tenant should not move old accounting rows into a new lease's ledger.

This chapter is an engineering explanation of the documented domain, with synthetic amounts. It is not accounting advice or a claim that every listed invariant has been exercised in this review.

## Payment is not allocation

A charge records an amount owed. A payment records money received. An allocation applies payment to a charge. Unapplied money remains received cash but does not automatically reduce a particular charge's balance.

For a synthetic charge of 1,000 and a payment of 700 with only 500 allocated to that charge, the charge's remaining balance is 500; the payment has 200 unapplied. Showing a mutable paid flag or subtracting the full payment from every charge would misrepresent the records.

## Revenue is a read model

The inspected Revenue architecture says the domain has no database models or write services. It reads Billing data through organization-scoped selectors and exposes summary and collection-row contracts. Operational actions lead back to the owning lease ledger.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  Charges[Posted lease charges] --> Selector[Scoped Revenue selectors]
  Allocations[Payment allocations] --> Selector
  Selector --> Summary[Summary and collection rows]
  Summary --> UI[React query and presentation]
  Selector --> AI[Deterministic analyst tools]
```

**Text alternative:** Posted charges and allocations feed organization-scoped Revenue selectors. The same structured read contracts support frontend summaries and deterministic AI analysis.

The documented selected-period equations use posted charges for expected amount and their allocations for collected amount. Outstanding is their difference. A no-charge gap is an operational finding, not invented revenue. Table rows and summary totals use consistent filters so separately implemented calculations do not drift.

## Mutations belong to the owning service

A billing service should validate organization scope, workflow rules, allowable allocation, and transaction boundaries. Database constraints protect structural invariants; locking and explicit concurrency policy protect operations that depend on changing balances.

The exact remedies depend on the implemented schema. Do not copy a lock excerpt without checking which rows and predicates prevent the race. An aggregate computed before acquiring the necessary lock can still be stale.

## Refresh downstream views deliberately

After posting a charge or allocating payment, refresh the relevant ledger, Revenue lists/summaries, and dashboard consumers. Organization and normalized filters belong in query identity. Use authoritative responses where possible and invalidate derived views whose totals may have changed.

An AI answer should rebuild facts rather than treat the last formatted response as financial memory. A document or frontend component should not create a parallel balance calculation.

## Verify the synthetic history

Test partial allocation, unapplied cash, two payments against one charge, tenant turnover with separate leases, filtering by period/entity, and cross-organization denial. Compare the list, summary, dashboard, and analyst tool under the same filters. A review of source documents alone does not establish these checks passed.

title: Private documents and reviewed intake
summary: Keep canonical files, extracted drafts, and confirmed financial records at distinct trust boundaries.
body:
## A file is evidence, not a financial record

EstateIQ documents store private evidence and metadata. Intake captures incoming artifacts and proposed values. Expenses owns confirmed spend. A receipt extraction may propose a category or amount, but confirmation must pass domain rules before it becomes financial truth.

The source inspection covered document storage documentation, targeted file-view code, and the intake draft-confirmation service. It did not upload real files or run extraction/provider workflows.

## Canonical files and private delivery

The documented upload pipeline validates supported PDF/image inputs, converts supported images to a canonical PDF, computes a hash, and records original plus canonical metadata. Storage paths include organization/document context. A path naming convention improves organization; authorization still happens in the backend.

EstateIQ's inspected `document_file_views.py` scopes DocumentFile queries by organization and builds a `FileResponse` with `nosniff`. Its current preview/download design streams through the authorized backend, rather than returning raw storage URLs.

That distinction corrects an important generic assumption: short-lived S3 URLs are one possible design, but this application's observed path is backend-authorized streaming. Both need a permission boundary; they have different revocation, bandwidth, and caching tradeoffs.

## From intake draft to expense

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  Incoming[Incoming document artifact] --> Validate[Validate and stage]
  Validate --> Extract[Extract proposed fields]
  Extract --> Draft[Reviewable expense draft]
  Draft --> Confirm[Explicit user confirmation]
  Confirm --> Lock[Scoped locked draft]
  Lock --> Workflow[Financial workflow]
  Workflow --> Expense[Owning expense service]
```

**Text alternative:** Incoming artifacts are validated and staged; extraction proposes fields in a review draft. User confirmation locks the scoped draft and delegates confirmed financial creation through the owning workflow/service boundary.

The inspected `expense_draft_confirmation_service.py` runs transactionally, obtains an organization-scoped locked draft, requires pending status, rejects an already linked expense, validates required confirmed fields, and delegates to Financial Workflows. Those are observable source behaviors, not an executed race-condition test result.

## Preserve the confirmation boundary

Required fields include a permanent document link, scope, amount, date, and category. Related organization-owned records must remain compatible with the selected organization. A confident extraction does not bypass review or establish that an accounting operation is valid.

The cross-domain workflow coordinates evidence links while the owning Expense service retains its write rules. If an operation fails, transaction and storage cleanup semantics must be understood separately: a database rollback does not automatically delete an object already uploaded to S3.

## Recovery and verification

Use synthetic PDFs/images for size/type checks, conversion failure, unsupported files, duplicate ingestion, expired staging cleanup, foreign document IDs, and preview/download denial. Submit confirmation twice and concurrently; check that the resulting durable expense behavior matches the service contract without duplicate financial records.

Inspect storage outcomes after partial failure and make abandoned-object cleanup observable. For preview, verify object URL cleanup and cancellation when changing organizations. For Q&A, verify the document-specific source boundary and image-only limitation.

title: Subscriptions, webhooks, and feature gates
summary: Separate SaaS entitlement from lease accounting and enforce access on the server.
body:
## Two different meanings of billing

EstateIQ's subscriptions domain concerns the owner paying the platform. The lease Billing domain concerns receivables from tenants. They have different customers, records, providers, and consistency expectations. Do not use one subscription status to infer that a lease payment settled.

The reviewed instructions describe plan limits, trial state, provider synchronization, and feature gates. This guide omits mutable commercial prices; inspect current seeded plans and product contracts when implementing.

## Provider events establish provider-backed state

Subscription instructions describe signature verification before processing Stripe webhook events. The inspected handler maps provider subscription data through configured plans to an organization's subscription and uses `update_or_create` to mirror state. It can synchronize a missing provider mirror before processing.

Repeated upserts help repeated events converge; they do not by themselves prove protection against stale out-of-order events, every concurrency race, or lost delivery. Record event identity, ordering policy, reconciliation, and observable failure handling where needed. A successful browser redirect is not proof that backend subscription state is synchronized.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  Checkout[Hosted checkout] --> Provider[Provider subscription]
  Provider --> Signature[Verified webhook]
  Signature --> Mapping[Resolve organization and plan]
  Mapping --> State[Project subscription state]
  State --> Gate[Server feature gate]
  Gate --> API[Permitted domain action]
```

**Text alternative:** The hosted provider emits a verified event that maps to organization/plan state. Backend feature gates consult the resulting state before the domain action. Frontend checkout return is presentation, not authoritative state.

## Gate order and separate authority

The documented policy checks a recognized demo organization first, then subscription standing, then plan limits. A demo exemption must not bypass authentication, membership, or organization-object isolation. Keep the exemption narrowly tied to intended synthetic demo behavior.

The inspected AI message view applies standing and usage checks before response construction. Its usage lookup is user-based, so quota semantics must be documented accurately. A frontend upgrade prompt is useful feedback, but the backend denies unsupported access even if the caller bypasses the UI.

## Trials and scheduled transitions

Local trials without a provider subscription and provider-backed trials have different transition owners. The instructions describe a management command for local expiration and webhook updates for provider-backed state. Do not apply both transitions blindly to the same subscription.

Treat scheduled expiration as idempotent maintenance with last-success monitoring. A missed trigger must have a recovery path, and grace-period decisions need explicit timestamps and timezone rules rather than scattered UI conditions.

## Frontend consistency

After a limit-changing action such as unit creation, refresh subscription status/usage consumers as well as the domain list. After checkout, refetch authoritative state and explain pending synchronization when appropriate. Avoid optimistically granting paid access from a redirect query parameter.

## Verify the provider boundary

Exercise invalid signatures, duplicate and out-of-order events, missing organization metadata, unknown price mappings, delayed synchronization, expired local trials, canceled access, grace-period boundaries, and foreign organization requests. Check logs and durable state rather than response codes alone.

The reviewed handler's own idempotency claim is a design intention supported by the upsert shape. This handbook review did not run webhook replay tests or inspect live provider settings.

title: Property, onboarding, finance, and tax workflows
summary: Connect the rest of the system without creating duplicate sources of truth.
body:
## Property structure before financial activity

Buildings and units supply stable property identity. Leasing connects people and contracts to those units. The documented occupancy rule derives from effective active leases rather than a manually maintained occupied boolean.

That matters during turnover: a unit's timeline persists while each lease keeps its own ledger. UI navigation should distinguish current operational context from historical records instead of opening a combined unit balance.

## Onboarding derives progress

The documented onboarding chain is building, units, lease, ledger activity, and expenses. Selectors derive setup status from organization-owned records and expose stable next-step contracts to clients and Copilot. Preferences and interaction events can persist; duplicate has-building or completed-finance booleans should not compete with domain truth.

A new organization with no data is a valid empty state. The UI should guide the next safe action rather than crash, render invented totals, or imply that a checklist established readiness.

## Expenses and owner-side property finance

Expenses owns confirmed spend, category/vendor relationships, and supporting evidence. Property Finance owns owner-side financing and recurring obligations such as mortgage, insurance, and property-tax records. Neither owns lease charges or payment allocation.

Reporting consumes deterministic selectors/contracts from these domains. Explain metric inclusion rules before combining spend, financing, and receivables: visually adjacent cards do not establish that their values share an accounting basis.

## Accountant preparation is composition

Tax Documents composes income, expenses, documents, buildings, and property-finance facts into review/readiness surfaces. Missing evidence and uncategorized records route back to their owning domains. This is not a tax-advice, deduction, filing, or compliance engine.

The inspected source documentation marks formal PDF/ZIP packet phases as planned. Preserve that status until an implemented export and failure exercise provide evidence. A packet-preview UI should not be described as a completed durable export job.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  Building[Building and units] --> Lease[Effective leases]
  Lease --> Ledger[Lease ledger]
  Ledger --> Reports[Deterministic reporting]
  Expense[Confirmed expenses] --> Reports
  Finance[Owner property finance] --> Reports
  Documents[Private evidence] --> Tax[Accountant preparation]
  Reports --> Tax
  Building --> Setup[Derived onboarding status]
  Lease --> Setup
  Ledger --> Setup
  Expense --> Setup
```

**Text alternative:** Property and lease facts support ledger activity and derived onboarding. Confirmed expenses and owner finance contribute to reporting. Reporting plus evidence support accountant preparation without moving ownership of the underlying facts.

## Build a vertical workflow

For a synthetic unit, create a lease through its owning service, post a documented charge, attach an authorized evidence document where needed, and observe the derived dashboard/setup state. If a mutation changes several read surfaces, invalidate every affected cache contract rather than maintaining duplicate state in components.

For an accountant-review item, deep-link to the exact record owner. Do not let a report silently edit a category or invent a missing receipt. Cross-domain coordination belongs in a workflow layer that delegates actual writes.

## Verification and limitations

Test lease date boundaries, turnover history, missing setup data, foreign property relationships, finance/expense scope, consistent selected periods, and links from review issues to authorized records. Confirm that deleting or archiving source data changes derived onboarding/readiness appropriately.

This chapter reconciles domain documentation. Detailed schema, algorithms, and deployment outcomes require their own code review and tests before labeling each workflow verified.

title: Feature controllers, cache contracts, and workspace UX
summary: Use EstateIQ patterns for typed transport, scoped server state, and deliberate visual hierarchy.
body:
## Build from contract to presentation

EstateIQ features use typed API modules, query hooks, controller/workspace hooks, pages, and presentational parts. A controller is valuable where multiple state sources and user actions meet. A visual card should receive explicit props rather than independently fetching a competing version of domain truth.

The handbook itself stays static and frontend-only. Axios and TanStack Query are taught here because EstateIQ uses a backend, not installed merely to make a documentation app look full-stack.

## Scope query identity

The inspected OrgProvider invalidates queries with the `org` prefix on workspace changes. Feature query keys should include organization and normalized filter values. Canonical period/filter inputs keep cache identity predictable when URLs and controls change.

**src/features/example/queryKeys.ts · synthetic excerpt**

```typescript
// src/features/example/queryKeys.ts — Partition a feature's server snapshots.
export const exampleKeys = {
  list: (orgSlug: string, period: string) =>
    ['org', orgSlug, 'example', 'list', period] as const,
};
```

A key convention helps switching behavior; it is not server authorization. Inspect each feature for keys outside the convention before assuming a prefix-based invalidation covers every view.

## A mutation has downstream consumers

A payment allocation can change the lease ledger, Revenue collection rows, summary totals, and dashboard consumers. Unit creation can change plan usage. Document confirmation can change expenses, evidence links, and review counts. Track affected contracts explicitly.

An authoritative mutation response can update a detail cache directly. Derived aggregates usually need invalidation or recomputation through their server source. Avoid optimistic financial totals unless the operation and rollback policy justify it.

## Workspace and transient state

The inspected layout owns one global Copilot drawer and uses current organization context. The feature owns conversation behavior. Document preview owns session chat and Blob lifecycle. Page/controller composition connects those behaviors without turning every presentational component into an orchestrator.

Local state includes open drawers, selected tabs, and editing inputs. Server state includes membership, quotas, financial records, and derived setup status. Do not make a local success banner the authority for a provider webhook or background job outcome.

## The EstateIQ visual language

Its visual reference uses zinc/near-black surfaces, subtle borders, generous rounded panels, cyan actions, emerald healthy state, amber attention, and red danger. Major headers explain the workspace and primary action; badges communicate scope or status. Dense content remains grouped into purposeful surfaces.

The handbook borrows those principles: a focused header, compact section navigation, stronger article identity, subdued surfaces, cyan interaction, and diagrams that respect the surrounding theme. A reference article still needs readable line length and prose rhythm; adopting dashboard styling does not require adding invented KPI cards.

## Verify behavior with design

Review empty, loading, partial, error, and stale-refresh states. Check keyboard focus, drawer dismissal, restored focus, mobile overflow, and contrast in both themes. Test an organization switch during in-flight requests and a mutation affecting more than one view.

Source inspection found concrete loading/error states in dashboard panels and structured metadata/action treatment in document headers. The handbook applies that hierarchy to reading and navigation; it does not reuse EstateIQ's business records or private assets.

title: 01 · Define the Reports feature
summary: Write the contract and a Foundry task brief before choosing models or components.
body:
## The outcome

Build one small feature all the way through: an active editor creates a draft report, lists reports in their workspace, and opens a report detail. An active viewer can read. Someone without membership cannot read or write. A request repeated after an uncertain response must not create a second draft.

Reports contain a title and a draft status. They do not calculate financial results, generate PDFs, or ask an AI provider for facts. Those extensions come after this slice has evidence behind it.

This is an authored reference design inspired by the EstateIQ boundaries. The Django and TanStack examples are unexecuted reference code. The [interactive Reports lab](/lab/reports) runs a browser-only simulation with synthetic records.

## Trace the feature

```mermaid
flowchart TB
 subgraph client["Browser · presentation and scoped snapshots"]
  Page[Reports page] --> Controller[Feature controller]
  Controller --> Query[Typed transport and query hooks]
 end
 Query -->|Identity plus nominated workspace| View
 subgraph api["Django · authority"]
  View[Authenticate and resolve active membership]
  View --> Input[Validate command serializer]
  Input --> Service[Authorize action and create draft]
  View --> Selector[Read through scoped selector]
 end
 subgraph durable["PostgreSQL · durable truth"]
  Service --> Constraint[Unique tenant plus actor plus creation key]
  Constraint --> Rows[Report rows]
  Selector --> Rows
 end
 Rows -->|Scoped response| Query
```

The browser chooses a workspace. The server proves the user belongs to it. Query keys prevent accidental cache mixing, while scoped database queries enforce access. Each has a different job.

## Freeze the API contract

The tutorial assumes an existing JWT-authenticated Django REST Framework application. A separate application must configure JWT authentication, a user model, installed apps, PostgreSQL, and migrations. Django session authentication is also possible, but needs its own CSRF and response-code contract; do not paste JWT expectations into it.

| Request | Allowed actor | Success | Important rejection |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| GET `/api/v1/reports/?limit=20&offset=0` | Active viewer or editor | 200 paginated list | 401 identity missing; 403 membership missing |
| POST `/api/v1/reports/` | Active editor | 201 new draft; 200 replay | 400 invalid input; 403 forbidden; 409 key conflict |
| GET `/api/v1/reports/{uuid}/` | Active viewer or editor | 200 detail | 404 object outside current scope |

Every request carries `X-Org-Slug`. The backend derives the tenant from authenticated membership; the body cannot grant tenant access. The command has exactly two fields:

```json
{
  "title": "Quarterly portfolio review",
  "creationKey": "20ee76c4-334d-46d5-a527-7650c52902e3"
}
```

The result is a report object with `id`, `title`, `status`, and `createdAt`. The list uses `count`, `next`, `previous`, and `results`. Field names stay consistent through serializers, TypeScript, and tests.

## Decide retry semantics

A creation key identifies one command by one authenticated actor in one tenant. A retry uses the same key and normalized title. A changed title with that key returns 409. A different actor cannot retrieve the original actor’s result by guessing their key.

A 503 or connection failure may happen after commit. Treat the outcome as unknown until the original command is replayed or reconciled. A form edit starts a new command only after that uncertainty is resolved. The lab deliberately refreshes its synthetic list immediately to make the committed row visible; a real client might still have a stale list.

## Give Foundry a concrete brief

Foundry helps coordinate the work and evidence. It does not replace backend permission checks. The handbook's local Foundry initialization does not imply that governed release automation has already been configured.

```text
Outcome: Editors create draft reports in their active workspace.

Scope:
- Reports model and reviewed migration.
- Scoped list/detail selectors and authorized create service.
- DRF contract; typed React transport, hooks, controller, and parts.
- Tenant, role, replay, conflict, and uncertainty checks.

Acceptance evidence:
- North member cannot retrieve a South report by UUID.
- Viewer reads but POST returns 403; outsider list returns 403.
- Same actor + tenant + creationKey returns the same ID on replay.
- Same key + different normalized title returns 409.
- Scope change clears old detail and pending command.
- PostgreSQL concurrent replay creates one row.
- Backend and browser test output attached to the implementation.

Review:
- Backend reviewer checks scope, transaction, constraint, migration.
- Frontend reviewer checks request identity, cache keys, recovery UX.
- Anthony owns acceptance and release authorization.

Non-goals: exports, AI-generated facts, worker deployment, billing.
```

Use the Foundry commands and task schema available in your installed version. This is a task brief, not an invented CLI invocation.

## Checkpoint

Before writing code, answer: who can create, where does tenant authority come from, and what happens if the write succeeds but the response disappears? Continue to [models and migrations](/guide/reports-data).

title: 02 · Model the tenant and report
summary: Express ownership and replay identity as database relationships and constraints.
body:
## Establish the application scaffold

Use a separate Django application for the backend tutorial. The handbook remains a static frontend. The reference paths below assume `apps.organizations` and `apps.reports` are installed Django apps with normal `__init__.py`, `apps.py`, and migration packages. If your application already owns organizations and membership, reuse its canonical models instead of duplicating them.

Target the Django 5.2 documentation series for these examples. Lock compatible Django, DRF, JWT, and PostgreSQL driver versions in the backend repository and test that lock. This chapter does not provide or claim a verified environment.

## Represent membership explicitly

```python
# apps/organizations/models.py — Canonical organizations and active roles.
from django.conf import settings
from django.db import models


class Organization(models.Model):
    slug = models.SlugField(unique=True)
    name = models.CharField(max_length=120)


class Membership(models.Model):
    class Role(models.TextChoices):
        VIEWER = "viewer"
        EDITOR = "editor"

    organization = models.ForeignKey(Organization, on_delete=models.CASCADE)
    user = models.ForeignKey(settings.AUTH_USER_MODEL, on_delete=models.CASCADE)
    role = models.CharField(max_length=12, choices=Role.choices)
    active = models.BooleanField(default=True)

    class Meta:
        constraints = [
            models.UniqueConstraint(
                fields=["organization", "user"], name="unique_org_member"
            )
        ]
```

Membership is a relationship, not a claim accepted from a browser dropdown. The lab's role selector is deliberately a simulation control.

## Keep durable command identity

```python
# apps/reports/models.py — Store a draft and the identity of its create command.
import uuid
from django.conf import settings
from django.db import models


class Report(models.Model):
    id = models.UUIDField(primary_key=True, default=uuid.uuid4, editable=False)
    organization = models.ForeignKey(
        "organizations.Organization", on_delete=models.PROTECT
    )
    created_by = models.ForeignKey(
        settings.AUTH_USER_MODEL, on_delete=models.PROTECT
    )
    creation_key = models.UUIDField()
    title = models.CharField(max_length=120)
    status = models.CharField(max_length=12, default="draft", editable=False)
    created_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)

    class Meta:
        constraints = [
            models.UniqueConstraint(
                fields=["organization", "created_by", "creation_key"],
                name="unique_report_create_command",
            ),
            models.CheckConstraint(
                condition=models.Q(status="draft"), name="report_is_draft"
            ),
        ]
        indexes = [models.Index(fields=["organization", "-created_at"])]
```

`PROTECT` makes deletion policy explicit: deleting an organization or creator cannot silently remove reports. That is a teaching choice, not a universal retention policy. Decide anonymization, archival, and deletion requirements for the real product.

The draft constraint fits this slice. Adding ready/failed states later requires a reviewed schema change. Do not expand a frontend enum and assume the database now accepts it.

## Review the migration

Run these commands in the separate backend repository after configuring the apps and database:

```bash
python manage.py makemigrations organizations reports
python manage.py sqlmigrate organizations 0001
python manage.py sqlmigrate reports 0001
python manage.py migrate --plan
python manage.py migrate
python manage.py check
```

Inspect generated dependencies, foreign keys, the replay uniqueness constraint, and the tenant index. Commit generated migrations with the code. For an existing table, inspect duplicate command identities before applying uniqueness; a migration should not discover the cleanup policy in production.

Django documents that `get_or_create` needs database uniqueness on its lookup fields to protect against competing inserts. Our lookup uses all three constrained fields. Review that relationship rather than relying on the method name. [Django QuerySet reference](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/5.2/ref/models/querysets/#get-or-create).

## Draw the ownership boundary

```mermaid
erDiagram
 ORGANIZATION ||--o{ MEMBERSHIP : has
 USER ||--o{ MEMBERSHIP : belongs_through
 ORGANIZATION ||--o{ REPORT : owns
 USER ||--o{ REPORT : creates
 REPORT {
  uuid id PK
  uuid creation_key
  string title
  string status
  datetime created_at
 }
 MEMBERSHIP {
  boolean active
  string role
 }
```

The ER diagram shows relationships; it does not prove an API query includes the tenant predicate. That proof belongs in the next chapter and its tests.

## Checkpoint
