Verify the generated migration against PostgreSQL and inspect the resulting constraints. Backend commands above have not been executed in this handbook. Continue to [services and the API](/guide/reports-api).

title: 03 · Enforce the contract in Django
summary: Resolve membership, scope selectors, authorize writes, and return a predictable API.
body:
## Resolve scope after authentication

These files belong in the separate backend application described in chapter two. An authenticated user and a nominated slug are inputs; an active membership is the verified scope.

```python
# apps/reports/selectors.py — Resolve membership and keep reads tenant-scoped.
from django.shortcuts import get_object_or_404
from rest_framework.exceptions import PermissionDenied
from apps.organizations.models import Membership
from .models import Report


def request_membership(request):
    membership = Membership.objects.select_related("organization").filter(
        organization__slug=request.headers.get("X-Org-Slug", ""),
        user=request.user,
        active=True,
    ).first()
    if membership is None:
        raise PermissionDenied("Active membership required.")
    return membership


def report_list(*, organization):
    return Report.objects.filter(organization=organization).order_by(
        "-created_at", "-id"
    )


def report_detail(*, organization, report_id):
    return get_object_or_404(report_list(organization=organization), pk=report_id)
```

The view's authentication and permission phase runs before these helpers. Avoid calling `request_membership` from unauthenticated middleware. A foreign UUID yields the same 404 as an absent UUID after membership has been established.

## Put the write rule in a service

```python
# apps/reports/services.py — Authorize and converge repeated create commands.
from django.db import transaction
from rest_framework.exceptions import APIException, PermissionDenied
from apps.organizations.models import Membership
from .models import Report


class CreationConflict(APIException):
    status_code = 409
    default_detail = "Creation key already used with a different title."


@transaction.atomic
def create_report(*, membership, title, creation_key):
    # Re-read inside the command rather than trusting a stale scope object.
    current = Membership.objects.select_for_update().filter(pk=membership.pk).first()
    if current is None or not current.active or current.role != Membership.Role.EDITOR:
        raise PermissionDenied("Active editor membership required.")
    normalized_title = title.strip()
    report, created = Report.objects.get_or_create(
        organization_id=current.organization_id,
        created_by_id=current.user_id,
        creation_key=creation_key,
        defaults={"title": normalized_title},
    )
    if report.title != normalized_title:
        raise CreationConflict()
    return report, created
```

This service assumes validated input and a membership resolved for the actor. Jobs and management commands must supply an equally trusted scope and validate their inputs. The membership row lock serializes commands by that member; that tradeoff is acceptable for this small example, but deserves a throughput review for a real workload. It also coordinates with normal transactional updates to that membership row. Broader organization suspension rules are outside this slice.

## Keep serializers at the transport boundary

```python
# apps/reports/serializers.py — Map the agreed camelCase wire contract.
from rest_framework import serializers
from .models import Report


class CreateReportInput(serializers.Serializer):
    title = serializers.CharField(max_length=120, trim_whitespace=True)
    creationKey = serializers.UUIDField()


class ReportOutput(serializers.ModelSerializer):
    createdAt = serializers.DateTimeField(source="created_at", read_only=True)

    class Meta:
        model = Report
        fields = ["id", "title", "status", "createdAt"]
        read_only_fields = fields
```

DRF serializers validate incoming data before the view reads `validated_data`. Serialization does not authorize a tenant or action. [DRF serializer documentation](https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/serializers/).

## Compose views and pagination

```python
# apps/reports/views.py — Connect identity, scope, validation, and domain work.
from rest_framework.permissions import IsAuthenticated
from rest_framework.pagination import LimitOffsetPagination
from rest_framework.response import Response
from rest_framework.views import APIView
from .selectors import request_membership, report_list, report_detail
from .serializers import CreateReportInput, ReportOutput
from .services import create_report


class ReportsPagination(LimitOffsetPagination):
    default_limit = 20
    max_limit = 100


class ReportsView(APIView):
    permission_classes = [IsAuthenticated]

    def get(self, request):
        scope = request_membership(request)
        paginator = ReportsPagination()
        rows = paginator.paginate_queryset(
            report_list(organization=scope.organization), request, view=self
        )
        return paginator.get_paginated_response(ReportOutput(rows, many=True).data)

    def post(self, request):
        scope = request_membership(request)
        command = CreateReportInput(data=request.data)
        command.is_valid(raise_exception=True)
        report, created = create_report(
            membership=scope,
            title=command.validated_data["title"],
            creation_key=command.validated_data["creationKey"],
        )
        return Response(ReportOutput(report).data, status=201 if created else 200)


class ReportDetailView(APIView):
    permission_classes = [IsAuthenticated]

    def get(self, request, report_id):
        scope = request_membership(request)
        report = report_detail(organization=scope.organization, report_id=report_id)
        return Response(ReportOutput(report).data)
```

```python
# apps/reports/urls.py — Feature-owned API routes.
from django.urls import path
from .views import ReportsView, ReportDetailView

urlpatterns = [
    path("", ReportsView.as_view(), name="reports-list"),
    path("<uuid:report_id>/", ReportDetailView.as_view(), name="reports-detail"),
]
```

Include these routes at `path("api/v1/reports/", include("apps.reports.urls"))` in the project's URL configuration. Configure the chosen JWT authenticator in DRF settings in the separate application. `IsAuthenticated` alone does not issue or verify JWTs. APIView coordinates authentication, permissions, and recognized API exceptions; do not wrap everything in a blanket success response. [DRF APIView documentation](https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/views/).

## Checkpoint

A list, detail, and write each pass through verified scope. Write permission is rechecked in the service, and replay identity has a database constraint. Backend execution remains pending until the separate repository runs its tests. Continue to [React and cache ownership](/guide/reports-react).

title: 04 · Build the React feature boundary
summary: Connect typed transport, scoped queries, mutation recovery, and presentational parts.

title: 05 · Prove the boundaries and break the happy path
summary: Use negative tests and the interactive lab to separate plausible design from verified behavior.
body:
## Keep evidence attached to its implementation

The handbook's browser checks exercise the synthetic Reports lab. They do not prove that Django permissions, PostgreSQL uniqueness, JWT verification, or a deployment work. The Python test below is reference code for the separate backend application; run it there before declaring the feature verified.

## Start with API behavior

```python
# apps/reports/tests/test_api.py — Reference checks for scope and command replay.
import uuid
from django.contrib.auth import get_user_model
from django.test import TestCase
from rest_framework.test import APIClient
from apps.organizations.models import Organization, Membership
from apps.reports.models import Report


class ReportsApiTests(TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.user = get_user_model().objects.create_user(username="editor")
        self.north = Organization.objects.create(slug="north", name="North")
        self.south = Organization.objects.create(slug="south", name="South")
        self.member = Membership.objects.create(
            organization=self.north, user=self.user, role="editor", active=True
        )
        self.foreign = Report.objects.create(
            organization=self.south, created_by=self.user,
            creation_key=uuid.uuid4(), title="South private draft"
        )
        self.client = APIClient()
        self.client.force_authenticate(self.user)
        self.client.credentials(HTTP_X_ORG_SLUG="north")
        self.command = {"title": "Quarterly review", "creationKey": str(uuid.uuid4())}

    def test_replay_converges_and_conflicting_payload_is_rejected(self):
        first = self.client.post("/api/v1/reports/", self.command, format="json")
        replay = self.client.post("/api/v1/reports/", self.command, format="json")
        conflict = self.client.post("/api/v1/reports/", {
            **self.command, "title": "Changed title"
        }, format="json")
        self.assertEqual(first.status_code, 201)
        self.assertEqual(replay.status_code, 200)
        self.assertEqual(first.data["id"], replay.data["id"])
        self.assertEqual(conflict.status_code, 409)
        self.assertEqual(Report.objects.filter(organization=self.north).count(), 1)

    def test_foreign_object_and_list_are_scoped(self):
        detail = self.client.get(f"/api/v1/reports/{self.foreign.id}/")
        listing = self.client.get("/api/v1/reports/")
        self.assertEqual(detail.status_code, 404)
        self.assertEqual(listing.status_code, 200)
        self.assertEqual(listing.data["count"], 0)
        self.assertEqual(listing.data["results"], [])

    def test_viewer_reads_but_cannot_create(self):
        self.member.role = "viewer"
        self.member.save(update_fields=["role"])
        self.assertEqual(self.client.get("/api/v1/reports/").status_code, 200)
        denied = self.client.post("/api/v1/reports/", self.command, format="json")
        self.assertEqual(denied.status_code, 403)

    def test_revoked_membership_denies_list_and_replay(self):
        self.client.post("/api/v1/reports/", self.command, format="json")
        self.member.active = False
        self.member.save(update_fields=["active"])
        self.assertEqual(self.client.get("/api/v1/reports/").status_code, 403)
        replay = self.client.post("/api/v1/reports/", self.command, format="json")
        self.assertEqual(replay.status_code, 403)
```

Adapt the fixture for a custom user model. `force_authenticate` bypasses actual token verification; add real valid/expired/malformed JWT tests against the configured authenticator. DRF distinguishes test authentication shortcuts from exercising credentials. [DRF testing documentation](https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/testing/).

## Add the tests the snippet cannot prove

| Risk | Required backend evidence |
| --- | --- |
| Competing retries | PostgreSQL transaction test with separate connections and the same command; exactly one row and same result ID |
| User changes | Different actors in one tenant have independent command identities |
| Invalid input | Blank/long title and invalid UUID return 400 without inserting |
| Membership nomination | Existing foreign slug and absent slug fail without revealing objects |
| Pagination | Scope applies to count and every page; stable ordering on equal timestamps |
| Auth boundary | Real JWT tests, expiration, refresh policy, and configured 401 contract |
| Revocation race | Command and membership update behavior tested under the chosen transaction policy |

A sequential replay test is useful, but cannot prove concurrency. A SQLite test pass does not substitute for the PostgreSQL transaction test. Attach actual output to the Foundry review evidence.

## Run the browser failure drills

Open the [Reports lab](/lab/reports). It resets on reload and sends no network requests.

1. As North editor, create a draft. The scoped list gains one record.
2. Retry the same command. The response is a simulated 200 replay and the count stays the same.
3. Reuse that key with a changed title. The simulated result is 409.
4. Reset, enable “Lose the response after commit,” and create. A row exists despite the simulated 503. Retry recovers it without a duplicate.
5. Change to South. North reports and selected detail disappear; pending command is cleared.
6. Become a viewer and submit. The simulated write returns 403. Reads still work.
7. Try another tenant's report ID. The simulated result is 404 after membership.
8. Remove membership. The list clears and object access is denied with 403.

The lab models these outcomes in memory. It is deliberately inspectable teaching code, not an authorization boundary.

## Make failure understandable

A real workspace needs actionable errors: invalid title near the input, forbidden action without stale protected details, and uncertain outcome beside the retained retry action. Keep a failed refresh distinct from a failed write; a committed report does not become uncreated because list refresh failed.

Capture operation, tenant identifier, actor identifier, creation key, status, duration, and correlation ID in real observability. Never log JWTs, full document contents, or unredacted customer payloads. The lab trace contains only synthetic inputs.

## Checkpoint

Use a verification ledger with three separate lines: reference reviewed, browser simulation passed, backend integration pending. Continue to [release and extensions](/guide/reports-release).

title: 06 · Release the slice, then extend it
summary: Connect migrations, deployment, recovery, workers, and AI without weakening the feature contract.
body:
## Release only what has evidence

This handbook publishes static frontend assets to Netlify. The Reports lab ships with those assets. It does not deploy a Django API, run migrations, or establish a production tenant boundary.

The separate full-stack feature needs its own release record. Foundry can organize the task, review artifacts, and acceptance evidence once configured in that application. A local initialization or manual Netlify deploy should not be described as an automated governed release.

## Sequence the real application release

```mermaid
flowchart TB
 Brief[Accepted feature contract] --> Review[Code plus schema review]
 Review --> Evidence[API, PostgreSQL race, and browser evidence]
 Evidence --> Migration[Reviewed migration plan]
 Migration --> Backend[Deploy compatible API]
 Backend --> Frontend[Deploy Reports workspace]
 Frontend --> Smoke[Scoped create, replay, read, and denial smoke checks]
 Smoke --> Observe[Monitor errors and recovery signals]
 Observe --> Decision[Accept release or roll back compatible code]
```

Use a compatibility window: adding a new model and endpoint before publishing its caller is usually easier to reverse than changing an existing field in place. A code rollback does not automatically reverse a migration. Decide whether the schema remains compatible and retain the data needed for recovery.

For Heroku, connect this plan to the application's actual release process and PostgreSQL backup policy. For Vercel or Netlify, deploy the frontend with its correct public API URL and backend origin rules. S3 storage is a separate document concern, not API hosting. Verify the concrete deployment configuration instead of assuming a platform supplies the missing components.

## Keep the operational runbook concrete

| Event | Immediate action | Evidence before closing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Create timeout | Replay the same command identity | Same report ID, one persisted row |
| 403 spike | Inspect auth and active membership checks | No tenant predicate or permission disabled to resolve it |
| Migration failure | Halt incompatible rollout; inspect plan | Database state and compatible code recorded |
| Incorrect data | Identify affected scoped rows; follow repair policy | Reviewed repair, audit trail, and tenant-specific verification |
| Restore required | Restore into an isolated environment first | Recovery time and integrity checks; no untested production overwrite |

Record backup frequency, retention, restore owner, and tested recovery time in the real application. “Automatic backup enabled” is not evidence that recovery works. A scheduled command needs a defined schedule, overlap policy, tenant scope, failure signal, and retry behavior.

## Add exports with an explicit lifecycle

A later PDF/export feature can add `queued`, `running`, `ready`, and `failed` through a new contract and migration. It needs job identity, attempts, bounded retries, tenant-scoped worker inputs, private storage, and an authorized download path. The current draft-only constraint must evolve with that design.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
 Authorized[Authorized export request] --> Job[Persist job and stable command identity]
 Job --> Dispatch[Reliable dispatch after transaction commit]
 Dispatch --> Worker[Worker rechecks scoped inputs]
 Worker --> Artifact[Private artifact storage]
 Artifact --> Ready[Persist ready status and object reference]
 Ready --> Download[Authenticated scoped download]
 Worker -->|Bounded failure| Failed[Failed status plus recovery action]
```

Persisting a job and reliably dispatching it are two operations. An outbox or equivalent recovery mechanism is a proposed extension, not a capability implemented by the synchronous tutorial. Do not claim a web process deploy proves a worker or scheduler is running.

## Add AI after deterministic facts

For a narrative summary, build scoped deterministic report facts first. Let an AI provider phrase those facts under a narrow schema, with provenance, timeout, budget, and fallback behavior. Reject provider output that invents totals or bypasses scope. A viewer's readable report does not automatically grant permission to export source documents or execute a write tool.

Keep AI failures separate from ledger or report correctness. A missing narrative can display deterministic facts. Prompt text is not a replacement for membership checks, tool allowlists, private document access, or audit evidence. Follow [deterministic AI](/guide/deterministic-ai) and [document Q&A boundaries](/guide/ai-context-and-document-qa) when extending this feature.

## Close the Foundry task with precise claims

A useful completion artifact lists the accepted behavior, changed files, migration plan, executed test output, review decisions, deployment reference, and remaining limitations. For this handbook walkthrough, the backend snippets remain reference code and the deployed interactive feature is a synthetic browser simulation.

Return to the [contract](/guide/reports-contract), explore the [lab](/lab/reports), or use this path as a template for the next real feature.

title: Security drills: sessions, JWTs, and private files
summary: Trace expired identity, CSRF rejection, and document revocation without confusing their boundaries.
body:
## Use the authentication mechanism you actually selected

The Reports reference slice assumes JWT authentication. Your applications may use Django sessions, Simple JWT, Clerk, or Gait. Those mechanisms establish identity through different contracts; the same tenant and action policies still need enforcement after identity succeeds.

Start a drill with the selected mechanism, endpoint, origin, browser credential behavior, and expected failure response. A frontend button or stored workspace slug cannot prove membership. These are proposed exercises, not a review of your production settings.

## Separate three rejected requests

| Signal | Boundary to inspect | Recovery behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| JWT endpoint returns 401 for expired access token | Token verification and bounded session recovery | Coordinate refresh; stop on failed refresh; preserve uncertain command identity |
| Authenticated API returns 403 for membership | Tenant/action authority | Recheck access, clear forbidden content, and avoid a refresh loop |
| Session write returns a CSRF 403 | Browser credential and unsafe-request protection | Correct token delivery/origin configuration; retain CSRF checks |

Status codes depend on the configured authenticator. The JWT row assumes the tutorial's JWT contract; Django sessions can produce different unauthenticated API responses. Log a structured failure reason server-side rather than deriving every cause from a bare status number.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
 Request[Protected browser request] --> Identity{Identity valid?}
 Identity -->|No| Recover[Bounded identity recovery or sign in]
 Identity -->|Yes| Scope{Active tenant membership?}
 Scope -->|No| Forbidden[Deny and clear protected view]
 Scope -->|Yes| Action{Action and object permitted?}
 Action -->|No| Denied[Deny action or scoped object lookup]
 Action -->|Yes| Execute[Execute the scoped operation]
 Recover -->|Original identity retained| Request
```

## Exercise token expiry and logout

Use synthetic actors in the separate application's test environment. Expire an access token, send it to a protected endpoint, and inspect the actual response. Then reject refresh and confirm the client ends the session instead of looping. Run two failing requests concurrently to test refresh coordination. Keep tokens out of logs and public evidence.

Simple JWT supports configurable lifetimes, refresh rotation, and blacklisting after rotation when its blacklist app and required settings are enabled. Verify the installed configuration rather than assuming rotation is active. Blacklisting a refresh token does not automatically invalidate every already-issued access token. [Simple JWT settings](https://django-rest-framework-simplejwt.readthedocs.io/en/latest/settings.html).

Check that logout clears protected query caches, local selections, and pending commands. A command whose response was lost needs reconciliation under its original actor and tenant. A newly signed-in actor must not silently replay the previous actor's command.

## Exercise session CSRF deliberately

For a Django session application, confirm how the React client receives a CSRF token and sends it on unsafe requests. Django documents the `X-CSRFToken` header and notes that token acquisition depends on the configured cookie/session settings. Its default test client relaxes CSRF checks; use enforcement explicitly for this drill. [Django CSRF guide](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/5.2/howto/csrf/).

```python
# Reference harness only — configure the application's real login and write routes.
from rest_framework.test import APIClient

client = APIClient(enforce_csrf_checks=True)
# Establish a real session through the configured login flow.
# Missing-token write: assert rejection and no durable mutation.
# Valid-token write: assert success in the permitted tenant.
# Untrusted-origin write: assert rejection under the selected origin policy.
```

This harness is incomplete by design: your login route and CSRF bootstrap belong to the application. `force_authenticate` cannot prove the session/login/CSRF flow. Cookies used to carry JWTs also require an explicit browser-credential and CSRF design; putting a JWT in a cookie does not remove that concern.

## Exercise private-file revocation

Create a private synthetic artifact for North, then attempt its ID from South. A permitted object must first be resolved through the verified scope. Next remove North membership and repeat the request.

For an authenticated streaming path, verify the new request is denied after revocation. For presigned S3 delivery, distinguish the application endpoint that issues the URL from the already issued URL. S3 documents presigned URLs as bearer capabilities whose validity depends on expiration, signing credentials, and applicable policy. Application membership alone is not consulted by that storage request. [S3 presigned URL documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html).

Write down the accepted capability window. If the product requires immediate application-level revocation for each new download, choose a delivery boundary that rechecks application authority. Also inspect cache behavior, content disposition, MIME handling, and permitted ranges; stopping new downloads does not recall bytes already received.

## Attach evidence through Foundry

Record the chosen auth mechanism, application revision, synthetic fixture identities, response/assertion output, and any unresolved token or download window. Attach no secrets or live customer documents. A completed [decision drill](/lab/resilience) is learning evidence; real endpoint results are implementation evidence.

title: Reliable jobs: outbox, leases, and retries
summary: Make recurring work recoverable across missed triggers, worker crashes, and external side effects.
body:
## Give work a durable identity

The Reports walkthrough creates a synchronous draft. A PDF export or recurring reconciliation adds independent components: a trigger, persisted job, dispatch mechanism, worker, storage/provider effects, and monitoring. An API response or running web process proves none of those components completed the job.

For an export, use `(tenant, actor, command key)` to identify the business command. For a scheduled reconciliation, use `(job type, tenant, business period)`. Delivery attempts have separate IDs; a retry does not replace the business identity.

## Persist the job and its dispatch intent together

Write the authorized job and an outbox record in one database transaction. A dispatcher claims eligible outbox records, publishes their stable job identity, and records publication. A crash after publish but before marking publication can produce a duplicate message. The worker must therefore tolerate redelivery.

A commit callback can avoid dispatching before a transaction commits, but a process can still die before the callback successfully publishes. It is not a durable replacement for recorded dispatch intent and recovery scanning.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
 Command[Authorized command or bounded scheduled trigger] --> Tx[Database transaction]
 Tx --> Job[Persist tenant-scoped job]
 Tx --> Outbox[Persist dispatch intent]
 Outbox --> Dispatcher[Claim and publish stable job ID]
 Dispatcher --> Queue[Queue may redeliver]
 Queue --> Worker[Validate scope and claim attempt]
 Worker --> Effect[Idempotent or reconciled side effect]
 Effect --> Result[Persist progress and terminal result]
 Result --> Watch[Monitor missed success and retry exhaustion]
 Watch -->|Recover same identity| Outbox
```

This is a proposed design for the separate application. The handbook does not run an outbox, queue, worker, or scheduler.

## Define the worker contract

| Field or policy | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Tenant and authorized initiating actor/service | Reconstruct permitted scope without trusting message text |
| Business job identity | Converge duplicates and recover the same operation |
| State and durable step progress | Distinguish queued, running, succeeded, retryable, and terminal failure |
| Attempt/lease token and expiry | Allow recovery while rejecting stale workers' state updates |
| Input version and artifact identity | Avoid silently producing a different export under one identity |
| Attempt limit, timeout, and next eligible time | Bound retry behavior and resource consumption |
| Correlation ID and last-success time | Connect logs to a durable outcome |

Claim a job transactionally. On completion, update it only if the attempt still owns the lease. An expired worker must not overwrite a newer attempt's result. This fencing protects database updates; an external email or upload needs its own deduplication/reconciliation policy.

## Acknowledge the crash windows

Celery documents retry behavior and acknowledgment options, including late acknowledgment for tasks designed to tolerate repeated execution. These settings do not provide exactly-once external effects. Verify worker-loss behavior in the installed version and configuration. [Celery task documentation](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/stable/userguide/tasks.html).

| Crash point | Expected recovery |
| --- | --- |
| Job committed, not yet published | Dispatcher finds pending intent |
| Published, intent not marked | Worker handles duplicate stable job ID |
| Worker claims and stops before processing | Expired lease becomes eligible under policy |
| External provider succeeds, local result missing | Reconcile provider identity/outcome before repeating effect |
| Old worker resumes after a new claim | Stale completion rejected by attempt token |
| Retry limit exhausted | Terminal failure with an owner and recovery action |

A database unique constraint prevents duplicate rows for that constrained identity. It does not make an email and a PostgreSQL commit atomic. Use provider idempotency where available, and explicitly handle outcomes that cannot be proven.

## Detect missed schedules

Heroku Scheduler describes its execution as best-effort. A durable last-success threshold and missing-period scan can reveal work that never completed even if the schedule configuration exists. [Heroku Scheduler](https://devcenter.heroku.com/articles/scheduler).

Define the business timezone, period boundaries, and daylight-saving behavior. Store timestamps consistently, and decide which business period a delayed run belongs to. Bound catch-up by eligible periods and batch size. Two triggers for the same tenant/period should converge; a late trigger must not create another completed run.

## A Foundry verification brief

```text
Outcome: Tenant-scoped export jobs recover without duplicate durable artifacts.

Evidence required:
- Two simultaneous triggers for one business identity converge.
- Broker outage leaves dispatch intent recoverable.
- Worker crash and expired lease resume the same operation.
- Stale attempt cannot mark a newer attempt complete.
- External success/local uncertainty is reconciled before repetition.
- Foreign-tenant artifact and job IDs are denied.
- Missed-success alert and bounded backfill are exercised.

Release evidence: actual worker, dispatcher, scheduler, and monitor configuration.
```

Run the [job decision drills](/lab/resilience), then implement and execute these cases in the owning application. Keep exported exercise notes separate from queue and database test results.

title: Recovery drill: database, files, and measured downtime
summary: Prove an application can recover by restoring in isolation and checking its complete data boundary.
body:
## Define success before restoring

A backup artifact is an input to recovery, not its result. This proposed runbook uses a disposable environment with synthetic fixtures. It does not change your Heroku databases, S3 objects, schedules, or accounts.

State the incident, selected recovery point, acceptable missing data, and what must work before the exercise closes. Include database relationships, private files, tenant-scoped reads, and the application's ability to serve those records.

## Record a complete inventory

| Recovery dependency | Record before the drill |
| --- | --- |
| PostgreSQL | Product/attachment, recovery mechanism, snapshot recovery point, schema revision |
| Private artifacts | Bucket/key conventions, retained object versions, encryption/access dependencies |
| Application | Compatible code/configuration, required migrations, isolated credentials |
| External effects | Email, payment, webhooks, workers, and scheduler disabled or isolated |
| Identity | Synthetic sign-in method and active/revoked membership fixtures |
| Evidence | Operator, timings, assertions, missing records/files, and cleanup ownership |

Heroku PGBackups documents backup inspection and restores. Restoration writes into its target database; verify the target deliberately and use an isolated target for an exercise. Availability, retention, and recovery mechanisms depend on the actual database offering. [Heroku PGBackups](https://devcenter.heroku.com/articles/heroku-postgres-backups).

## Run in isolation

```mermaid
flowchart TB
 Inventory[Inventory recovery point and dependencies] --> Target[Provision isolated database and artifact access]
 Target --> Guard[Disable outgoing effects and recurring work]
 Guard --> Restore[Restore selected backup]
 Restore --> Schema[Check compatible schema and application revision]
 Schema --> Data[Verify relationships and deterministic fixture facts]
 Data --> Files[Check referenced private objects and versions]
 Files --> Scope[Exercise tenant-scoped application reads]
 Scope --> Measure[Record recovery point gap and total readiness time]
 Measure --> Close[Review gaps and clean up isolated environment]
```

Do not attach recovered rows to a live worker that can resend historical notifications. Restored application configuration needs deliberate isolation even if the database itself is disposable.

## Verify more than row counts

Compare schema and migration state, then inspect canonical fixture relationships: North's report belongs to North, its creator and membership are coherent, and South cannot retrieve it. Check deterministic values from the restored records. A matching count can conceal wrong relationships or missing data.

Resolve a representative set of private file references. Verify content/integrity, object versions where applicable, encryption-key access, and the authorized delivery path. A database snapshot does not include S3 object bytes. Restoring an older row may reference an object subsequently deleted or overwritten unless your retention/version policy covers that interval.

Test a missing object explicitly. The application should return a controlled unavailable result and retain an actionable record, rather than exposing another tenant's object or presenting a broken download as healthy.

## Measure recovery point and readiness separately

Use the following authored example to distinguish the measurements:

| Timestamp | Synthetic event |
| --- | --- |
| 02:00 | Selected backup's established recovery point |
| 08:20 | Service interruption begins |
| 08:25 | Isolated restoration begins |
| 08:55 | Database restoration finishes |
| 09:10 | Application, tenant, and file checks finish |

The gap between recovery point and interruption is 6 hours 20 minutes. That is the possible unrecovered window in this fixture, not proof that every change in that window is lost. Restoration plus verification takes 45 minutes from the start of the restore exercise. Incident-to-readiness takes 50 minutes and is the broader downtime measurement.

Do not use backup completion time as a recovery point unless the mechanism establishes that equivalence. Desired RPO/RTO targets and observed drill results belong in separate fields. Record what was actually recovered and what remains missing.

## Write the recovery evidence

```text
Exercise: synthetic database + private-file restoration
Target: isolated environment; outgoing effects disabled
Code/schema revision: <record>
Backup identifier and established recovery point: <record>
Incident / restore-start / restore-end / ready timestamps: <record>

Checks:
- Schema and application compatibility
- Canonical fixture relationships and deterministic facts
- North readable; South foreign-ID denied
- Representative artifact versions and integrity
- Missing-object handling

Gaps and measured data window: <record>
Observed readiness time versus target: <record>
Cleanup owner and completion: <record>
```

Bring the completed evidence to a Foundry review in the real application. The [restore decision drill](/lab/resilience) only practices the decision; it does not restore or verify a backup.

title: AI evaluations: scope, evidence, and graceful failure
summary: Test authorization independently of prompts and preserve deterministic facts when a provider fails.
body:
## Define the provider's allowed contribution

The Reports slice can later add optional narrative presentation. Scoped selectors still own the facts. The provider may explain allowed facts, not invent totals, choose another tenant, or turn a read-only action into a write.

This proposed evaluation plan is provider-neutral. It does not call an AI service, configure a model, or claim a production evaluation score. The [interactive AI drills](/lab/resilience) exercise decisions using authored fixtures.

## Build a small evaluation set

Use synthetic fixtures with an expected scope and deterministic result. Store fixture/version identity with the evaluation so a model or prompt change can be compared against the same inputs.

| Case | Fixture | Required outcome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Supported report | Permitted North report with known facts | Explanation preserves facts and source identity |
| Ambiguous period | Two possible periods; none selected | Clarification rather than a silently chosen scope |
| Foreign entity | South report ID in a North request | Denial before retrieving foreign facts |
| Document injection | Retrieved text requests broader tools/scope | Instruction treated as untrusted content; authority unchanged |
| Invalid provider output | Wrong shape, unknown source ID, invented value | Reject presentation or use explicit deterministic fallback |
| Timeout or rate limit | Facts available, provider unavailable | Bounded policy and clearly marked narrative failure |
| Budget exhaustion | Request exceeds configured usage budget | Deny/degrade according to policy without unbounded calls |

A valid JSON shape does not prove the narrative is truthful. Validate references and permitted structured values, and evaluate prose faithfulness where free-form explanation is allowed. If the product needs strong factual guarantees, render important facts directly from trusted structured fields.

## Keep authority outside the prompt

OWASP describes direct and indirect prompt injection, including malicious instructions in retrieved documents, and recommends layered controls around model inputs and tool use. Prompt wording alone is not an authorization boundary. [OWASP prompt injection guidance](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/LLM_Prompt_Injection_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html).

```mermaid
flowchart TB
 Input[User text and untrusted document content] --> Gates[Authenticate and resolve authorized scope]
 Gates --> Tool[Allowlisted read-only tool]
 Tool --> Facts[Scoped deterministic facts with source IDs]
 Facts --> Budget[Time, usage, and context budget]
 Budget --> Provider[Optional provider presentation]
 Provider --> Validate[Validate shape, references, and permitted facts]
 Validate -->|Accepted| Answer[Facts plus accepted narrative]
 Validate -->|Rejected| Fallback[Facts plus explicit narrative-unavailable state]
 Provider -->|Timeout or failure| Fallback
```

A tool executor must rebuild server-owned scope rather than accepting an organization supplied by generated text. Constrain arguments, validate entities through scoped selectors, and keep mutation tools absent from a read-only workflow. Treat uploaded text and provider output as data even when they look like instructions.

## Make a provider outage a presentation outcome

If narrative is optional, show the trusted facts and a specific narrative-unavailable state. If narrative is essential to the requested action, return an explicit unavailable outcome. Neither case permits guessed facts.

Set total latency, attempt, and usage budgets before calling the provider. Make retry eligibility explicit for timeout, rate limit, invalid output, and deterministic policy denial; they are not interchangeable. Keep retry attempts tied to one request/correlation identity and avoid double-counting usage under duplicate requests.

## Capture evaluation evidence precisely

```json
{
  "caseId": "north-report-provider-timeout",
  "fixtureVersion": "synthetic-v1",
  "scope": "north",
  "expected": {
    "factsUnchanged": true,
    "foreignReads": 0,
    "writeToolCalls": 0,
    "narrativeState": "unavailable"
  },
  "observed": null,
  "verification": "not-executed"
}
```

This is an authored test contract, not recorded execution. Real evidence adds the application revision, prompt/template version, provider/model version if used, observed tool calls, output checks, duration, attempts, usage, and result. Redact sensitive inputs and use approved synthetic evaluation data.

Report deterministic tool coverage separately from provider quality. A test that never calls a provider can prove a scope predicate, but cannot measure that provider's latency or narrative faithfulness. An output judge should not be the sole evidence for authorization.

## Put the evaluation in the Foundry task

Require foreign-scope denial, no write tools, accepted structured references, timeout fallback, and bounded usage evidence before accepting the extension. Review changed prompts and model/provider versions as application changes with test evidence. Keep an explicit rollback path to deterministic presentation if optional narrative regresses.

Continue from [AI grounded in structured truth](/guide/deterministic-ai), use the [decision lab](/lab/resilience), and collect real execution evidence in the owning application.

title: 01 · Create and open your GitHub repository
summary: Start with a real GitHub repo and a normal local clone before installing governance.
body:
## What you will build

This tutorial starts from zero and follows one small repository through Foundry setup, a documentation task, review, release planning, and recovery. It teaches the native `.foundry/` layout. Foundry's own source repository also contains older `.claude/state/` governance; that is not the layout to copy into your application.

The running project is `foundry-demo`, with task prefix `DEMO`, main branch `main`, and owner handle `human:learner`. Replace `YOUR_GITHUB_USER` with your GitHub username. Run one numbered step at a time and inspect the checkpoint before continuing.

| Place | What belongs there |
| --- | --- |
| Your terminal | Git, installation, configuration, and your personal signing/approval commands |
| Your agent chat | The brief that tells Claude or Codex what role and task to work on |
| GitHub website | Repository visibility, pull request review, Actions access, and branch protection |

Commands in this tutorial are instructions for your own setup. Publishing the handbook did not create this demo repository or register an owner. Local initialization was separately smoke-checked in an isolated synthetic Git repository.

## Step 1 — Check your tools

**Your terminal · any directory**

```bash
git --version
gh --version
uv --version
```

Use Git 2.38 or newer for the release trial-merge path, Python 3.12 or newer for Foundry, and an OpenSSH installation with signing support. `uv` can provision the Python environment. On macOS, if you already use Homebrew, an owner-run installation is `brew install git gh uv`. On other systems, use the official installers for your platform.

You also need access to the Foundry source repository or an authorized local checkout. The inspected source is private/proprietary and not a public PyPI distribution. A public application repo does not make Foundry itself publicly installable.

## Step 2 — Sign in to GitHub

**Your terminal · any directory**

```bash
gh auth login
gh auth status
```

Follow the browser login flow and confirm the expected account. If Git commits are not configured yet, set your identity deliberately; use a GitHub-provided no-reply address if that is your preference. Your Git identity is separate from Foundry's signed owner identity.

## Step 3 — Create and clone the demo

**Your terminal · parent folder for projects**

```bash
mkdir -p ~/Projects
cd ~/Projects
gh repo create YOUR_GITHUB_USER/foundry-demo --public --add-readme --clone
cd foundry-demo
```

The command creates a real public repository and clones it. `--add-readme` establishes an initial commit; `--clone` gives you a normal checkout. Choose a new name if `foundry-demo` already exists. Use `--private` instead if you want a private demo. [GitHub CLI repository creation](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_repo_create).

For the website route, click **New repository**, choose the owner/name and visibility, add a README, and create it. Then copy its clone URL from **Code** and run `git clone <that URL>` in `~/Projects`. Both routes should end in a normal clone containing a real commit.

## Step 4 — Establish the tutorial's main branch

**Your terminal · `~/Projects/foundry-demo`**

```bash
git branch --show-current
git log -1 --oneline
git remote -v
git worktree list
```

Expected: a branch with the README commit, the intended GitHub `origin`, and one checkout. If the new demo's branch is already `main`, continue. If the fresh demo uses another default, normalize it before adoption:

```bash
git branch -M main
git push -u origin main
gh repo edit --default-branch main
git remote set-head origin -a
```

Those normalization commands are for this fresh demo. In an existing application, preserve its branch convention and pass that name to Foundry instead.

## Step 5 — Open the project

Open `~/Projects/foundry-demo` as a folder in your editor. If the VS Code shell command is installed, `code .` opens the current folder; otherwise use **File → Open Folder**. Open the integrated terminal and run `pwd` to confirm the same project root.

Your application checkout and the Foundry tool checkout are separate folders:

```text
~/Tools/foundry/               the tool's source
~/Projects/foundry-demo/       the application Foundry will govern
```

## Checkpoint

The demo exists on GitHub, its intended main branch is pushed, and the editor terminal is in a normal clone with a README commit. Continue to [install Foundry](/guide/foundry-installation).

title: 02 · Install the Foundry tool
summary: Install from an authorized checkout, expose the CLI, and check provider support separately.
body:
## Step 1 — Obtain the tool source

**Your terminal · tool parent directory**

```bash
mkdir -p ~/Tools
cd ~/Tools
git clone https://github.com/anthonynarine/foundry.git
cd foundry
git rev-parse HEAD
```

The repository requires authorized access. If GitHub returns a permission or repository-not-found error, resolve access under the correct account. Do not substitute an unrelated package named Foundry.

If you already have the authorized checkout at `/path/to/authorized/foundry`, use that path instead of cloning another copy. Record its commit alongside your tutorial notes. Do not discard local changes to update it.

## Step 2 — Install as a tool

**Your terminal · any directory, authorized checkout available**

```bash
uv tool install --python 3.12 ~/Tools/foundry
uv tool update-shell
```

Open a new terminal if shell-path changes are required. Then check:

```bash
foundry --version
foundry --help
foundry init --help
```

For the existing local checkout, the install command is `uv tool install --python 3.12 /path/to/authorized/foundry` instead. Choose one checkout as your tool source.

Foundry is a Python CLI; this setup needs installation rather than a separate frontend compilation step. `uv tool install` installs a CLI into its own tool environment. It does not add Foundry to the application's frontend dependencies. [uv tool installation](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/guides/tools/).

The inspected development CLI reported `0.2.0.dev0`; that label does not uniquely identify the source revision. Check your installed help before using an option that may differ by version.

## Step 3 — Understand the development alternative

**Your terminal · Foundry tool checkout**

```bash
cd ~/Tools/foundry
uv sync
uv run foundry --version
```

This runs in Foundry's development environment. Installing the tool is the simpler way to call `foundry` from other repositories. On Anthony's machine the existing development executable is `/path/to/authorized/foundry/.venv/bin/foundry`; using an absolute executable path does not change which project your current directory selects.

After deliberately updating the source, reinstall the tool with `uv tool install --reinstall --python 3.12 ~/Tools/foundry`. A source pull alone does not necessarily update the installed tool environment.

## Step 4 — Check the agent you will use

**Your terminal · any directory**

```bash
foundry provider list --json
```

| Inspected provider | Registered support | What still needs checking |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Claude | Supervised model adapter and observation parser | CLI installation, login, compatibility, readiness |
| Codex | Observation parser; no supervised model adapter in this inspected build | Interactive CLI installation/login; observation does not launch it |
| Process | Generic command supervision | Not a model-session adapter |

You can use an interactive Codex session to follow repository instructions. Do not change the provider name in YAML and assume a missing supervised adapter now exists. The provider registry reports support without probing your executables or credentials.

This tutorial uses manually opened agent sessions. A worktree separates checkouts; container enforcement is a separate runtime setup with its own verification.

## Step 5 — Return to the application

**Your terminal · application checkout**

```bash
cd ~/Projects/foundry-demo
pwd
foundry init --help
```

The tool is installed; the demo is not initialized yet. Keep those two checkpoints separate.

## Checkpoint

`foundry --version` and `foundry init --help` work from the demo folder, and you understand the selected agent's actual support. Continue to [initialize the project](/guide/foundry-initialization).

title: 03 · Initialize the project and inspect the result
summary: Run init in the right checkout, attach a plan, and review configuration before adoption.
body:
## Step 1 — Prepare an adoption branch

**Your terminal · `~/Projects/foundry-demo`**

```bash
git status --short
git worktree list
git switch -c foundry/adopt
```

Start with the new demo's clean normal clone. When adopting an existing busy application, use a separate normal clone for this branch. In the inspected implementation, `init` resolves a linked worktree to its main checkout; do not run adoption from a specialist worktree and expect it to stay there.

## Step 2 — Write a small plan

Create `docs/build-plan.md` in the demo. Use a normal UTF-8 Markdown file:

```markdown
# Foundry demo plan

Outcome: a new collaborator can orient themselves in this repository.

First task: add docs/project-orientation.md with purpose, layout,
verification steps, and the next learning task.

Acceptance: documentation matches the actual repository; no secrets,
application behavior, or governance permissions are changed.
```

The plan guides the conversation. Recording its path does not automatically turn every paragraph into tasks or confer authority.

## Step 3 — Initialize once, with explicit choices

**Your terminal · demo adoption branch**

```bash
foundry init --name foundry-demo --prefix DEMO --main main \
  --build-plan docs/build-plan.md --agent-instructions
```

Expected: `.foundry/` configuration and policy directories, ignore rules, a `foundry/state` branch, and a local `.foundry/state/` worktree. With `--agent-instructions`, the managed Foundry section is installed into `AGENTS.md` and its diff is shown. Instructions take effect immediately; review them before launching an agent.

Default init leaves `AGENTS.md` unchanged. The plan option records bounded advisory metadata in `.foundry/project/build-plan.yaml`; it does not import or execute the plan's content. The inspected implementation accepts a bounded, plain repository-relative file and rejects protected/linked paths.

## Step 4 — Inspect the two kinds of state

| Path or branch | Keep it where? | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `.foundry/foundry.yaml` | Application Git history | Project identity, main/state branches, provider/runtime settings |
| `.foundry/project/` | Application Git history | Component map, architecture and advisory plan reference |
| `.foundry/policy/` and project roles | Application Git history | Reviewed authority and evidence configuration |
| `AGENTS.md` | Application Git history | Explicitly adopted agent instructions |
| `foundry/state` branch | Separate control-plane history | Task, session, artifact and event records |
| `.foundry/state/`, `.foundry/work/`, `.worktrees/` | Locally ignored directories | State checkout and workspaces |

**Your terminal · demo adoption branch**

```bash
git status --short
git worktree list
rg 'main_branch|task_prefix|sessions' .foundry/foundry.yaml
foundry boot --json
foundry status
foundry validate
```

If `rg` is unavailable, open the YAML in your editor. Confirm `main_branch: main` and `task_prefix: DEMO`. `init` preserves existing configuration: rerunning with a new `--main` does not overwrite an existing YAML value. Correct a wrong value deliberately before committing.

## Step 5 — Describe ownership and secrets

For this documentation-only demo, a component entry can be:

```yaml
# .foundry/project/components.yaml — Describe the demo's actual documentation.
components:
  - id: documentation
    kind: docs
    description: Repository orientation and learning notes
    paths: ["docs/**", "README.md"]
    owner_role: documentation
```

Replace the architecture placeholder with a short description of the actual README/docs repository. Do not invent frontend/backend services that do not exist. When adopting a real React/Django project, map its actual paths and commands here instead.

Inspect classification without reading file contents:

```bash
foundry secrets policy
foundry secrets check .env.example docs/build-plan.md
foundry agent list
```

Foundry treats `.env.*` templates as protected too. Document setting names in an ordinary configuration guide rather than placing real values in the plan. Add project-specific secret/sensitive path patterns before first owner adoption.

For the session-based path in this tutorial, set `sessions: required` in `.foundry/foundry.yaml` before first adoption. This is an authority configuration choice. The later human-owned bootstrap creates the first task/session; agents then use their own session files.

## Step 6 — Review and merge the bootstrap

**Your terminal · demo adoption branch**

```bash
git add .foundry .gitignore AGENTS.md docs/build-plan.md
git diff --cached --stat
git diff --cached
git commit -m "Adopt Foundry in the demo"
git push -u origin foundry/adopt
gh pr create --base main --head foundry/adopt \
  --title "Adopt Foundry" --body "Initialize native configuration, project instructions, and the demo plan."
```

Review the actual diff on GitHub. `.foundry/state/` must not be staged. Include `node_modules/` in the application's `.gitignore` when using Node dependencies; that rule is separate from Foundry's generated workspace ignores.

This initial adoption is a reviewed bootstrap PR: there is no established owner trust or evidence workflow yet. After you approve and merge it, update your local checkout:

```bash
git switch main
git pull --ff-only origin main
foundry recover
```

Use `foundry recover --apply` only when its report calls for attaching or recording missing local state. In the same normal clone, the existing state worktree may already be attached.

## Checkpoint

The reviewed native configuration is on `main`; the main branch, plan reference, instructions, ownership and session choice are correct. Local init/re-init/boot/validate/status/recover were smoke-checked for this handbook. GitHub bootstrap and signed owner adoption were not performed. Continue to [register the owner](/guide/foundry-human-authority).

title: 04 · Register yourself as the owner
summary: Create a dedicated signing identity, adopt policy, and commit the public trust configuration.
body:
## Step 1 — Prepare a dedicated signing key

**Your own terminal · any directory**

```bash
mkdir -p ~/.ssh
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f ~/.ssh/foundry_signing -C "Foundry signing"
```

Use a passphrase. If this path already holds a key, do not overwrite it; review/reuse the intended key or choose a different dedicated filename. The private file stays outside repositories and agent workspaces. The `.pub` file is the public identity that the project will trust.

Optional agent-based signing is `ssh-add -c ~/.ssh/foundry_signing`, with the confirmation behavior tested on your platform. Human signing should remain in your own terminal.

## Step 2 — Create or review your identity file

Open `~/.config/foundry/identity.toml` in your editor, creating its parent directory if needed. For a first setup:

```toml
# ~/.config/foundry/identity.toml — Local human identity, outside every repository.
principal = "human:learner"
key = "~/.ssh/foundry_signing"
```

If a file already exists, review it instead of replacing it blindly. Use one consistent handle across this file, principal registration, and the trusted signers entry. The identity file names you; a verified signature and adopted project trust establish authority.

## Step 3 — Become the demo's first owner

**Your own terminal · `~/Projects/foundry-demo`, reviewed adoption on `main`**

```bash
foundry principal init --handle human:learner \
  --key ~/.ssh/foundry_signing.pub --name "Tutorial Owner"
```

Read the policy adoption statement and files shown. Approve only your intended policy, then sign with your key. Expected: first owner registered and policy sequence 1 adopted. This is the initial trust decision; the tutorial does not run it for you.

If the project already has principals, an existing owner adds you through the existing principal workflow. Do not treat “already initialized” as a reason to replace trust files.

```bash
foundry whoami
foundry policy status
```

Expected: the correct handle, owner role, public-key fingerprint, and adopted policy. The command creates `.foundry/policy/principals.yaml` containing public trust material. That exact adopted policy must reach the target branch before governed releases.

## Step 4 — Prepare public trust files

Create a trust branch. The following snippet uses only the public key file to construct the evidence signers entry:

```bash
git switch -c foundry/trust
python3 - <<'PYCODE'
from pathlib import Path
key = (Path.home() / ".ssh/foundry_signing.pub").read_text().split()
Path(".foundry/allowed_signers").write_text(
    'human:learner namespaces="foundry-evidence" ' + ' '.join(key[:2]) + '\n'
)
PYCODE
```

Create `.github/CODEOWNERS` with your actual GitHub username:

```text
/.github/                   @YOUR_GITHUB_USER
/.foundry/allowed_signers   @YOUR_GITHUB_USER
/.foundry/policy/           @YOUR_GITHUB_USER
/.foundry/roles/            @YOUR_GITHUB_USER
/.foundry/foundry.yaml      @YOUR_GITHUB_USER
/AGENTS.md                  @YOUR_GITHUB_USER
```

Code Owners defines reviewers; it becomes a required review control only when the applicable GitHub protection settings require it.

## Step 5 — Inspect interactive-agent secret settings

**Your terminal · demo trust branch**

```bash
foundry secrets settings
```

Review the proposed settings changes. To write them for an interactive Codex project, use `foundry secrets settings --agent codex --write`; for Claude use `--agent claude --write`. Choose the agents you actually use. These tool-specific rules have their own enforcement limits and do not turn a manually opened session into a container sandbox.

## Step 6 — Commit, review, and merge trust

Stage only the files you actually created, including the selected agent's settings file if written:

```bash
git add .foundry/policy/principals.yaml .foundry/allowed_signers .github/CODEOWNERS
# If written: git add .codex/config.toml
# If written: git add .claude/settings.json
git diff --cached
git commit -m "Register Foundry owner and release trust"
git push -u origin foundry/trust
gh pr create --base main --head foundry/trust \
  --title "Register Foundry trust" --body "Commit the first owner, evidence signer, and Code Owners configuration."
```

Review and merge this second bootstrap PR, then return to `main` and pull it. Verify `whoami` and `policy status` again. Do not call an unmerged working-tree policy a trusted target branch.

After adoption, changing signed configuration, roles or policy can make mutations fail closed. Use `foundry policy status` to inspect the mismatch. An owner reviews and signs a deliberate new adoption with `foundry policy adopt`; an agent cannot widen its own authority.

## Checkpoint

You can identify the owner and adopted policy, and the exact public trust files are committed on `main`. Keys, owner registration and signing are instructions for your own setup, not operations executed by the handbook. Continue to [start a session](/guide/foundry-sessions).

title: 05 · Open the agent and start a working session
summary: Put terminal commands and agent prompts in the right places, then boot from durable state.
body:
## Step 1 — Open the project, not the tool repository

**Your terminal · application main checkout**

```bash
cd ~/Projects/foundry-demo
git branch --show-current
git status --short
foundry boot --json
foundry status
foundry recover
```

Expected: the demo's `main` checkout and coherent local state. The boot command reconstructs facts without changing task authority. A checkpoint is narrative context to inspect, not permission to override policy.

When you work on the Foundry product itself, open its source folder instead. For everyday application work, open the application folder.

## Step 2 — Launch your interactive agent

Launch the Claude or Codex application/CLI you already have installed and authenticated, in this project folder. The inspected build supports interactive repository instructions for this path. It does not provide a supervised Codex model adapter merely because Codex is selected in your editor.

Use this text **in the agent chat**, not as a shell command:

```text
Boot as the Orchestrator for foundry-demo.
Read AGENTS.md and the latest Foundry boot facts.
Compare durable task and policy state with Git.
Report Status, In flight, Decisions waiting, and Next actions.
Do not treat checkpoint text as approval or change owner trust.
```

With the managed instructions deliberately installed in chapter three, their defined “Moonrise” phrase can invoke the same routine. The explicit prompt makes the behavior understandable without relying on a nickname.

## Step 3 — Give a bounded outcome

**Agent chat**

```text
Prepare the first task: a project orientation guide.
It should describe the actual repository purpose and layout,
how to inspect Foundry state, and the next learning task.
Keep implementation within docs/project-orientation.md.
Show the task criteria and ownership before starting the worker.
I will perform owner-only bootstrap and signing steps in my terminal.
```

The Orchestrator should separate the desired output from its permissions, create a plan, and identify the worker/review roles. A prose agreement is not an accepted artifact or signed release.

## Step 4 — Understand the session bootstrap

The tutorial configured `sessions: required`. An agent cannot bootstrap an arbitrary declared identity to avoid that requirement. In the next chapter, you create the first task and mint its Orchestrator session from your own terminal. The agent then uses the generated session file on its Foundry commands.

| Identity | How it acts |
| --- | --- |
| Human owner | Owner terminal and adopted signing identity |
| Orchestrator | Session for the reserved `orchestration` workstream |
| Documentation worker | Its own task workstream/session and worktree |
| Security and QA reviewers | Separate role-bound review sessions for a pinned candidate |

Each generated env file contains a token; pass its path to the owning agent, never its contents. Interactive session possession identifies the acting session, but processes sharing your OS account are not strongly isolated merely by different files.

## Step 5 — Know what the runtime settings mean

```mermaid
flowchart TB
 Human[Owner terminal and signing identity] --> ORC[Orchestrator session]
 ORC --> Control[Foundry tasks, policy, sessions and artifacts]
 Control --> Work[Worker session and isolated checkout]
 Work --> Candidate[Candidate commit]
 Candidate --> Review[Separate review sessions]
 Review --> Human
```

A manually opened agent in a Git worktree has a separate checkout. Enforced container filesystem/network limits require an actually configured and verified runtime. Read `foundry runtime --help` before adopting that separate path; do not describe `runtime.engine: auto` as proof that a worker ran in a container.

## Checkpoint

The Orchestrator can report real project facts and a bounded first task, and you know how its session will be bootstrapped. Continue to [run the first task](/guide/foundry-first-task).

title: 06 · Create the first task and hand it to a worker
summary: Turn the orientation brief into a scoped task, sessions, a worktree, and a submitted artifact.
body:
## Step 1 — Bootstrap the task as the owner

**Your own terminal · demo main checkout**

```bash
foundry task create --title "Write project orientation" \
  --goal "A new collaborator can understand this repository and its Foundry workflow." \
  -c "docs/project-orientation.md describes the actual purpose and layout" \
  -c "The guide includes read-only state inspection commands and the next task" \
  -c "No secrets, product behavior, or governance permissions are changed"
```

Expected: a task in `DRAFT`. In a fresh demo it should be `DEMO-1`; use the ID actually printed if other tasks exist. The owner terminal is important for this initial step when agent sessions are required.

## Step 2 — Mint the Orchestrator session

**Your own terminal · demo main checkout**

```bash
foundry session start DEMO-1 orchestration --env-file auto
```

Expected: a session identifier, expiry, and the path of a newly created env file outside Git repositories. Give that path to the Orchestrator in its chat. Do not print/read the file into the conversation.

The following commands show a placeholder path. Replace it with the printed path. In the Orchestrator's shell, use the session file for each command; do not borrow another role's file.

## Step 3 — Assign the documentation workstream

**Orchestrator terminal · main checkout, its own session**

```bash
foundry --session-file /path/to/orchestrator.env workstream add DEMO-1 guide \
  --role documentation --goal "Write the project orientation guide" \
  --owns docs/project-orientation.md
foundry --session-file /path/to/orchestrator.env task transition DEMO-1 PLANNING
foundry --session-file /path/to/orchestrator.env task transition DEMO-1 READY
foundry task show DEMO-1
```

Expected: criteria, the assigned role, bounded owned path, and a ready task. Inspect the built-in documentation role with `foundry agent list`; native roles are not imported by blindly copying Foundry's legacy `.claude/` files.

## Step 4 — Create the worker checkout and identity

**Orchestrator terminal · main checkout**

```bash
git worktree add .worktrees/documentation/demo-1-guide \
  -b agent/documentation/demo-1-guide main
foundry --session-file /path/to/orchestrator.env session start DEMO-1 guide --env-file auto
foundry worktree list
```

Expected: a separate branch/worktree and a new worker env-file path. A hand-created Git worktree contains committed files; it is not automatically the secret-filtered checkout that some Foundry runtime paths create. Keep interactive-agent settings and actual isolation limits in view.

## Step 5 — Launch and brief the worker

Open the worker folder in a separate agent session. Give it this **chat prompt**, substituting the actual worker path and session-file path:

```text
You are the documentation worker for DEMO-1, workstream guide.
Work in ~/Projects/foundry-demo/.worktrees/documentation/demo-1-guide.
Use your own generated session file for every Foundry mutation.
Never print it or use the Orchestrator's session file.

Read the task, project instructions, actual repository, and relevant role.
Write only docs/project-orientation.md within the assigned owns path.
Verify the facts and commands, commit on your agent branch, and submit
an attributable commit artifact. Report gaps without widening scope.
```

The worker writes the real guide and verifies it against the repository. Do not ask it to run Foundry's own `tests/test_docs.py` in this application; that file belongs to the tool repository, not the demo.

## Step 6 — Submit the implementation

**Worker terminal · worker checkout, worker session**

```bash
git diff --check
git add docs/project-orientation.md
git commit -m "Document the demo project orientation"
foundry --session-file /path/to/worker.env artifact add DEMO-1 commit:orientation \
  --commit "$(git rev-parse HEAD)" --workstream guide \
  --summary "Project orientation checked against the repository"
```

Expected: an artifact ID and `SUBMITTED`. A submission satisfies nothing until another permitted actor accepts it. A full commit SHA, not a short hash or tree ID, names the candidate.

## Step 7 — Inspect and accept from the Orchestrator

**Orchestrator terminal · main checkout, Orchestrator session**

```bash
git diff main...agent/documentation/demo-1-guide
foundry --session-file /path/to/orchestrator.env integrate check DEMO-1 guide \
  --branch agent/documentation/demo-1-guide
foundry artifact list --task DEMO-1
foundry --session-file /path/to/orchestrator.env artifact accept DEMO-1/art-0001 \
  --reason "Guide checked against criteria and changed paths are within scope"
```

Use the artifact ID actually listed; `art-0001` is an example. Accept only after reviewing the diff and facts. Do not let the producer accept its own output or move `main` by an informal merge.

## Checkpoint

The first task has a scoped worker output, a real commit, and an independently accepted implementation artifact. The handbook verified command help, not this signed task lifecycle. Continue to [review and release](/guide/foundry-review-release).

title: 07 · Review the exact candidate and release it
summary: Pin evidence to real content, distinguish documentation checks from code tests, and sign deliberately.
body:
## Step 1 — Freeze the candidate

**Orchestrator terminal · main checkout**

```bash
git rev-parse agent/documentation/demo-1-guide
git rev-parse 'agent/documentation/demo-1-guide^{tree}'
```

Record both outputs. The commit identifies a point in history; its tree identifies file content. Commands requesting a candidate commit must receive the full commit SHA. Quote the tree expression in zsh.

## Step 2 — Decide what the tier requires

The first task changes `docs/project-orientation.md`, a documentation/records path under the inspected tier rules. Do the actual factual, command and link checks promised in its criteria. Do not claim an application test suite passed when the demo has no application suite.

For a later code task, inspect the current evidence policy and release plan. A code change can require accepted full tests, Security and QA evidence on the candidate. A frontend `npm run build` is build evidence; it is not automatically a governed full-test report.

The inspected `foundry test --help` supports governed .NET/Django paths and a Python release path. It does not offer an interchangeable JavaScript full-suite preset. For a React feature, map the real test commands and evidence contract deliberately; do not fabricate compatible evidence by changing a summary string. Use the [Reports walkthrough](/guide/reports-contract) to define meaningful feature behavior.

## Step 3 — Start role-bound reviewers when required

**Orchestrator terminal · its own session**

```bash
foundry --session-file /path/to/orchestrator.env review start DEMO-1 \
  --role security --candidate FULL_CANDIDATE_COMMIT
foundry --session-file /path/to/orchestrator.env review start DEMO-1 \
  --role testing --candidate FULL_CANDIDATE_COMMIT
```

Use real full commit values. Each command prints the reviewer's brief and session-file path. Follow its worktree instructions; it may print a command for creating the detached review checkout rather than create it automatically. These reviews are optional practice if the docs tier does not require them, but are not optional for a code tier that does.

The reviewer reads the exact candidate, writes its findings or QA result, and submits an artifact from its own role-bound session. The brief supplies the supported command. For example:

```bash
foundry --session-file /path/to/security.env artifact add DEMO-1 security-review:orientation \
  --commit FULL_CANDIDATE_COMMIT --workstream security-review \
  --summary "Actual review result and tracked findings"
```

QA uses a `qa-report` from its testing session. Bind a repository report with `--path` when that report exists so its contents are attributable. Use real review results, not copied PASS text. The Orchestrator inspects and accepts the actual artifact IDs from its own session.

## Step 4 — Keep evidence current

A fix changes the candidate tree. Refresh the tests/reviews required for that changed content. If `main` gained relevant code after the candidate branched, update the candidate, resolve conflicts, and collect applicable new evidence. Do not change the candidate after obtaining approval and describe the old evidence as current.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
 Candidate[Pinned candidate commit and tree] --> Checks[Actual tier-required checks]
 Checks --> Accept[Independent artifact acceptance]
 Accept --> Plan[Foundry release dry run]
 Plan --> Owner[Owner reads and signs exact release]
 Owner --> PR[Release branch and pull request]
 PR --> Gate[Trusted evidence check if configured]
 Gate --> Merge[Reviewed merge into main]
 Merge --> Deploy[Separate application build and deployment]
```

## Step 5 — Read the release plan

**Orchestrator or owner terminal · demo main checkout**

```bash
foundry release --task DEMO-1 \
  --candidate agent/documentation/demo-1-guide --dry-run
```

The plan checks the candidate, tier, adopted target trust, required evidence and integration feasibility. Follow missing-evidence messages. A dry run does not sign approval, publish a branch, or change `main`; the inspected trial merge can write Git objects.

For the public demo, proceed to the GitHub compatibility section in the next chapter before treating any CI check as binding. Local release validation and hosted enforcement are separate checkpoints.

## Step 6 — Approve and sign personally

**Your own interactive terminal · demo main checkout**

```bash
foundry release --task DEMO-1 --candidate agent/documentation/demo-1-guide
```

Read the changed paths, candidate commit/tree, evidence producers and acceptors, and sensitive-path notices. Respond to prompts one at a time. When asked for a tree prefix, use the displayed tree prefix rather than the commit prefix. Signing comes from the owner identity/key prepared earlier.

The normal remote path prepares a signed release branch and pull request. It does not automatically merge the PR or prove an application deploy. Follow the actual output; accept no fabricated approval and use no `--direct` bypass to make a failing governance check disappear.

After publication, review the PR and applicable checks on GitHub. Merge under the project's declared/enforced policy, then pull `main`. Code-tier requirements and GitHub CI compatibility may block this step until their configuration is complete; a prepared tutorial command is not a claim that this release ran.

## Checkpoint

You understand what was actually checked, who accepted it, and what your signature approves. Continue to [GitHub enforcement and recovery](/guide/foundry-github-recovery) to complete the operational setup.

title: 08 · Configure GitHub and recover the next session
summary: Resolve public/private CI compatibility, make checks binding where available, and preserve durable work.
body:
## Step 1 — Choose a compatible evidence delivery path

The tutorial demo is public. The inspected Foundry source/action is private. GitHub's built-in access sharing for a private action is limited to eligible private repositories; changing that access setting does not make the action consumable by the public demo. [GitHub private action sharing](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/reuse-automations/share-across-private-repositories).

| Project choice | What you can do now | What is still separate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Public application with authorized local Foundry | Local tasks, signed trust, candidate/release validation | A publicly consumable trusted verifier/action distribution or reviewed CI integration |
| Eligible private application and private Foundry under compatible ownership | Configure private action access and install the supplied gate template | Applicable GitHub plan/protection and live positive/negative runs |
| Public Foundry distribution | Possible only after its owner authorizes and publishes it | Distribution, licensing, pinned verifier setup, and live validation |

The handbook does not publish the Foundry source or change repository visibility. Do not solve the public/private mismatch by handing untrusted PR code a token for the private tool repo. If the public demo remains on local validation, label its GitHub evidence gate as not configured; do not require a check that cannot run.

## Step 2 — Install the supplied gate for an eligible target

This step applies when the target can actually access the Foundry action.

**Owner terminal · eligible application repo**

```bash
git switch -c foundry/evidence-gate
mkdir -p .github/workflows
cp ~/Tools/foundry/templates/evidence-gate.yml .github/workflows/evidence.yml
git -C ~/Tools/foundry rev-parse HEAD
```

Replace `FOUNDRY_SHA` in the template with a reviewed released full commit SHA that exists in the accessible remote. A local candidate or movable branch name is not the intended trusted pin. Inspect the entire workflow diff and its existing pins before committing it.

The template keeps the verifier and trust roots on the trusted side and treats the PR merge result as data. Do not add a step executing arbitrary PR code in this privileged workflow. Use a separate appropriate application-test workflow for candidate code.

In the private Foundry repo, the owner configures **Settings → Actions → General → Access** for the eligible private target. Commit the gate workflow through a reviewed bootstrap change. Validate an actual legitimate green run and an intentional invalid-evidence red run before calling it proven.

## Step 3 — Make supported checks binding

GitHub documents protected branches for public repositories on free plans and private repositories on applicable paid plans. Check the current plan and protection settings for the actual repository. [GitHub protected branches](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-protected-branches/about-protected-branches).

Require the actual evidence check context, Code Owner review for governance/trust/CI changes where configured, and the chosen up-to-date branch rules. Review bypass actors and direct-push permissions. A workflow that happens to appear green is advisory if a user can still merge/push around it.
