Confirm behavior with a deliberate blocked path. A single-owner project also needs a workable independent review arrangement; configure required reviewers according to the repository's real participants rather than leaving a rule no one can satisfy.

Records/docs still need a route through protected `main`. They do not become exempt because they are small: prepare their branch and the evidence required for their tier. Deployment remains a separate product action; a merged Foundry release does not publish Netlify, Heroku or Vercel by itself.

## Step 4 — Record a checkpoint before leaving

**Agent chat**

```text
Prepare a checkpoint with Status, In flight, Decisions waiting,
and Next actions. Include exact task/branch/candidate references,
actual check results, uncommitted work, and active sessions.
Do not grant approval or change policy through the note.
```

A checkpoint file has four headings:

```markdown
## Status
Record completed work and actual evidence.

## In flight
Record task, workstream, branch, candidate and any active processes.

## Decisions waiting
Record owner decisions without inventing approval.

## Next actions
Record bounded continuation steps under existing authority.
```

For a complete first-task path, the owner prepares `docs/session-checkpoint.md` with those headings in their own checkout, then records it from the owner terminal:

```bash
foundry checkpoint --from docs/session-checkpoint.md --task DEMO-1
```

The documentation worker owns only `docs/project-orientation.md`, so it must not silently create the checkpoint file. The owner path above avoids widening that worker's scope. An agent-recorded checkpoint must use its own existing session and matching workstream, with explicit ownership for any input file it creates. `--commit` is a separate capability/branch choice; default recording does not commit product files or push state.

## Step 5 — End authorized sessions

Inspect `foundry session list` and actual worktree status. End a finished worker through its session or the Orchestrator:

```bash
foundry --session-file /path/to/orchestrator.env session end SESSION_ID --remove-env
```

Use the actual session ID. End the Orchestrator last. Do not stop another process merely because a prose note says to; verify ownership and that work is safely handed off first.

## Step 6 — Return after a crash

**Your terminal · application checkout**

```bash
git status --short
git worktree list
foundry boot --json
foundry status
foundry recover
foundry validate
```

Inspect before applying recovery. `foundry recover --apply` is the deliberate mutation path when missing attachments or lost state need recording. Preserve unknown uncommitted work, inspect its branch/handoff, and mint a new session rather than reusing an expired token.

The local `foundry/state` branch and unpushed worker branches do not magically travel with a fresh clone. Establish an approved backup/push policy for that control-plane history and worker work. A clone can recreate local attachments; it cannot reconstruct records that existed only on a lost disk. Never put session-token files or private keys into that backup branch.

## Final checkpoint

Record each setup stage as completed, blocked, or still unverified: GitHub repo, tool installation, native init, owner trust, sessions, task/artifact path, required evidence, compatible CI/protection, and recovery storage. Local init is verified by this handbook's smoke check; owner signing, GitHub gate, and governed task/release execution require your actual setup evidence.

Return to [the first chapter](/guide/foundry-repository) or apply the workflow to the [Reports feature](/guide/reports-contract).

title: Gaming platform: system design
summary: A five-game platform with shared social features, authoritative multiplayer state, poker tournaments, and a separate AI assistant.
body:
## More than a game board

This repository has grown into a gaming platform: Tic-Tac-Toe, Connect Four, Checkers, Sudoku, and Poker share an account and social experience. React presents the interface; Django owns persisted domain state; Channels carries live commands and updates. Redis supports channel delivery and ephemeral coordination. Poker adds table-specific rules and a multi-table tournament domain.

The architecture below summarizes the inspected source. It is a source review, not a production audit or a new backend test run.

## Platform architecture

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  GamingPlatform[Gaming platform browser] --> Rest[DRF HTTP endpoints]
  GamingPlatform --> Socket[Channels WebSocket consumers]
  Rest --> Domains[Accounts games invites chat tournaments]
  Socket --> Domains
  Domains --> Database[Relational database]
  Socket <--> Redis[Redis channel layer and coordination]
  Rest --> Assistant[Trinity retrieval assistant]
  Assistant --> Retrieval[FAISS retrieval and model provider]
```

**Text alternative:** The React browser uses HTTP for API operations and WebSockets for real-time interactions. Both enter a Django application with game and social domains backed by a relational database. Channels uses Redis for delivery and coordination. Trinity has a separate retrieval/model path.

## Ownership map

| Area | Responsibility | Boundary |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Browser | Routes, boards, animations, controls, responsive shell, server snapshots | A displayed legal action is not permission to execute it |
| Accounts | Identity, tokens, user records | Identity must be followed by room/table authorization |
| Invites and lobby | Creation, acceptance, roster, start coordination | Scope by game type and game ID |
| Game domains | Moves, turn order, rules and results | A client submits intent; the server decides validity |
| Poker | Seats, stacks, cards, betting rounds, timers and hand results | Produce a separate safe payload for each viewer |
| Tournament services | Registration, seating, blind levels, elimination and balancing | A tournament outlives any one table connection |
| Social features | Friends, presence, direct/group chat and notifications | Room membership and message visibility need their own checks |
| Trinity | Retrieval-backed answers | Assistant output cannot decide game state or authorization |

## Shared shell, distinct game engines

The React application uses contexts for account, UI, notifications, friends and direct messaging. Game pages add their own state and board components. A common shell reduces duplicated navigation, while different game engines keep Sudoku rules separate from poker betting.

The backend registry in `utils/game_registry.py` currently maps Tic-Tac-Toe, Connect Four, Checkers and Poker to their model and game factory. Sudoku is a separate domain; it is not listed as an invite-capable multiplayer registry entry. Extending the platform means deliberately choosing which common workflow a new game participates in.

## Deployment topology

The inspected `Procfile` runs migrations in a release command and serves the backend with Daphne against `ttt_core.asgi:application`. That ASGI application routes HTTP through a WSGI adapter and WebSockets through origin validation, JWT middleware and Channels routing. A WSGI-only development server does not provide this socket path.

The database configuration uses `DATABASE_URL` when supplied, with a SQLite fallback. PostgreSQL is necessary when relying on actual row-lock behavior in concurrent poker workflows. Redis is a separate dependency; it is not the durable game database. The frontend is a separate CRA build. This handbook does not verify the gaming project's currently deployed hosts or worker count.

## Design decisions to carry forward

Keep gameplay ownership on the server, room identifiers namespaced, and per-viewer state serialization explicit. Separate durable state from broadcast delivery. Separate tournament continuity from the lifetime of a table socket. Keep visual animation a representation of state rather than the mechanism that advances it.

Read [the multiplayer flow](/guide/gaming-multiplayer-flow), [poker and tournament design](/guide/gaming-poker-tournaments), and [security and AI boundaries](/guide/gaming-security-ai) next.

title: Gaming platform: multiplayer flow
summary: Trace create, invite, accept, lobby, start, move, and reconnect across HTTP and WebSockets.
body:
## One shared entry path

A generic lobby workflow lets several games share invites without sharing their rules. The inspected registry covers Tic-Tac-Toe, Connect Four, Checkers and Poker. Each registry entry resolves a model, factory and seat mapping. The lobby receives a game type and game ID rather than assuming every ID belongs to Tic-Tac-Toe.

## From invitation to play

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant Host as Host browser
  participant API as Django HTTP API
  participant Guest as Invited browser
  participant Lobby as Lobby consumer
  participant Game as Game consumer
  Host->>API: Create game and invitation
  API-->>Host: Game identity and join information
  Guest->>API: Accept invitation
  Guest->>Lobby: Connect to typed lobby
  Host->>Lobby: Connect and request start
  Lobby->>Lobby: Check roster and start rules
  Lobby-->>Host: Start event with game type
  Lobby-->>Guest: Start event with game type
  Host->>Game: Connect to game channel
  Guest->>Game: Connect to game channel
  Host->>Game: Submit move intent
  Game->>Game: Validate player turn and rules
  Game-->>Host: Updated state
  Game-->>Guest: Updated state
```

**Text alternative:** The host creates a game and invite over HTTP. The guest accepts, both connect to the typed lobby, and the server checks the start transition. Both then connect to the appropriate game consumer. Move intentions are validated server-side before updated state is sent.

## Namespacing prevents cross-game collisions

Different game tables can each have row ID `4`. A bare room ID cannot distinguish them. `scoped_lobby_id(game_type, lobby_id)` produces a game-type-qualified identifier for lobby coordination. Invite guards also compare the expected game type. This is an object-boundary problem analogous to tenant isolation, even though a gaming room is not an organization tenant.

Lobby WebSocket routes use `ws/lobby/<game_type>/<lobby_id>/`. Poker table routes use `ws/poker/<game_id>/`; other game consumers have their own routes. Namespacing a channel group prevents accidental broadcast collisions; it does not replace participant authorization.

## Transport roles are specific to an operation

HTTP covers account operations, game creation and invite acceptance. WebSockets support live lobby coordination and gameplay commands as well as notifications. Do not claim that WebSockets only announce changes: game consumers also receive actions and persist resulting game state.

A successful socket send means bytes were sent, not that a move was accepted. Render server responses, expose rejected moves clearly, and recover from a fresh authorized snapshot after connection loss.

## Connection ownership in React

Account-level sockets should follow authenticated provider lifetime. Lobby sockets follow lobby route lifetime; table sockets follow active table membership. Tear down old subscriptions when the user changes game, logs out or moves tables. Otherwise old event handlers can update the wrong board or double-count badges.

## Verification scenarios

| Scenario | Expected property to verify |
| --- | --- |
| Two games have the same numeric ID | Lobby groups remain distinct |
| Invite has the wrong game type | Join is refused |
| Nonparticipant requests a move | No game-state mutation |
| Same player sends two overlapping actions | Server turn/rule checks determine the result |
| Reconnect after a missed update | Fresh authorized state replaces stale browser state |
| Leave one lobby and open another | Old socket callbacks cannot mutate the new lobby |

These are proposed verification cases. This handbook did not run the gaming backend or a two-player session.

title: Gaming platform: poker & tournaments
summary: Design for private cards, locked state transitions, tournament continuity, and table reassignment.
body:
## A table and a tournament are different aggregates

`PokerGame` owns a table's hand, seats, stacks, betting and community cards. The multi-table tournament domain owns the wider competition: entries, tables, registration, blind progression and elimination. The older scheduled single-table match workflow remains separate from the MTT routes; similar names do not make them interchangeable.

## Tournament continuity

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Entry[Registered tournament entry] --> Waiting[Tournament channel while unseated]
  Waiting --> Seat[Initial seating after commit]
  Seat --> Table[Poker table connection]
  Table --> Complete[Hand completion service]
  Complete --> Balance[Elimination and table balancing]
  Balance --> Table
  Balance --> Moved[Table reassigned event]
  Moved --> Table
  Balance --> Eliminated[Eliminated entry]
  Eliminated --> Waiting
```

**Text alternative:** A registered entrant can receive tournament events before seating through a tournament channel. Once assigned, they connect to a poker table. Completed hands feed elimination and balancing, which may move the entrant or eliminate them. An eliminated entrant can still qualify for the tournament channel.

## Lock, validate, persist, publish

Poker consumer paths use `transaction.atomic()` and `select_for_update()` to serialize competing changes to a game row. PostgreSQL actually enforces these row locks; SQLite does not provide an equivalent test of this behavior. Locking reduces concurrency races, while domain validation still decides whether an action is legal.

Tournament start wraps initial seating in a transaction and schedules reassignment broadcasts with `transaction.on_commit()`. Subscribers should not be told they have a seat before the seating record exists. Post-commit delivery still has a failure window if the process dies before dispatch; an outbox would be a future reliability improvement, not an implemented component claimed here.

## Private cards need a per-viewer payload

`poker_payload(game, user)` produces the payload used by REST and WebSocket paths. It replaces another player's unrevealed cards with placeholders before delivery and derives legal actions for the requesting user. Showdown and voluntarily shown cards have explicit reveal behavior.

The shared event should cause each connection to construct its own safe view. Broadcasting one player's already-serialized snapshot to everyone would bypass this boundary. Hidden CSS and blurred cards provide no protection for information already delivered to the browser.

## Two connections solve two different gaps

| Connection | Use | What it does not own |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ws/poker/<game_id>/` | Table state and gameplay; also tournament events while seated | Identity of the tournament independent of its current table |
| `ws/poker/mtt/<tournament_id>/` | Tournament snapshot and events for a registered entry, including unseated or eliminated entries | Table actions, cards and turn timers |

The table consumer can redirect a reconnect aimed at a stale table to the entrant's current table. The tournament channel handles the separate case where the entrant has no table at all. The source describes closing the tournament-only connection once a table connection takes over; keeping both can double-deliver tournament events.

## Timers are the scaling boundary

Turn and next-hand timers are held in process-local dictionaries and use in-process scheduling. A restart loses those schedules, and multiple ASGI workers do not share those dictionaries. The documented bot harness requires a single ASGI worker. Do not draw a distributed timer service into the current-state architecture.

A future design could persist deadlines and use a recoverable dispatcher, with each execution rechecking the current hand and turn under a lock. Until implemented and exercised, that is a proposal.

## Meaningful invariants

Verify chip conservation at appropriate hand boundaries, valid seat occupancy, legal phase progression, elimination rank consistency, and correct table reassignment. The repository documents multi-client bot runs, but this handbook did not repeat them. Historical clean runs do not certify every current route, deployment topology or reconnect path.

title: Gaming platform: security & AI
summary: Separate user identity, participant authority, private game state, and retrieval-backed assistance.
body:
## Identity is only the first gate

The platform uses SimpleJWT for HTTP authentication and a JWT WebSocket middleware for socket identity. The ASGI router wraps sockets in `AllowedHostsOriginValidator`. Consumers must still check the authenticated user's right to join a room or act at a table.

An origin check restricts where a browser connection may originate; it does not establish table membership. A signed token proves identity; it does not establish whose turn it is.

## Separate the assistant from gameplay authority

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Browser[React browser] --> Gameplay[Authorized game consumer]
  Gameplay --> Rules[Deterministic game rules]
  Rules --> State[Persisted game state]
  Browser --> Ask[Trinity question endpoint]
  Ask --> Retrieval[FAISS document retrieval]
  Retrieval --> Model[Model generated answer]
  Model --> Advice[Advisory text only]
```

**Text alternative:** Gameplay goes through an authorized consumer and deterministic rules to persisted state. Trinity questions use a separate retrieval and model pipeline that produces advisory answers. There is no depicted model-to-game-state mutation path.

The inspected Trinity chain uses LangChain RetrievalQA with FAISS and an OpenAI model. That is distinct from game-playing opponents implemented in game logic. The assistant should explain rules; authoritative winners, card visibility and legal moves stay in deterministic game code.

## Security review scope

Public architecture notes describe trust boundaries and verification priorities. Location-specific findings and private remediation details are retained outside the published handbook. This chapter does not assert that all security work is complete or that the application is production-certified.

Review identity transport, room/action authorization, sensitive logging, assistant abuse controls and restart-safe scheduling in the actual application. Record detailed results in its restricted engineering evidence rather than a promotional page.

## Assistant boundaries to document

Treat retrieved documents as untrusted content. Keep secrets out of the index and prompts. Bound input length, retrieval size, request rate and provider spending. Provide a clear unavailable state when the provider fails. A polished assistant drawer does not demonstrate any of these controls; inspect the endpoint and its data sources.

## Verification priorities

Test anonymous and nonparticipant denial, private-card payloads for different viewers, invite game-type mismatch, revoked or expired identities at connection boundaries, and MTT start authority. For AI, test provider failure, oversized questions and sensitive error redaction. Use dummy identities and synthetic questions. The handbook records these as work to verify, not checks already executed.

title: AuthFlow: browser & console design
summary: A React account experience and workspace console with memory access tokens and a server-owned refresh cookie.
body:
## The browser-facing part of Gait

AuthFlow is the React frontend for Gait's authentication and security service. Its current routes go beyond the original login demo: accounts and two-step setup, onboarding, application setup, organization consoles, findings, members, and operator-only security screens.

The source README describes an older browser-token model. The inspected current interceptor and token store are the stronger authority for the transport design below.

## Session transport

## Project architecture

```mermaid
%% handbook-project:authflow
flowchart TB
  N0[Account UI] --> N1[Gait account API] --> N2[Session outcome]
  N3[Console route] --> N4[Membership gate] --> N5[Scoped responses]
  N6[Memory access token] --> N7[Coordinated refresh] --> N8[Auth host cookie]
```

**Text alternative:** Account UI → Gait account API → Session outcome. Console route → Membership gate → Scoped responses. Memory access token → Coordinated refresh → Auth host cookie. These are responsibility lanes; the detailed diagram below describes the connected workflow.

## Detailed flow

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant UI as React browser
  participant Memory as Access token memory
  participant API as Gait auth API
  participant Session as Server session
  UI->>API: Login with cookie transport
  API->>Session: Establish authenticated session
  API-->>UI: Access token and HttpOnly refresh cookie
  UI->>Memory: Keep access token in memory
  UI->>API: Authorized API request with Bearer access token
  UI->>API: Reload or expired token: cookie refresh request
  API->>Session: Validate and rotate refresh state
  API-->>UI: New access token
  UI->>Memory: Replace access token
```

**Text alternative:** Login establishes a server session. JavaScript receives an access token kept only in memory; the auth host owns an HttpOnly refresh cookie. After reload or expiry, a coordinated refresh obtains another access token. The server validates refresh state.

## Component ownership

| Area | Owns | Authority boundary |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Auth contexts and hooks | Account/session UI and API calls | Backend decides identity and session validity |
| Axios clients | Bearer attachment, cookie transport and bounded retry | A refresh response must actually contain an access token |
| Refresh coordinator | Browser refresh coordination | Coordination does not replace server rotation rules |
| Console layout | Organization route and workspace navigation | Backend validates organization membership |
| Findings and application pages | Presentation of server contracts | Displayed evidence keeps its original trust level |
| Operator route guard | Operator navigation availability | Every operator API still needs server authorization |

`tokenStorage.js` keeps access tokens in a module variable and clears legacy token cookies. `axios.js` uses a separate session client to prevent interceptor recursion; an authenticated request retries once after refresh. Logout clears local state and broadcasts signed-out state after attempting server logout.

## Account, console, operator

`/account` covers a person's own security settings. `/console/:orgSlug` covers an organization workspace. Operator routes are wrapped in `RequireOperator`. These are three different scopes, not three visual versions of the same permission.

The route organization slug is a selection hint. It must not be trusted as proof that the user belongs to that organization. Likewise, hiding a staff page cannot protect its API.

## Availability is part of the design

The inspected feature-status source is dated 2026-09-28 and labels product sign-in and built-in check packs early access. That is the source's status snapshot, not a fresh live availability check. Explain access requirements in user-facing flows rather than promising universal availability from the existence of a route.

Continue with [the backend authority](/guide/gait-backend-design) and [the SDK integration boundary](/guide/gait-sdk-design).

## Refresh coordination across browser tabs

The current coordinator shares one in-flight refresh promise inside a tab and uses the Web Locks API to serialize refreshes across tabs when supported. The backend rotates refresh state, so overlapping use of the same old credential can be treated as replay. Older browsers without Web Locks retain only the in-tab guarantee; they can be signed out if concurrent refresh triggers replay revocation.

Use [the refresh and revocation chapter](/guide/gait-refresh-revocation) to follow this boundary. Clearing browser state alone does not prove that server-side logout succeeded.

title: gait-sdk: verification & signal design
summary: A Python library inside your API: verify identity, check live sessions, and report application security signals.
body:
## A library inside the application process

The SDK is not another hosted service. Framework adapters run inside a Django REST Framework or FastAPI application and translate a presented token into a verified identity. The consuming application still owns organization membership, roles and object access.

## Identity and authority

## Project architecture

```mermaid
%% handbook-project:sdk
flowchart TB
  N0[Framework adapter] --> N1[Configured verifier] --> N2[Verified identity]
  N3[Verified identity for sensitive action] --> N4[Application rules] --> N5[Live session check]
  N6[Application check] --> N7[Machine credential] --> N8[Reported evidence]
```

**Text alternative:** Framework adapter → Configured verifier → Verified identity. Verified identity for sensitive action → Application rules → Live session check. Application check → Machine credential → Reported evidence. These are responsibility lanes; the detailed diagram below describes the connected workflow.

## Detailed flow

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Caller[Caller with Bearer token] --> Adapter[Django or FastAPI adapter]
  Adapter --> Verify[Configured token verifier]
  Verify --> Identity[Verified identity]
  Identity --> Authorize[Application membership and object rules]
  Authorize --> Sensitive[Optional live session check]
  Sensitive --> Mutation[Application mutation]
  Verify -. key retrieval or introspection .-> Gait[Gait identity service]
  Sensitive --> Gait
```

**Text alternative:** A framework adapter invokes the configured verifier and returns a verified identity. Application rules authorize the requested object. Sensitive operations then check the live session before mutation. Verification may use local cached public keys or remote introspection.

## Two deliberate verification modes

The README defaults to introspection, which asks Gait's `whoami` endpoint. The inspected Django adapter caches successful Bearer introspection results for 45 seconds; it does not make an upstream request for every ordinary call. Its uncached sensitive-action check is a separate contract. Explicit JWKS mode verifies RS256 access tokens locally against configured issuer, audience and public keys. Do not depict every mode as network-free. JWKS mode still fetches keys initially and on cache refresh.

The documented JWKS contract checks signature, key ID, issuer, audience, expiry, issue time, access-token use and required identity/session identifiers. Key-set refresh and bounded stale-key behavior are explicit. Verification failure does not silently switch to introspection.

## Revocation and sensitive actions

Local signature validity cannot reveal a newly revoked session by itself. `require_live_session` performs an uncached live check for sensitive operations. The documented order is identity, application authorization, live-session check, then mutation. Provider unavailability denies a sensitive operation rather than approving it from an old answer.

Key users by verified issuer and opaque subject. Avoid parsing subjects or deriving application roles from unverified token fields.

## Machine identity is a separate flow

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Check[Application self check] --> SDK[Explicit SDK signal call]
  SDK --> Credential[Application credential authentication]
  Credential --> Scope[Server derived application workspace environment]
  Scope --> Evidence[Customer reported evidence]
  Evidence --> Finding[Control and finding lifecycle]
```

**Text alternative:** A backend explicitly reports a self-check using an application credential. Gait derives scope from that credential and persists customer-reported evidence that feeds control and finding state.

The SDK does not automatically observe every request. `send_security_signal` is an explicit call site. Its public parameters do not let the caller choose an organization, environment or trust level. The credential must stay on the backend, never in a frontend build.

An application-reported PASS is an assertion by that application, not proof independently collected by Gait. Exact signal retries are deduplicated by application, signal type and source reference in the documented contract.

## What the consuming service must still build

The service must map identity to its own memberships, enforce permissions, decide which operations require a live check, handle provider failures, and produce accurate bounded self-checks. The SDK supplies verification and transport; it cannot make those domain decisions.

## Connect the three repositories

Follow [the complete authentication walkthrough](/guide/gait-auth-walkthrough) to connect browser login, refresh rotation, identity verification and application authorization. Product sign-in remains an early-access capability in the inspected source status; configured JWKS verification requires a compatible issuer and published signing keys.

title: django_auth: Gait service design
summary: Server-controlled sessions, account security, workspace isolation, and evidence-backed security findings.
body:
## The authority behind the console

The `django_auth` repository is Gait's identity and security backend. It owns authentication and server session state, account-security workflows, workspace/application records and security evidence. AuthFlow presents this data; gait-sdk verifies users or reports application signals from consuming backends.

This overview uses public-safe source and code summaries. Confidential security triage, plans and internal findings are excluded.

## Service boundaries

## Project architecture

```mermaid
%% handbook-project:gait
flowchart TB
  N0[Account requests] --> N1[Session and protection] --> N2[PostgreSQL state]
  N3[Console requests] --> N4[Scoped membership] --> N5[Controls and findings]
  N6[Application credential] --> N7[Derived signal scope] --> N8[Evidence provenance]
```

**Text alternative:** Account requests → Session and protection → PostgreSQL state. Console requests → Scoped membership → Controls and findings. Application credential → Derived signal scope → Evidence provenance. These are responsibility lanes; the detailed diagram below describes the connected workflow.

## Detailed flow

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  Console[AuthFlow browser] --> Account[Account and session API]
  Console --> Workspace[Workspace and application API]
  Account --> Session[AuthSession and token lifecycle]
  Account --> Protection[Recent auth MFA and abuse controls]
  Workspace --> Membership[Membership and scoped permissions]
  Client[Application with gait-sdk] --> Signals[Credential authenticated ingestion]
  Signals --> Scope[Derived application organization environment]
  Scope --> Evidence[Customer reported security evidence]
  Membership --> Findings[Scoped control and finding views]
  Evidence --> Findings
  Account --> DB[PostgreSQL]
  Workspace --> DB
  Findings --> DB
```

**Text alternative:** The console uses account/session APIs and workspace APIs. The backend enforces session, recent-authentication and membership boundaries. Applications submit signals through a separate credential-authenticated endpoint; scope comes from the application credential and evidence remains customer-reported. PostgreSQL persists state.

## Browser session authority

`user/refresh_cookie.py` defines a host-only HttpOnly refresh cookie scoped to `/api/auth/`. Cookie-authenticated requests require an allowed Origin and the custom auth header before reading or rotating that cookie. Secure and SameSite settings depend on deployment configuration; HttpOnly alone is not CSRF protection.

JavaScript uses a memory access token. The server controls refresh state and logout. Recent-password or recent-MFA policies protect sensitive account actions independently of merely holding an access token.

## Workspace isolation

People, organizations, memberships, applications and environments are distinct records. Workspace pages select a scope; backend permissions decide access. A server-to-server application credential represents an application, not an organization administrator or a human user.

`security/tenant_ingestion.py` derives scope, organization and environment from the verified application. The caller's payload cannot select those boundaries. This keeps reported evidence attached to the credential's actual workspace and environment.

## Evidence has provenance

Customer signals feed evidence, control and finding state while retaining their customer-reported trust level. Internal evidence and customer assertions must remain distinguishable. A finding's existence, acknowledgment or accepted-risk state each mean something different; none should be presented as a completed independent fix.

The SDK does not provide a generic privileged Observatory client. Console reading and application signal reporting are different API surfaces and identities.

## Bounded automation

The source overview describes capability-bound security agents and execution flags. Treat analysis, recommendation, execution and deployment approval as distinct stages. An AI conclusion cannot grant itself a production capability. This handbook does not assert that a security fleet is currently enabled or that any agent executed a production change.

## Operational design

The repository describes Heroku application hosting, PostgreSQL, SMTP and RabbitMQ event integration. These are source-described dependencies, not a checked live deployment inventory. Verify session denial, workspace isolation, application-credential revocation, signal replay and evidence provenance against the deployed configuration before making operational assurance claims.

## Audience belongs to the session

The inspected token implementation supports legacy HS256 and configured RS256 issuance. In the RS256 path, a registered relying-party audience is selected from the sign-in Origin and stored on the session; refresh preserves that audience. A caller does not choose authority by adding an audience field to its request body.

Gait restricts relying-party audiences to the session/identity endpoints they need. A product token is not automatically a console-admin credential. Consuming applications still own their organization membership and domain roles. See [the verification chapter](/guide/gait-api-verification) and [application authorization](/guide/gait-app-authorization).

title: Foundry: engineering control plane
summary: Durable repository state, isolated workstreams, scoped agent capabilities, and evidence tied to a reviewed candidate.
body:
## The system that builds the other systems

Foundry belongs in this catalogue as an engineering platform. It operates during development and release coordination rather than on the normal browser-to-application request path. Its durable unit is repository state: assignments, decisions, audit events, handoffs and evidence that survive a model session.

The current source review checked revision `713e176`. The existing setup tutorial records an earlier revision and its isolated initialization smoke check; those results do not automatically certify newer release paths.

## Control plane and delivery

## Project architecture

```mermaid
%% handbook-project:foundry
flowchart TB
  N0[Human outcome] --> N1[Tasks and policy] --> N2[Git backed state]
  N3[Isolated workspace] --> N4[Candidate artifacts] --> N5[Verification evidence]
  N6[Candidate review] --> N7[Human approval] --> N8[Release integration]
```

**Text alternative:** Human outcome → Tasks and policy → Git backed state. Isolated workspace → Candidate artifacts → Verification evidence. Candidate review → Human approval → Release integration. These are responsibility lanes; the detailed diagram below describes the connected workflow.

## Detailed flow

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  Human[Anthony human outcome and authority] --> Plan[Plan and task scope]
  Plan --> Control[Foundry control plane]
  Control --> Workspace[Isolated workstream and runtime]
  Workspace --> Candidate[Candidate commit and artifacts]
  Candidate --> Review[Independent review and verification]
  Review --> Approval[Human approval tied to candidate]
  Approval --> Release[Governed release checks]
  Control <--> Durable[Git backed state and audit history]
  Release --> Product[Product build and deployment integration]
```

**Text alternative:** A human defines an outcome and scope. Foundry coordinates isolated work, collects candidate artifacts, and tracks independent review and human approval. Durable Git-backed state supports recovery. Product build and deployment integration follows its own configured release contract.

## Components and ownership

| Component | Owns | Boundary |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Core and state | Tasks, workstreams, events, checkpoints | Chat memory is not durable state |
| Authority and policies | Principals, capability checks and approvals | Role labels alone do not grant authority |
| Workspaces and runtimes | Isolated execution and scoped work | A worker does not accept its own candidate |
| Providers | Model/runtime integration | Provider-neutral design does not imply equal adapter support |
| Evidence and observation | Artifacts, verification and recorded results | A recorded claim is not an executed check |
| Release | Candidate checks and governed integration | CI and deployment need actual configured contracts |
| Secret guard | Protected paths and execution boundaries | Prompts cannot substitute for deterministic enforcement |

## Native and legacy enforcement differ

The README distinguishes native projects with registered principals and SSH-signed approval from Foundry's older repository layout. Design descriptions must name that boundary. Do not present every recorded approval line as a cryptographic authorization or every possible provider as a supervised adapter.

A useful artifact binds a result to a concrete commit/tree, test command and output. If the candidate changes after review, the old review does not describe the new tree. Recovery should re-read state, ownership and evidence before continuing work.

## Foundry connects to projects through development

Foundry can coordinate changes to a frontend, SDK or backend repository without becoming part of their user-authentication stack. The gaming platform's game consumer, Gait's account/session service and EstateIQ's domain services still own their respective runtime decisions.

Containerized execution and broker-mediated external actions belong to the governed design; the available enforcement depends on the actual runtime and policy path in use. This handbook's manual Netlify publication is not evidence that it completed Foundry's governed release flow.

## Start with a concrete repository

Use [the eight-step Foundry tutorial](/guide/foundry-repository) for GitHub repository creation, installation, initialization, human authority, sessions, tasks, review and recovery. The tutorial already distinguishes what its smoke check executed from what remains a guided exercise.

## Session lifecycle and runtime observations

The refreshed source adds runtime-bound activity observations. A session record can say it is active while a runtime sample cannot establish a current supervisor identity. The activity projection checks a unique runtime/session backlink, task assignment, lifecycle, runtime metadata and the sampled identity; ambiguous or unavailable observations stay labeled as such.

An observed-live supervisor is not proof that a model is making progress, produced a correct artifact, or has release authority. Recorded usage, process observation, task completion and candidate acceptance remain different facts. This review inspected the code; it did not launch a runtime or replay real session records.

title: My Django + React folder structure
summary: One repository, backend and frontend directories, and three focused .gitignore files.
body:
## One project, two runtimes

```text
project-name/
├── .gitignore
├── README.md
├── docs/
├── backend/
│   ├── .gitignore
│   ├── .venv/                  # local, ignored
│   ├── manage.py
│   ├── requirements.txt
│   ├── config/                 # settings, URLs, ASGI, WSGI
│   └── apps/
│       ├── __init__.py
│       └── tasks/              # models, API, services, tests
└── frontend/
    ├── .gitignore
    ├── package.json
    ├── package-lock.json
    ├── index.html
    ├── public/
    └── src/                    # see the frontend structure guide
```

Run `git init` once at the project root. Do not initialize nested repositories in backend and frontend. Initialize Foundry at that same root when using its workflow; follow the [Foundry tutorial](/guide/foundry-repository) for generated governance files.

```bash
# Terminal — create the repository layout, before scaffolding either runtime.
mkdir project-name
cd project-name
git init
mkdir backend frontend docs
```

## Root .gitignore: shared local files

```gitignore
# /.gitignore — Shared local environment and OS files.
.DS_Store
Thumbs.db
.env
.env.*
!.env.example
.idea/
```

## Backend .gitignore: Python and generated data

```gitignore
# /backend/.gitignore — Python environments and generated runtime files.
.venv/
venv/
__pycache__/
*.py[cod]
.pytest_cache/
.coverage
htmlcov/
*.sqlite3
*.sqlite3-journal
media/
staticfiles/
```

Keep migrations, source static assets, dependency inputs and lockfiles committed. `media/` above is uploaded runtime data; `staticfiles/` is collected output. Do not use either path for source code.

## Frontend .gitignore: JavaScript dependencies and output

```gitignore
# /frontend/.gitignore — Installed packages and generated browser artifacts.
node_modules/
dist/
build/
coverage/
.vite/
playwright-report/
test-results/
*.log
```

Commit `package-lock.json`, configuration and safe `.env.example` files. Never put a secret in a Vite environment variable: values exposed to frontend code are public.

Nested ignore rules apply relative to their own directory. They do not stop tracking files already committed; inspect `git ls-files` and use `git check-ignore -v` to check a rule before changing tracking. See the [Git ignore reference](https://git-scm.com/docs/gitignore).

## Grow the backend deliberately

The [setup guide](/guide/django-setup) creates `apps/tasks` directly, with `AppConfig.name = "apps.tasks"`. Keep `config/` for application wiring and settings. Keep each domain's models, serializers, views, selectors, services and tests together. Introduce packages such as `api/` or `services/` when the files become large, rather than creating empty layers in advance.

## Keep frontend conventions consistent

Use the same [frontend directory structure](/guide/frontend-folder-structure) whether React sits inside this repository or has its own repository. The runtime commands change working directory; the responsibilities stay the same. The handbook itself remains frontend-only.

title: My frontend project structure
summary: A standalone React layout with feature ownership, Axios transport and TanStack Query.
body:
## Start with a standalone React project

A frontend-only application has no empty backend directory. Its repository root is the frontend root. In a full-stack repository, this same tree lives inside `frontend/`.

```text
frontend-project/
├── .gitignore
├── .env.example
├── README.md
├── package.json
├── package-lock.json
├── index.html
├── vite.config.ts
├── tsconfig.json
├── public/                       # files served without module imports
└── src/
    ├── main.tsx                  # mount React
    ├── app/
    │   ├── App.tsx               # application composition
    │   ├── routes.tsx            # routing
    │   └── providers.tsx         # shared providers
    ├── api/
    │   └── client.ts             # Axios instance and transport policy
    ├── features/
    │   └── tasks/
    │       ├── api.ts            # task request functions and DTOs
    │       ├── queries.ts        # keys and TanStack Query hooks
    │       ├── TasksPage.tsx
    │       ├── components/
    │       └── TasksPage.test.tsx
    ├── components/
    │   └── ui/                   # reusable controls without feature rules
    ├── hooks/                    # genuinely shared React behavior
    ├── lib/                      # shared non-React helpers
    ├── assets/                   # imported images and fonts
    ├── styles/
    └── test/                     # shared test setup and fixtures
```

Create folders when they have a responsibility to hold. A small app can begin with `app`, `features`, `components` and `styles`; it does not need an empty architecture skeleton.

## Scaffold and keep generated configuration

```bash
# Terminal — new standalone application; use the full-stack frontend path instead if needed.
npm create vite@latest frontend-project -- --template react-ts
cd frontend-project
npm install
npm install axios @tanstack/react-query
npm run dev
```

This intentionally uses the current scaffold, not a promise of identical generated files forever. Review its Node requirement and commit the resulting lockfile. Keep a single package manager for the project. Add a routing library when the application needs multiple routes; `app/routes.tsx` is a placement convention, not a file Vite generates.

## Give Axios and TanStack Query separate jobs

Axios owns requests, base URL, cancellation and transport-level error handling. TanStack Query owns remote snapshots, loading/error states and invalidation. Feature modules own endpoint functions and keys. React state owns open menus, form drafts and selected tabs. See the [working connection example](/guide/react-api-connection).

A shared client should not import a page or a feature. A reusable button should not import task queries. Cross-feature behavior belongs in explicit application composition or a deliberate public feature interface; avoid reaching into another feature's private component files.

## Standalone .gitignore

```gitignore
# /.gitignore — Local files and generated output for a frontend-only repository.
node_modules/
dist/
build/
coverage/
.vite/
playwright-report/
test-results/
*.log
.env
.env.*
!.env.example
.DS_Store
```

Commit package manifests, lockfiles, source assets and safe environment examples. This is one `.gitignore` for a standalone frontend. The [full-stack layout](/guide/full-stack-folder-structure) uses three because it has a shared root and two runtimes.

## Verify the boundaries

Check that a clean clone can install and build, a direct route reload works on the host, every screen has loading/error/empty states, and a user change clears sensitive cached data. Test organization switching during an in-flight request where applicable. Directory names help navigation; backend access checks still enforce security.

title: Gait: follow authentication across three projects
summary: Connect the browser, session authority and consuming API without confusing their responsibilities.
body:
## Three projects, three responsibilities

AuthFlow implements the inspected browser account and console experience. django_auth owns Gait identity, sessions and security state. gait-sdk verifies identity inside a consuming API; it does not replace that API's domain permissions.

This walkthrough explains inspected source paths. It is not an OAuth authorization-code tutorial or proof that a product has completed integration. A product origin and audience must be explicitly configured; an AuthFlow console token is not automatically valid for every application.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Browser
    participant G as Gait authority
    participant A as Consuming API
    participant D as Application database
    B->>G: Login and optional second factor
    G-->>B: Access token and refresh cookie
    B->>A: Bearer access token
    A->>G: Introspect identity when required
    G-->>A: Verified identity or denial
    A->>D: Check application membership and role
    A->>G: Uncached live-session check for sensitive action
    G-->>A: Active, revoked or unavailable
    A->>D: Mutate only after required checks pass
    A-->>B: Application result
```

## Follow the path

1. [Login and session establishment](/guide/gait-login-session).
2. [Refresh, concurrency and logout](/guide/gait-refresh-revocation).
3. [API identity verification](/guide/gait-api-verification).
4. [Application authorization](/guide/gait-app-authorization).
5. [Failure and integration checks](/guide/gait-auth-failure-checks).

For source ownership and deployment limits, read the [AuthFlow](/guide/authflow-design), [Gait backend](/guide/gait-backend-design) and [SDK](/guide/gait-sdk-design) case studies. No tokens, credentials or live identity calls are collected by this handbook.

title: Gait login and session establishment
summary: Trace password and second-factor handling into the browser session.
body:
## Establish the browser session

The inspected AuthFlow login sends the configured API's `/login/` request with cookie session transport. A response requiring two-factor authentication switches the UI to a second-factor step. `/two-factor-login/` accepts an OTP or recovery code. Wrong-code, expired-login and rate-limit states need distinct feedback.

The access token stays in module memory. The refresh credential uses an HttpOnly cookie; it is not returned to application code for localStorage persistence. Reload recovery therefore depends on the refresh path, not a token surviving in browser storage.

## Keep browser protections explicit

The inspected refresh cookie is host-only and restricted to `/api/auth/`. Cookie-based refresh validates an allowed Origin and the expected Gait request marker before consuming cookie credentials. Secure and SameSite settings must fit the deployed origins. HttpOnly prevents ordinary JavaScript reads; it does not replace cross-site request protections.

## Audience is authority configuration

The backend selects the configured relying-party audience from the sign-in Origin and preserves it with the session. Request body input must not pick arbitrary audiences. The consuming API must expect the intended audience. Source support for RS256 does not prove a deployment has published keys or selected that mode.

Check login success, invalid password, second-factor transition, recovery-code consumption and throttling with synthetic accounts in the actual integration. These are proposed checks; the handbook did not run them.

title: Gait refresh, browser tabs and logout
summary: Understand rotating cookies, coordination limits and server-side revocation.
body:
## Restore without persisting the access token

The inspected AuthFlow Axios layer uses a separate session client for `/auth/refresh/`, with the configured base URL providing `/api`. A failed authenticated request can refresh and retry once. A dedicated client avoids recursively triggering the same refresh interceptor.

An in-flight promise coordinates refresh calls within one tab. Where available, the Web Locks API serializes refresh across browser tabs. Without Web Locks, the in-tab guard alone does not guarantee cross-tab safety with a shared rotating cookie.

## Rotation belongs to the authority

The inspected rotating backend path locks session state, records hashed refresh credentials and tracks consumption. Reuse of consumed credentials can revoke the session. A late browser request must not be treated as harmless simply because the user appears logged in elsewhere.

## Logout has two outcomes to verify

AuthFlow attempts `/auth/logout/` and clears memory and client query state in cleanup. Local cleanup still happens if that network request fails. It removes the visible local session but does not prove the authority revoked the server session.

Sensitive actions should use the SDK's separate uncached session check. A cached identity or locally valid access token may remain usable for ordinary verification until its applicable cache/expiration policy catches up.

Test simultaneous requests, two tabs, replay, refresh outage, logout outage and reload. Do not claim immediate global revocation solely from the browser's signed-out screen.

title: Gait API verification: introspection and JWKS
summary: Choose a verification mode and understand freshness and failure behavior.
body:
## Integrate inside the consuming backend

The SDK is a library, not a separate server process. Configure it in the API that receives the bearer token. Introspection is the inspected default; explicit JWKS mode requires compatible issuer configuration and published signing keys. Do not silently downgrade verification modes when a provider is unavailable.

Introspection asks the authority about a token. The inspected Django authentication adapter caches successful bearer introspection for up to 45 seconds per process, with a bounded cache. Therefore “introspection mode” does not mean every ordinary API request performs a fresh authority call.

## Local verification has a different freshness boundary

Configured JWKS mode checks signature, issuer, audience, timing and required identity/session claims. A locally verified token is not evidence that the session is still active at this moment. Key caching and signature validation cannot independently observe every session revocation.

## Sensitive operations require the live guard

The inspected `require_live_session(request)` performs an uncached authority check bound to the verified subject. Invalid or revoked sessions are rejected; provider unavailability fails closed with an unavailable response rather than permission to mutate.

For the intended sensitive workflow: verify identity, enforce domain permissions, require a live session, then execute the protected change. No JWT parsing shortcut should bypass signature or authority checks. Configure error handling so an invalid credential and an unavailable verification service remain distinguishable.

This explains SDK source behavior; confirm the installed SDK version and actual issuer settings before applying it to a deployment.

title: Gait identity meets application authorization
summary: Keep membership, roles and record ownership inside the application.
body:
## Map a verified identity to an application principal

Use a stable issuer and subject pair as the external identity boundary. Email is a mutable attribute, not a substitute for stable identity or an automatic permission grant. Resolve the local application user deliberately and handle disabled or unlinked accounts.

The Gait session is not the application's financial ledger, property membership or game role. Read those permissions from the application's authoritative records.

## Apply the checks in order

1. Verify the credential using the configured SDK mode.
2. Resolve the local principal and active membership in the requested organization.
3. Check operation-specific roles and retrieve the target record through a scoped query.
4. For a sensitive action, perform the uncached live-session check.
5. Apply the transactional domain operation and return its authoritative result.

A UI-selected organization is untrusted input. A valid subject cannot cross into another organization's record by changing a URL. Deny before mutating; checking after an update is too late.

## Separate application signals

SDK security signals use application credentials and server-derived organization, application and environment scope. Customer-reported observations are not independently verified findings. Signal reporting does not grant the caller end-user privileges or replace access checks.

Test a valid identity with a foreign organization, removed membership, insufficient role and disabled local account. Use the [EstateIQ tenancy chapter](/guide/estateiq-tenant-boundary) as a related boundary study, without assuming EstateIQ currently uses this exact Gait integration.

title: Gait authentication integration checks
summary: Verify denials, outages and cache behavior before trusting the connected flow.
body:
## Run these in the consuming integration

These are proposed checks, not backend test results. Use disposable accounts and synthetic organization data, with the installed SDK and configured authority.

| Scenario | Expected boundary | Evidence to collect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Expired or malformed access token | Reject identity | No domain write |
| Wrong audience in configured verification mode | Reject identity | No fallback to a permissive mode |
| Valid identity, foreign organization | Deny domain access | No foreign rows or writes |
| Removed membership | Deny application operation | Current membership consulted |
| Revoked session during cached identity window | Sensitive live guard rejects | No protected mutation |
| Authority unavailable during required live check | Fail closed as unavailable | No mutation and no false logout diagnosis |
| Concurrent refresh in two tabs | Follow rotation/coordination policy | No silent credential corruption |
| Logout request fails | Local cleanup, server status unresolved | UI does not claim verified revocation |
| Retry after a committed command's response is lost | Apply command idempotency policy | No duplicate side effects |

## Distinguish the evidence

A unit test with a mocked verifier proves local branching. An integration test with a real authority tests transport and configuration. A browser test checks cookies, origins and tab coordination. None alone certifies the other layers.

The handbook's own browser suite verifies presentation and navigation only. Source inspection confirms the described code paths, not production key publication, provider availability or successful application integration.

title: Recipe: add a protected REST endpoint
summary: Add one operation with validation, scoped lookup and an explicit API contract.
body:
## Before you start

Use an existing Django/DRF application with authentication and a Task model. The [starter API](/guide/django-first-api) supplies the owner-scoped model, serializer and ViewSet. This excerpt adds a read-only completed-task endpoint; it does not expose general model editing.

## Files and implementation

Create `backend/apps/tasks/completed_views.py`, then mount the view from your existing app URL configuration.

```python
# backend/apps/tasks/completed_views.py — Return only the caller's completed tasks.
from rest_framework.decorators import api_view, permission_classes
from rest_framework.permissions import IsAuthenticated
from rest_framework.response import Response
from .models import Task
from .serializers import TaskSerializer

@api_view(["GET"])
@permission_classes([IsAuthenticated])
def completed_tasks(request):
    rows = Task.objects.filter(owner=request.user, completed=True).order_by("-id")[:100]
    return Response(TaskSerializer(rows, many=True).data)
```

Add a `path("completed-tasks/", completed_tasks)` entry to `apps/tasks/urls.py` while preserving its router routes; the project already mounts that app under `/api/`. Import `path` and the new view there. This example deliberately returns at most 100 rows; use a pagination contract when clients need the full collection.

## Verify in the application

Create completed and incomplete tasks for two users. Check that only the caller's completed tasks appear, anonymous access is denied, and POST is rejected. If the domain is organization-scoped, resolve active membership and apply organization scope as well. A valid identity alone is insufficient.

Continue with [view choices](/guide/django-views) and [serializer/permission boundaries](/guide/django-rest-boundaries).

title: Recipe: add scheduled backend work
summary: Separate the command, durable business job and scheduler that invokes it.
body:
## Before you start

Choose the scheduler available on your deployment platform and decide how missed or duplicate invocations are handled. A management command is an entry point; it is not a scheduler or a durable worker by itself.

## File and integration excerpt

Create the app's `management/` and `management/commands/` packages with `__init__.py` files. This harmless command is a smoke check for command discovery and scheduler invocation, not a production job runner.

```python
# backend/apps/tasks/management/commands/scheduler_probe.py — Verify a scheduler can invoke Django.
from django.core.management.base import BaseCommand
from django.utils import timezone

class Command(BaseCommand):
    help = "Print an invocation timestamp without changing application records."

    def handle(self, *args, **options):
        self.stdout.write(f"Scheduler probe invoked at {timezone.now().isoformat()}")
```

```bash
# Terminal — backend/, then the same environment through your chosen scheduler.
python manage.py scheduler_probe
```

Commit the command and configure the scheduler explicitly on the host. Keep credentials in its environment configuration. For real work, call a tested service or enqueue a durable job with a business identity; avoid burying the operation inside scheduler configuration.

## Verify

Confirm invocation time and exit status, timezone, disabled schedules and overlapping executions. Then test duplicate delivery, process failure and missed-run reconciliation for the actual operation. A timestamp only proves invocation—it does not prove business completion.

Use [reliable jobs](/guide/reliable-job-lifecycle) for outbox, leases and idempotency, and [scheduling and backups](/guide/backup-and-scheduled-tasks) for operational setup.

title: Lumen: the flagship clinical platform
summary: Source-backed service boundaries and a planned Gait-secured AWS deployment.
body:
## The flagship

Lumen is Anthony's flagship vascular ultrasound reporting platform. The owner intends to deploy its HTTP services to dedicated EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer and secure application identity through Gait. **The AWS architecture is proposed, not deployed or verified.**

## What the source establishes

| Boundary | Inspected responsibility | Design implication |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `lumen_ui` | React/Vite, Axios and organization-aware request context | Serve a static build; never put server secrets in it |
| `lumen_reports` | Django/DRF, reporting domains, organizations and facilities | Clinical workflow and permission authority |
| `lumen_media` | FastAPI, verified identity, exam authorization and object storage | File access needs the same tenant/facility boundary |
| `lumen_policy` | Shared deterministic authorization policy | Reuse policy without granting broad database privileges |
| Deployment wiring | Reverse proxy, health probes and staged database initialization | Container wiring is not an AWS deployment |
| Gait integration | Django SDK wiring and a Media verification adapter | Test each integration; do not assume identical cache/error behavior |

Older README diagrams name `lumen_ai`, but that directory is absent in the inspected checkout. AI is a future, separately gated tier in this design. Existing integration and production-build readiness still require a fresh application audit; this handbook did not run Lumen tests.

## Project architecture

```mermaid
%% handbook-project:lumen
flowchart TB
    Browser[React workspace] --> Reports[Django clinical workflows]
    Reports --> Clinical[Scoped clinical records]
    Gait[Gait verified identity] --> Membership[Organization and facility authorization]
    Membership --> Media[Private media access]
    Plan[Planned AWS ingress] --> Instances[Dedicated EC2 service instances]
    Instances --> Operations[Audit and recovery controls]
```

## Follow a clinical workflow

Resolve the authenticated identity, select the organization, prove active membership and apply facility/exam policy before reading or changing clinical records. Report calculations and workflow transitions remain server-owned. A browser form or AI suggestion cannot grant a role, finalize a report or bypass a locked state.

The Reports permission code sets transaction-local PostgreSQL tenant context only after membership succeeds. Media reads Reports-owned authorization facts and applies the shared policy before storage access. Those source boundaries complement each other; neither private networking nor a Gait token replaces them.

## Infrastructure is the next design layer

The [AWS topology](/guide/lumen-aws-architecture) maps ALB listeners and per-service target groups to private EC2 instances. The [security plan](/guide/lumen-aws-security) defines account, network, identity, data and operational controls. The [release gates](/guide/lumen-aws-release) describe the evidence required before real use.

This case study contains no patient data, production identifiers, internal security findings or cloud credentials.

title: Lumen on AWS: ALB and dedicated EC2 services
summary: A proposed AWS topology with public ingress, private service instances and explicit data boundaries.
body:
## Proposed topology, not deployed infrastructure

The owner's baseline is **one dedicated EC2 instance per application server, behind an ALB**. Use separate target groups for distinct services. This keeps service deployment boundaries explicit. A single instance per service is still a single point of failure; the resilient target repeats each critical tier across Availability Zones.

```mermaid
%% handbook-lumen-aws
flowchart TB
    Browser[Browser] --> Edge[HTTPS ALB with WAF]
    Edge --> UITG[UI target group]
    Edge --> ReportsTG[Reports target group]
    Edge --> MediaTG[Media target group]
    UITG --> UI[Private EC2: UI]
    ReportsTG --> Reports[Private EC2: Django]
    MediaTG --> Media[Private EC2: FastAPI]
    Reports -. verified identity .-> Gait[Gait authority]
    Media -. verified identity .-> Gait
    Reports --> DB[Private PostgreSQL]
    Media --> DB
    Media --> Storage[Private S3]
    Future[Future AI tier: approval required]
```

## Route services deliberately

Proposed names below are placeholders, not provisioned domains. Prefer host-based routing to avoid silently assuming ALB strips a path prefix.

| Listener rule | Target group | Dedicated private EC2 service |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `app.lumen.example` | UI | Nginx serving the React build and selected same-origin proxies |
| `reports.lumen.example` | Reports | Production Django/DRF process |
| `media.lumen.example` | Media | Production FastAPI process |
| Future AI host, disabled initially | AI, only after approval | Future isolated service; absent from this checkout |
| Unknown host | Fixed denial response | No arbitrary default forwarding |

An HTTPS listener uses a managed certificate covering the chosen names. Publish only the intended application endpoints; restrict administration and internal docs separately. [AWS listeners](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/load-balancer-listeners.html) evaluate configured rules and route to [target groups](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/load-balancer-target-groups.html).

The current Nginx config rewrites `/media-api/` to Media's `/api/` and proxies `/auth/` to Gait. Preserve or deliberately replace that behavior. A path-forwarding rule is not equivalent to a rewrite. Public Reports/Media hosts need exact browser CORS/CSRF decisions; a same-origin UI proxy needs correct upstream authentication and forwarding-header handling. Select one documented browser contract before deployment.

## Subnets and service placement

Place the internet-facing ALB in public subnets spanning at least two supported Availability Zones. Place EC2 services in private application subnets with no public IPs or direct internet ingress. Use separate private database subnets for the recommended RDS PostgreSQL tier. Object storage is S3, reached through a constrained endpoint policy where suitable; it is not an instance inside the VPC.

Use one target group and deployment policy per service. Start with a single registered instance only for an explicitly limited initial environment. The production target uses independently replaceable instances in multiple AZs, registered through service-specific Auto Scaling groups. The ALB spanning zones does not make a singleton Reports or Media instance redundant. See [ALB zone behavior](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/load-balancer-subnets.html).

## Gait is an authority, not an ALB shortcut

Gait verifies identity; Lumen still owns organization, facility, exam and operation permissions. Keep Gait as a separately operated dependency with a defined TLS endpoint and bounded egress. Moving it to AWS is a separate project decision. Do not claim ALB's built-in authentication automatically integrates with the current Gait API.

The UI login/refresh transport, Reports SDK version and Media adapter must pass one end-to-end production-shaped contract. An outage must not cause protected operations to bypass verification. Sensitive actions need the installed integration's explicit freshness/revocation policy; do not assume a cached identity check is live session validation.

## State and non-HTTP integrations

Recommended managed tiers are private RDS PostgreSQL and private S3 with service-specific access. Preserve Reports-owned clinical truth and Media's narrow authorization-fact reads; separate roles and ownership even if sharing a database. Redis/cache and durable workers are optional tiers whose delivery and recovery policy must be defined before enabling them.

HTTP APIs and WebSocket upgrades fit an ALB. A raw HL7/MLLP TCP listener does not become an HTTP service by putting it in a target group. Keep such integrations on a separate private/VPN-connected interface and assess an NLB only if required; see [NLB protocol support](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/network/introduction.html). Clinical integration readiness is not established by this diagram.

## Connections, health and resilience

Encrypt browser-to-ALB and ALB-to-service traffic. HTTPS target groups encrypt the second hop, but ALB does not validate target certificates; that is not mutual TLS identity proof. If authenticated end-to-end service identity is required, design and verify an appropriate additional control.

Reports source distinguishes shallow liveness from a deeper database/Redis probe. Choose per-service readiness endpoints and timeouts based on actual dependencies, with no sensitive response data. ALB health routing is not authorization: AWS documents fail-open routing if every registered target is unhealthy. Services must deny unauthorized operations regardless of target health. See [health-check behavior](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/target-group-health-checks.html).

Configure deregistration/draining around in-flight clinical writes, uploads and any supported live connections. A reconnect or retry needs domain idempotency and a fresh authorized snapshot. The [security plan](/guide/lumen-aws-security) makes the network and runtime controls concrete.

title: Lumen AWS security plan
summary: Proposed controls for accounts, private networking, Gait identity, clinical data and operational recovery.
body:
## Security target and scope

This is the proposed security baseline for Lumen's AWS deployment, not a security certification or an implemented control inventory. It follows a layered approach: assume a stolen user session, a compromised application instance, an operator mistake and a failed external dependency are all possible. Limit each one's authority and preserve evidence.

Lumen handles sensitive clinical information. Use synthetic data until infrastructure, application controls and organizational/vendor approvals have been independently checked. Gait and AWS services do not, by themselves, establish regulatory compliance. The [AWS Security Pillar](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/security-pillar/welcome.html) provides the broader review framework.

## 1. Separate accounts and administrative authority

Separate production from development/test accounts and data. Use an organizational security/logging boundary where practical. Protect the root identity, avoid root access keys and use federated short-lived operator sessions with MFA. Define least-privilege deploy, read-only, incident-response and database-migration roles. Require explicit approval for production changes and restrict who can change IAM, keys, logs and backups.

The build role should publish reviewed artifacts; it should not inherit unrestricted clinical database access. Foundry agents receive scoped development authority, not standing production credentials. Use CI federation to obtain short-lived AWS credentials rather than storing long-lived access keys in the repository. See [AWS IAM recommendations](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/best-practices.html).

## 2. Public edge, private services

Attach a WAF policy to the ALB, tune managed and application-specific rules with representative synthetic requests, and add rate controls for login, expensive actions and uploads. WAF reduces some edge threats; it does not validate clinical permissions or make an uploaded file safe. Avoid blanket body-size or inspection assumptions for large medical media. See [AWS WAF web ACLs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/web-acl.html).

Proposed network rule matrix:

| Destination | Allowed source | Allowed purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ALB listener | Intended clients, HTTPS 443 | Public application ingress; optionally HTTP only to redirect |
| UI instance service port | ALB security group | Static delivery and selected proxy routes |
| Reports service port | ALB group and explicitly approved internal callers | Clinical API only |
| Media service port | ALB group and approved proxy callers | Media API only |
| PostgreSQL port | Reports and Media groups only | Separate restricted database roles |
| Cache/broker, if introduced | Specific producer/consumer groups | Authenticated encrypted application use |
| AWS interface endpoints | Approved application groups on HTTPS | Only required service APIs |
| SSH/RDP | None | Use controlled Session Manager access |

Avoid broad VPC-CIDR grants, a shared all-services security group and unrestricted lateral traffic. UI has no database permission. Media receives no clinical write authority merely because it can read authorization facts. Block unnecessary public IPv4 and IPv6 paths.

Restrict egress to required service endpoints, Gait and approved providers. NAT supplies outbound connectivity; it is not a destination allowlist. Security groups do not implement hostname-based filtering: use a controlled egress proxy/firewall or a well-defined network design where domain restrictions are required. Use [VPC endpoints](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/privatelink/privatelink-access-aws-services.html) and endpoint policies for supported AWS APIs, with DNS/routing and service-specific access reviewed.

## 3. Harden each EC2 role

Use reviewed, patched images and immutable replacement deployments. Run application processes without root privileges, encrypt EBS volumes, restrict attached instance profiles and require [IMDSv2](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/configuring-instance-metadata-service.html). Test the metadata hop policy with the actual container layout rather than choosing it blindly.

Use [Session Manager](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/session-manager.html) with narrow operator roles, session limits and encrypted audit destinations instead of public SSH. Command-content recording is not available for SSH/port-forwarding sessions; restrict those modes rather than claiming they provide a full command transcript. Emergency access needs time bounds, approval and post-event review.

Build once, scan dependencies/images, record the artifact digest and deploy that exact candidate. Configure rollback without destructive automatic database reversal. No secrets in AMIs, build arguments, frontend bundles, user-data output or container images.

## 4. Gait identity plus local clinical permissions

Require MFA and recent-authentication evidence for privileged clinical/organization administration according to the approved Gait integration policy. Enforce that policy in the backend, not just a browser prompt; verify which endpoints and SDK versions actually support it before enabling those operations.

Verify credentials in each application service through its tested integration. Validate intended issuer/audience and session semantics for the configured mode. Preserve the distinction between invalid identity, insufficient domain permission and an unavailable authority. Fail required verification closed; neither a network outage nor a successful health probe can authorize access.

Resolve organization from the requested scope, then verify current membership, role and facility/exam policy. Scope records before lookup. Preserve tenant-aware query keys and cancel/clear private UI data when identity or organization changes. Recheck sensitive actions according to an explicit live-session policy, plus operation-specific authorization.

Verify CSRF protection for cookie-authenticated writes, exact origins for cross-origin browser calls and deliberate trusted-proxy handling. Do not trust arbitrary forwarded identity, IP or organization headers from the public client. Keep login/refresh behavior consistent between production UI builds and all API adapters.

## 5. Encrypt and constrain data access

Use private RDS networking, encrypted database storage and backups, verified TLS connections and separate application/migrator/owner roles. Never give web processes database-superuser or unrestricted RLS-bypass authority. Preserve transaction-local tenant context and test connection-pool reuse between tenants. Follow [RDS TLS configuration](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/UsingWithRDS.SSL.html).

Enable S3 Block Public Access at the intended account/bucket boundaries and use policies that deny insecure transport. Use narrowly scoped instance roles, explicit encryption/key policies and opaque object keys. A private bucket still requires application authorization before access or URL issuance. Presigned links remain bearer capabilities until their effective expiration or applicable policy change; set a deliberate lifetime. See [S3 public-access controls](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/access-control-block-public-access.html).

Use [Secrets Manager](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/secretsmanager/latest/userguide/best-practices.html) with per-service secret access, rotation and reload/recovery procedures. Restrict KMS decrypt authority as carefully as secret retrieval. Rotating a database credential without updating the running clients is an outage, not a completed control.

## 6. Clinical media and AI boundaries

Apply size/type limits, safe parsing and quarantine/scanning policies appropriate to the actual upload formats. Verify authorization before presigning, listing or downloading media. Redact clinical identifiers from object names, URLs and operational logs; protect the underlying clinical record and required audit history separately.

No clinical payload goes to a future external AI provider by default. AI remains disabled until permitted data classes, approved vendors, access policy, retention and evaluation are explicitly resolved.
