Never let generated text grant access, modify deterministic measurements or finalize a clinical record without the authorized workflow.

## 7. Evidence, alerting and incident response

Use CloudTrail for AWS control-plane activity with deliberate coverage and a protected logging destination. S3 object data events require explicit selection and cost/volume planning; they are not guaranteed by default trail creation. CloudWatch application telemetry and Lumen's clinical access/change audit are separate layers. [CloudTrail](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-user-guide.html) does not substitute for a patient-record access trail.

Collect redacted application events, deploy identities, infrastructure changes and security alarms. Avoid credentials, patient identifiers and signed URLs in logs. ALB/WAF logs can themselves contain sensitive request metadata; restrict their contents where supported and strictly control storage/access/retention. Retain required evidence under an approved policy instead of choosing arbitrary durations here.

Alert on unexpected administrative access, public exposure, suspicious identity failures, disabled logging, denied storage access, unhealthy targets and backup failures. Assign an owner and runbook to each actionable alarm. Plan isolation of a compromised instance, credential revocation, evidence preservation, replacement deployment and communication.

## 8. Recovery and availability

Use multiple instances/AZs for critical service tiers and a recommended Multi-AZ database configuration where the availability requirement justifies it. Multi-AZ improves availability but is not a backup. Define acceptable recovery time and data loss, retain protected database/object backups and test restoration into an isolated environment. Consider account-separated copies and deletion-resistant policies where required by the threat model.

Test the complete authorization state after recovery: clinical rows, media references, organization/facility membership, RLS policies and service grants. Do not reopen the application simply because the database accepts connections. The [release gate chapter](/guide/lumen-aws-release) records the checks that turn this design into reviewable evidence.

title: Lumen AWS release gates and recovery evidence
summary: Make the proposed architecture reviewable before deploying clinical workloads.
body:
## Keep the implementation status honest

Every control below is **planned and unverified by this handbook**. The Lumen checkout and its deployment notes establish source context; historical test counts or local container success are not current AWS evidence. No AWS account, instance, ALB, key, database or policy was changed here.

## Phase 1: decisions before provisioning

Record the AWS account/environment boundaries, region/AZ choices, public names, Gait endpoint and browser authentication contract. Approve the clinical data inventory and allowed processing/storage locations. Decide which tiers require multi-AZ operation and define recovery targets. Keep AI and raw HL7 ingress disabled until their separate boundaries are designed.

## Phase 2: reviewed infrastructure

Implement the [topology](/guide/lumen-aws-architecture) through reviewed infrastructure as code. Check planned changes for public instance/database exposure, excessive IAM, unintended routes and public buckets. Create the required secrets, keys, log destinations and alarms through authorized workflows; never paste their live values into handbook examples.

## Phase 3: application compatibility

Build the actual production UI and test login, refresh, logout and direct reload against Reports and Media. Confirm SDK/adapter identity shape, audience, error contracts and freshness behavior. A working development login does not prove a production build works.

Preserve Lumen's staged database initialization contract: provision required roles, apply Django and Media schema changes, apply RLS, restore runtime grants and verify the result. The inspected deployment script explicitly requires that sequence. Do not replace it with a generic bare migration command. Adapting the bootstrap to RDS requires reviewing its supported administrative privileges; RDS administration is not identical to a self-managed PostgreSQL superuser.

## Phase 4: adversarial and failure verification

| Check to execute | Required evidence |
| --- | --- |
| Internet probes against private service/database ports | No direct reachability outside approved ingress |
| ALB listener rules and unmatched host | Correct service mapping and explicit default denial |
| Wrong issuer/audience, expired/revoked session | Protected operations denied under configured verifier policy |
| Foreign organization and facility/exam IDs | No unauthorized rows, files or mutation |
| Gait timeout or invalid upstream response | No verification bypass; useful failure classification |
| Reused DB connection under another tenant | No retained tenant context or cross-tenant results |
| Unauthorized S3 access or leaked object identifier | Denial; documented signed-link expiry behavior |
| Instance loss and replacement | Correct target registration, readiness and recovery |
| All targets unhealthy | Services still enforce authorization despite ALB routing behavior |
| Upload/clinical mutation interrupted during deploy | Defined retry/idempotency and no corrupted state |
| Secret rotation and credential revocation | New credentials work; removed authority is denied |
| Database and object restoration | Consistent clinical/media links and restored authorization controls |
| Logging/alert simulation | Protected useful evidence without sensitive payload leakage |

Run these against synthetic data in a production-shaped environment before approval. Record the exact candidate, infrastructure revision, environment, test time, result and responsible reviewer. A checked planning list is not an executed test.

## Phase 5: controlled rollout

Deploy reviewed immutable artifacts, apply the approved schema plan, register targets, check readiness and promote deliberately. Observe clinical workflows and deny unexpected access before opening broader traffic. Preserve a rollback path compatible with the schema changes. Avoid unreviewed emergency edits directly on instances.

## Recovery exercise

If a Media instance fails, remove or drain it according to the incident and deployment policy, preserve necessary evidence, replace it with the approved image and verify membership/exam authorization before returning it to service. A replacement instance should recover from durable storage and secrets rather than copied local uploads or handwritten configuration.

If a credential is compromised, containment and revocation come before casually restoring the same instance image with the same secret. Coordinate Gait/session response and AWS service-role response according to which authority was affected.

## Release decision

Proceed only when required technical evidence and applicable organizational/vendor approvals are complete. This handbook describes a design and proposed checks, not approval to process real clinical data or a claim of compliance.

title: Troubleshoot: browser request blocked or rejected
summary: Separate transport, CORS, CSRF, credentials and API permission failures.
body:
## Symptom

The browser reports a network/CORS failure, a session write returns 403, or a request works in curl but fails in React. Do not assume all three have the same cause.

## 1. Inspect the actual request chain

Open DevTools Network and record the frontend origin, API URL, method and status without copying credentials. Check whether OPTIONS ran, whether the actual request followed, and whether either redirected. A path mistake can route an API request into the frontend HTML fallback.

| Observation | Next check |
| --- | --- |
| HTTPS page calls HTTP API | Mixed-content blocking; fix the API URL/TLS |
| OPTIONS redirects to login | Proxy/preflight route handling |
| No actual request after preflight | Allowed origin, method and requested headers |
| Actual request returns 401/403 | Read its safe error contract and server-side classification |
| JSON client receives HTML | Host/path routing or SPA fallback |
| Server returns 500 without CORS headers | Investigate the backend error as well as middleware placement |

## 2. Follow the chosen authentication transport

For bearer auth, confirm the intended API receives the header; do not expose its value in notes. For cookie sessions, inspect cookie presence, credentials policy and applicable browser restrictions. Verify CSRF origin and token handling for unsafe requests. `withCredentials` does not create a login, and a trusted origin does not remove the CSRF token requirement.

The [CORS guide](/guide/django-cors) explains exact origins, middleware and deployment choices. The [React connection](/guide/react-api-connection) uses a development proxy; its success does not establish production cross-origin behavior.

## 3. Correct the narrow mismatch

Fix the URL, configured origin, preflight route or authentication/CSRF flow established by the evidence. Do not enable every origin, disable CSRF, or retry a failed write blindly. A request can commit even if the browser cannot expose its response; inspect the durable outcome before resubmission.

## Verify the correction

Repeat the original request from the intended deployed origin. Confirm a forbidden origin remains unreadable, missing/invalid credentials remain denied, and an unsafe session write with a missing token remains rejected. Check that no extra record was created during retries.

These are proposed application checks. The handbook does not intercept your browser requests or inspect a running API.

title: Troubleshoot: Gait login, token or permission denial
summary: Locate identity, session freshness and local authorization failures without weakening verification.
body:
## Symptom

Login appears successful but the API denies access, refresh repeats, or a protected operation stops working during a provider outage.

## 1. Identify the failing boundary

| Boundary | Evidence to inspect |
| --- | --- |
| Browser login/second factor | Status and safe error code; pending step and configured transport |
| Refresh | Retry count, rotation behavior and cross-tab coordination |
| Token verification | Configured issuer/audience/mode, expiry, installed SDK/adapter version |
| Session freshness | Whether this operation requires an uncached live-session check |
| Application authorization | Current local account, active organization/facility membership and operation role |

Do not paste a JWT into public decoding tools or the manual. Inspect only required claims in an approved local workflow. Decoding a token is not signature verification.

## 2. Distinguish invalid from unavailable

An invalid credential, a valid identity lacking permission and an unavailable verification service need different handling. Inspect the installed adapter's actual mapping instead of inferring everything from a status number. Django session authentication can return 403 for anonymous requests; not every denial triggers a bearer refresh.

The inspected SDK's Django introspection adapter can cache successful identity checks. A cached success is not a current session-liveness result. See [verification modes](/guide/gait-api-verification) and the [connected walkthrough](/guide/gait-auth-walkthrough).

## 3. Fix the contract, not the denial

Match the product's intended origin/audience registration, production browser transport and backend verification policy. Ensure refresh retries are bounded and use a separate transport path to avoid interceptor recursion. Repeated requests from two tabs require an explicit rotation/coordination policy.

If membership or a role was removed, denial may be the correct result. Never bypass domain permission checks because Gait recognizes the user. Do not switch to a permissive verifier when the authority is unavailable.

## Verify the correction

Test a synthetic valid account, wrong audience where applicable, expired token, removed membership, foreign record and provider outage. Confirm required live-session failures prevent mutation. On logout, clear private client state and distinguish local cleanup from verified server revocation.

Lumen's production-shaped identity compatibility is a [release gate](/guide/lumen-aws-release), not something established by this manual's source inspection.

title: Troubleshoot: ALB errors and unhealthy targets
summary: Separate load-balancer failures from target application responses and permission denials.
body:
## Symptom and scope

An AWS-hosted application returns 502/503/504, a target is unhealthy, or only one service hostname fails. This is a diagnostic reference for the **planned Lumen AWS architecture**, not a record of a live incident or a deployed ALB.

## 1. Identify which layer generated the response

Compare the request's host/path and time window with approved ALB access-log fields, target status and application correlation evidence. An application-generated error and an ALB-generated error can have the same visible status but different causes. Keep sensitive request metadata out of shared notes.

The [AWS ALB troubleshooting reference](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/load-balancer-troubleshooting.html) is the upstream source for service-specific failure causes. A gateway status is a starting signal, not a diagnosis.

## 2. Inspect the target path

Check the listener rule, target group, protocol, port and registered target. Compare readiness behavior with process liveness. Inspect service binding, target security group, ALB egress and network routing. A target can serve its root page while its real API dependency is unavailable.

```bash
# Read-only AWS CLI example — substitute an authorized account's identifiers and region.
aws elbv2 describe-target-health   --target-group-arn '<target-group-arn>'   --region '<aws-region>'   --query 'TargetHealthDescriptions[].{State:TargetHealth.State,Reason:TargetHealth.Reason}'
```

The placeholders are intentional. This command is not executed by the handbook and does not repair anything.

## 3. Investigate the matching evidence

| Evidence | Investigation |
| --- | --- |
| No targets registered | Deployment registration and intended target group |
| Health-check mismatch | Actual path, host handling, matcher and dependencies |
| Target connection failure | Service listener, protocol/port and narrowly scoped network rules |
| Request times out | Application/dependency timing and configured timeout relationship |
| Only one host/path fails | Listener priority, forwarding and backend URL contract |
| Target returns an authorization error | Application/Gait policy, not automatic load-balancer failure |

ALB routing can fail open when all targets are unhealthy; service authorization must still hold. HTTPS target groups also do not establish backend certificate validation. See the [planned topology](/guide/lumen-aws-architecture).

## Verify without opening the perimeter

Correct the demonstrated cause, then check the original authorized request, a denied application request and a deliberately unregistered/unmatched route. Keep EC2 and database services private. During a rollout, verify target draining and retry/idempotency behavior before repeating a clinical write. Record any actual AWS validation separately from this proposed design.

title: Troubleshoot: stale or incorrect React query data
summary: Trace the authoritative response, query identity and invalidation before forcing a reload.
body:
## Symptom

A successful save is not visible, switching organizations shows an old list, or the UI changes only after a full reload.

## 1. Establish whether the write succeeded

Inspect the authoritative mutation response and a scoped read of the resulting record. A stale cache and a server-side failure need different corrections. A lost response can follow a committed write; do not automatically submit it again.

## 2. Inspect the exact query identity

Compare the key used by the reader with the key targeted by the mutation. Include the current user or organization and normalized filters that change the representation. Check whether the query is enabled and whether the component observes the intended QueryClient/provider.

```typescript
// frontend/src/features/reports/queryKeys.ts — Keep list identity explicit.
export const reportKeys = {
  list: (orgSlug: string, status: string) =>
    ['org', orgSlug, 'reports', 'list', { status }] as const,
};
```

Do not include unstable timestamps or unrelated UI state just to force fresh fetches. Conversely, omitting organization identity can mix snapshots across workspaces. Keys partition client data; backend authorization remains required.

## 3. Follow downstream consumers

A mutation may affect a detail view, several filtered lists and derived aggregates. Update a known detail entry with an authoritative representation or invalidate the relevant scoped consumers. Await invalidation when a subsequent redirect depends on its completion. See the [query mutation recipe](/guide/recipe-query-mutation).

Invalidating is not a promise that every disabled or unobserved query immediately sends a request. Inspect the query's lifecycle and actual network activity. A UI holding a copied local snapshot may also ignore a correctly refreshed cache.

## Verify the correction

Test the original mutation, a filtered list, organization change during an in-flight request, logout and a different user's next session. Confirm old requests cannot repopulate the active view with private data. Avoid a global browser reload as the only evidence of a cache fix.

The [frontend contract guide](/guide/frontend-state-contracts) explains server-state ownership, downstream consumers and workspace behavior. This chapter does not run queries against any project backend.

title: Troubleshoot: a job is missing, late or duplicated
summary: Separate scheduler invocation, delivery attempts and durable business outcomes.
body:
## Symptom

A scheduled task appears not to run, a report processes twice, or a retry repeats an external effect.

## 1. Trace one business operation

Record a safe business-job identifier, scheduled occurrence, attempt identifier and environment. Check scheduler invocation, enqueue/outbox state, delivery, worker start, lease/claim, durable result and any external side effect separately.

A scheduler timestamp proves invocation. A broker acknowledgement proves a delivery event under its contract. Neither alone proves the business operation completed.

## 2. Find the missing or repeated boundary

| Observation | Next evidence |
| --- | --- |
| No invocation | Scheduler enabled state, timezone and intended release/configuration |
| Invocation but no job | Enqueue failure, transaction rollback or unpublished outbox entry |
| Queued but not claimed | Worker process, routing, credentials and queue subscription |
| Claimed but unfinished | Crash, timeout, expired lease or external-provider failure |
| Result exists but attempt retries | Acknowledgement/response loss and idempotency policy |
| Effect happened twice | Deduplication identity, lock/constraint and external-provider replay semantics |

## 3. Recover according to the operation

Before replaying, inspect the authoritative result. Reuse the same business identity where the contract supports exact replay, and reject the same key with a conflicting payload. Bound retries and quarantine exhausted attempts for explicit handling.

Do not delete deduplication state, purge queues or mark a clinical/financial operation complete solely to clear an alert. Preserve enough evidence to reconcile the durable record with any external effect. For a required future schedule occurrence, distinguish catching up a missed event from accidentally rerunning a completed one.

## Transaction timing matters

Publish after commit to avoid workers observing rolled-back records. A post-commit callback alone cannot recover from a process crash before delivery; use durable intent/outbox where loss is unacceptable. The [Django transaction reference](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/5.2/topics/db/transactions/) explains commit callback behavior; [reliable jobs](/guide/reliable-job-lifecycle) covers the wider lifecycle.

## Verify the correction

Exercise duplicate delivery, crash before/after commit, external response loss, worker restart, overlapping schedules and a missed occurrence using synthetic data. Confirm one intended durable effect, a truthful terminal state and an operator-visible failure when recovery is exhausted. These are proposed checks, not jobs executed by the handbook.

title: Troubleshoot: a migration or release schema check fails
summary: Inspect migration state, privileges and application compatibility before retrying a deployment.
body:
## Symptom

A deploy fails during schema changes, the application reports a missing column, or authorization breaks after a migration.

## 1. Preserve the first error and target identity

Record the release revision, intended database/environment, migration name and safe error category. Confirm the command used the expected settings and database role without printing a connection string or password.

```bash
# Read-only framework diagnostics — backend/ in the intended application environment.
python manage.py showmigrations --plan
python manage.py makemigrations --check --dry-run
```

`showmigrations` reads migration history. The second command checks whether model changes need migration files; it does not prove the existing database schema matches them. Neither command applies a migration or replaces the project's release process.

## 2. Classify the failure

| Observation | Investigate |
| --- | --- |
| Missing migration file | Candidate/branch contents and committed dependencies |
| Applied history disagrees | Database target and release/migration history |
| Constraint or backfill failure | Existing data, bounded repair plan and concurrent writes |
| Lock wait or timeout | Blocking transactions and operational migration strategy |
| Permission/view errors | Role ownership and restored grants/RLS policy |
| New code sees old schema | Rollout ordering and compatibility window |

Do not reach for `--fake`, drop a database, edit applied migration history or grant superuser as a generic fix. Those actions can hide a mismatch or destroy evidence. Diagnose and review a repair suitable to the actual environment.

## 3. Respect the application's migration contract

Lumen's inspected initialization sequence includes roles, Reports migrations, Media schema, RLS, runtime grants and verification. A bare migrate can be insufficient for its full authorization contract. Its proposed RDS deployment also needs a privilege-compatibility review. Follow the [Lumen release gates](/guide/lumen-aws-release), not a generic reset recipe.

For safer changes, separate expanding the schema, backfilling records and enforcing the final constraint when necessary. Plan coexistence of old/new application versions and a rollback compatible with the data change.

## Verify the correction

Use a representative isolated database to test the migration and application compatibility. Recheck constraints, tenant policies, service grants and affected queries. Validate backup restoration before destructive changes. A successful migration exit code alone does not prove clinical/tenant authorization still works.

The handbook executes no database commands; these examples require the application's approved diagnostic access.

title: API contracts: make client and server agree
summary: Define representations, validation errors, pagination, retries and compatibility before implementing both sides.
body:
## Write the contract before the integration

For each operation, record the URL/method, authentication, authorized scope, input, output, expected errors, side effects and retry policy. Include an example using synthetic records. The contract is a shared dependency of the React request function, Django serializer/view and tests.

The starter Tasks API is deliberately simple and unpaginated. The conventions below describe choices for a larger application; they do not silently change that starter's response shape.

## Keep representations explicit

List writable fields and distinguish server-managed IDs, timestamps, organization and workflow status. Give money, dates, timezones and missing values explicit representations. Validate related IDs against the same authorized scope. TypeScript types document the client expectation but do not validate arbitrary JSON at runtime.

Use serializers and a published schema to expose the intended representation. Validate responses at sensitive or untrusted boundaries where runtime validation is justified. Do not return raw model dictionaries with accidental internal fields.

## Pick one list contract

A conventional paginated response can use the DRF page-number structure:

```json
{
  "count": 1,
  "next": null,
  "previous": null,
  "results": [{ "id": 42, "title": "Synthetic task", "completed": false }]
}
```

Choose bounded page sizes, permitted filters and stable ordering. Document whether changing data can move records between pages; choose cursor semantics deliberately for rapidly changing collections. A frontend expecting an array must be updated when pagination is introduced. See the [DRF pagination reference](https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/pagination/).

## Make errors actionable

Define field errors, operation errors and unavailable dependencies separately. DRF's default responses do not automatically use a custom application envelope. If the team chooses one, implement the serializer/exception mapping consistently and test it.

```json
{
  "code": "validation_failed",
  "message": "Check the highlighted fields.",
  "fields": { "title": ["Enter a title."] },
  "request_id": "synthetic-request-42"
}
```

This is a proposed envelope, not an existing default. Keep raw exceptions, credentials and sensitive record contents out of the public response. A safe correlation identifier should lead an authorized operator to protected evidence.

## Decide retries and idempotency

A timeout does not prove a write failed. For commands that need safe replay, define key scope, payload fingerprint, retention, in-progress behavior and replay response. The same key with conflicting input must not perform a different operation. Use durable uniqueness/transaction rules rather than only a client-side disabled button.

Document whether an operation finishes immediately or accepts a job whose status must be observed. A successful HTTP acceptance response is not completed background work. Follow the [Reports contract](/guide/reports-contract) for a worked example.

## Evolve without surprise

Adding an optional response field is different from renaming a required field, changing pagination or altering permissions. Plan a compatibility window and explicit versioning/deprecation policy for breaking changes. Update consumers and contract tests together; an OpenAPI document alone does not prove deployed compatibility.

## Verify

Check successful and invalid input, forbidden/read-only field injection, anonymous and foreign-scope access, pagination boundaries, retry after response loss and old/new client behavior. These are proposed application checks, not tests executed by this handbook.

title: Database changes: expand, backfill, then enforce
summary: Plan schema evolution around live data, old clients, permissions and recovery.
body:
## Treat a migration as a release operation

Record the affected table size, existing data, dependent code, lock/concurrency behavior, expected duration and failure plan. Review generated migrations before applying them. Use a representative isolated database and the production database engine for meaningful rehearsal.

## A safe change has stages

For a new required field on existing rows, a useful pattern is:

1. **Expand:** add a compatible nullable/default-capable representation as appropriate to the database and workload.
2. **Deploy compatible code:** support old and new records during the transition and prevent creation of new invalid data.
3. **Backfill:** update existing rows in bounded, restartable batches with a measured load policy.
4. **Verify:** check remaining nulls/invalid values and race conditions with concurrent writes.
5. **Enforce:** add the intended constraint and retire the compatibility code in a reviewed later step.

This is a planning pattern, not a claim that every schema change requires five releases. Select the actual database operation after inspecting generated SQL and its locking behavior.

## Keep data migrations historical

Use Django's migration app registry for model state inside `RunPython`; importing today's application model can make an old migration depend on future code. Preserve dependencies when a migration touches another app. Define reversibility honestly: a destructive transformation may need restoration rather than a meaningful reverse function. See [Django's migration guidance](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/5.2/howto/writing-migrations/).

A large backfill can be better represented as separately supervised work than one long transaction. Define progress, retry, idempotency and how the final constraint is gated on completion.

## Preserve authorization infrastructure

Schema changes can affect views, grants, RLS and runtime roles as well as columns. Test the application under its actual restricted database roles. For Lumen, preserve the staged schema/RLS/grant verification process described in its [AWS release plan](/guide/lumen-aws-release); do not replace it with a generic migration command.

## Separate code rollback from data rollback

Can the previous application revision still run after the new schema change? Can the new revision tolerate records created by the old one? Answer those questions before rollout. Removing a column or rewriting clinical/financial data may make a simple code rollback insufficient.

Take the appropriate protected recovery point, verify restoration beforehand and define who can authorize a destructive recovery. Do not automatically reverse migrations after an application error without assessing what data was written.

## Release evidence

Record the candidate and migration set, reviewed SQL/plan, rehearsal results, data validation, permissions checks, deployment sequence and recovery decision. Exercise interruption during backfill and verify restart behavior. Use the [migration troubleshooting guide](/guide/troubleshoot-migrations) when the actual environment differs from the plan.

No migration, database or backup operation is executed by this handbook.

title: Testing strategy: prove the right boundary
summary: Choose checks by risk and distinguish source review, isolated tests and live integration evidence.
body:
## Start with what could go wrong

Name the invariant before selecting a test tool: another organization cannot read this row; an exact retry cannot create a second charge; an unavailable identity service cannot authorize a protected operation. A test is useful when its failure would reveal a meaningful regression.

## Match the evidence to the claim

| Check | What it can establish | What it does not establish alone |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Type/static checks | Certain structural/type mistakes | Runtime authorization or actual provider configuration |
| Unit test | A deterministic rule under selected inputs | Real database, network or framework wiring |
| Database/service test | Constraints, transactions and workflow behavior | Browser cookies or deployed networking |
| API test | Request validation, scoping and response contracts | Real identity verification if authentication is bypassed/mocked |
| Integration test | Actual component interoperability in the tested environment | Every failure mode or production equivalence |
| Browser test | User flow, rendering, navigation and selected interactions | Backend security when data/providers are synthetic |
| Concurrency/failure test | Behavior under a controlled race or crash window | All possible interleavings |
| Deployment smoke check | Selected live routes and configuration | Complete security review or recovery readiness |

Source inspection helps explain behavior; it is not an executed test. Preserve that distinction in release notes.

## Build a small risk-based matrix

For a protected write, cover valid input, invalid input, unauthenticated identity, insufficient role, foreign tenant/related ID, exact retry, conflicting replay and failure after commit. For a read, check list/detail scoping, pagination, query cost and private-file behavior.

Use the target database for locks, RLS and database-specific constraints. Transaction-wrapped test helpers can hide the absence of a required production transaction; choose the appropriate framework test class for the behavior. Review the [Django testing overview](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/5.2/topics/testing/overview/) alongside the application's test setup.

## Test the interface independently too

Check loading, empty, error, stale-refresh and unavailable-auth states. Verify keyboard use, mobile containment and direct route reloads. Exercise user/organization changes while requests are in flight. A screenshot can catch visual regressions but does not prove a command was authorized.

## Keep fakes truthful

A mocked token verifier is appropriate for testing local permission branches. Add a separate real-authority integration check for issuer/audience, cookies, revocation policy and outage behavior. A browser-only lab should call its data synthetic, not imply a production database transaction occurred.

## Record useful evidence

State the candidate revision, environment, command/check, outcome and relevant limitation. Prefer focused checks that prove the changed behavior. Broaden testing when changes, failures or unresolved risks justify it, rather than repeatedly running unrelated suites.

The [Django starter test](/guide/django-testing-delivery), [Reports verification](/guide/reports-verification) and [Lumen release gates](/guide/lumen-aws-release) show different levels of evidence. This manual's own browser checks verify the handbook's presentation and interactions.

title: Operational runbooks: respond, recover, verify
summary: Use defined response paths for deploy failures, identity outages, credentials and data restoration.
body:
## Before an incident

Know the owner, environment, last accepted revision, safe diagnostic access, alert source and escalation path. Each application needs its own operational values and approved access; this chapter provides the structure, not live credentials or a claim that a recovery was executed.

Use the same sequence: establish impact, preserve safe evidence, contain the failure, recover deliberately, verify the original and denied paths, then record follow-up work.

## Failed deployment

**Recognize:** distinguish a build failure, rejected migration, unhealthy target and application regression. Record the candidate and first failure rather than repeatedly deploying a moving branch.

**Recover:** stop promotion, preserve the previous known working artifact and check schema compatibility before rollback. Restore target routing according to the approved deployment policy. Avoid destructive database reversal as an automatic response to a web-process failure.

**Verify:** check the affected feature, authentication, tenant boundaries, target readiness and in-flight command outcomes. Follow [migration troubleshooting](/guide/troubleshoot-migrations) or the [ALB path](/guide/troubleshoot-alb) for the failing boundary.

## Gait or identity provider unavailable

**Recognize:** separate unreachable authority, invalid credentials and local permission denial. Inspect safe timing/status evidence and the configured adapter contract.

**Recover:** preserve fail-closed behavior where verification is required. Do not grant access from an unverified token or disable a live-session guard to restore availability. Restore the approved dependency or configuration and communicate the degraded experience.

**Verify:** use a synthetic valid account and invalid/revoked identity, plus sensitive operation checks. Confirm the UI does not mislabel every unavailable response as a wrong password. See [authentication troubleshooting](/guide/troubleshoot-authentication).

## Suspected compromised credential

**Contain:** identify which authority is affected: user session, application credential, AWS role, database password or deployment identity. Restrict affected capabilities and preserve approved evidence. Do not copy the credential into a ticket or chat.

**Recover:** coordinate revocation/rotation with the responsible identity or platform owner, update consumers deliberately and replace compromised hosts/artifacts as required. Do not assume changing one secret instantly invalidates every previously issued session or temporary credential; verify the actual policy and effective revocation.

**Verify:** prove removed authority is denied, intended new authority works and protected logs/configuration were not silently altered. Review possible exposure and required communication through the incident process. Lumen's AWS controls remain [planned](/guide/lumen-aws-security).

## Database outage or inconsistent state

**Recognize:** distinguish connectivity, resource pressure, locks, schema failure and suspected corruption. Avoid replaying uncertain clinical/financial writes without inspecting durable outcomes.

**Recover:** select a tested failover or restoration path appropriate to the fault. Multi-AZ availability is not a substitute for a backup. Isolate a restored copy and verify it before reconnecting normal application traffic.

**Verify:** check constraints, tenant membership/policies/grants, job/outbox state and file references, not just a successful database connection. Use the [recovery runbook](/guide/recovery-runbook) for restoration evidence.

## Private files missing after restore

**Recognize:** separate a missing object, stale identifier, expired signed link and correct permission denial. Preserve the record/object mapping and approved audit evidence.

**Recover:** reconcile database and storage recovery points. Restore the required protected objects through the approved process; do not make a bucket public or bypass document authorization to test access.

**Verify:** read a synthetic authorized document and reject a foreign tenant's request. Confirm metadata, retention and clinical record relationships remain consistent.

## Close the incident with evidence

Record impact, timeline, affected revisions, containment/recovery actions, actual verification and unresolved work. Update the relevant troubleshooting guide after reviewing what happened. Do not mark a drill, synthetic exercise or written checklist as proof of a real recovery.

title: Git: repository to pull request
summary: Start a repository, commit a focused change, open a PR, and merge with confidence.
body:
## When to use this

Use this path at the start of a build, before Foundry assigns work. Git records revisions; GitHub hosts collaboration. A commit is local until pushed. A pull request proposes a branch change for review; it does not deploy by itself.

## 1. Create or clone

For a new project, create an empty GitHub repository with your chosen visibility. Leave its initial README unchecked when pushing an existing local project. Replace OWNER and REPO below. First check `git status`: if you are already in a repository, do not initialize a nested one.

```sh
mkdir build-demo
cd build-demo
git init -b main
git config user.name "Your Name"
git config user.email "your-public-or-noreply-email@example.com"
```

Create a README and the [root, backend and frontend ignore files](/guide/full-stack-folder-structure) before staging. Review what will be public. `.gitignore` does not remove an already tracked secret; rotate an exposed credential.

```sh
git status --short
git add README.md .gitignore
git diff --staged
git commit -m "Initialize project"
git remote add origin https://github.com/OWNER/REPO.git
git push -u origin main
```

For an existing remote, use `git clone https://github.com/OWNER/REPO.git` instead, then `cd REPO`. Authenticate through your approved GitHub credential setup; never embed a token in the URL.

## 2. Branch and make one change

Start with a clean working directory and an up-to-date main. Edit README.md after creating the branch.

```sh
git switch main
git pull --ff-only origin main
git switch -c feat/build-notes
git diff
git add README.md
git diff --staged
git commit -m "Document local build steps"
git push -u origin feat/build-notes
```

Run the project's checks before pushing. Stage named paths so unrelated edits stay out of review. See the [Git tutorial](https://git-scm.com/docs/gittutorial).

## 3. Review a pull request

On GitHub, open **Compare & pull request**. Select base `main` and compare `feat/build-notes`; inspect Files changed. Describe the problem, resulting behavior and actual checks run. Use a draft while work remains. Review the final commit and wait for required checks before merging. See [GitHub's PR steps](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/how-tos/create-pull-requests/creating-a-pull-request).

Choose the repository's agreed merge method. A merge commit preserves branch topology; squash combines the PR into one commit; rebase-and-merge replays commits. After a squash merge, Git may not recognize the original branch as merged, so `branch -d` can refuse deletion. Verify the PR before deciding on cleanup.

## 4. Handle a conflict deliberately

To bring current main into your feature branch, start clean, then:

```sh
git fetch origin
git switch feat/build-notes
git merge origin/main
```

If Git reports conflicts, inspect `git status`, edit each conflicted file, remove conflict markers, and preserve the intended behavior from both changes. Stage resolved paths, rerun checks, then `git commit` and push the branch. To abandon this unfinished merge, use `git merge --abort`; starting clean makes recovery predictable. See [merge documentation](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-merge).

## Verify and recover

After the PR merges, switch to main and `git pull --ff-only origin main`. Confirm the merged behavior and a clean `git status`. If a pull refuses to fast-forward, inspect the history instead of forcing it. If you committed to the wrong branch, preserve the commit on a new branch before changing anything. Use the [command reference](/guide/git-command-reference) for safer undo choices.

title: Git command reference
summary: Find everyday Git commands by intent, with clear boundaries for destructive operations.
body:
## Choose the intent first

These are reference commands, not a script to run from top to bottom. Replace uppercase placeholders with your actual paths or revisions. Read `git status` before changing state. Search the handbook for a command or symptom to return here.

## Inspect without changing files

| Intent | Command | Read the result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Working directory and staging | `git status --short --branch` | Confirm the branch and pending files |
| Unstaged edits | `git diff` | Not yet selected for the next commit |
| Staged edits | `git diff --staged` | Exactly what the next commit records |
| Branch history | `git log --oneline --graph --decorate -15` | Follow recent commits and pointers |
| PR-sized comparison | `git diff origin/main...HEAD` | Changes since the branches' common ancestor |
| Remote names | `git remote -v` | Check destinations; do not share credential-bearing output |
| Worktree locations | `git worktree list` | Find where branches are checked out |

The [Git command index](https://git-scm.com/docs) links to each command's full options.

## Save, share and integrate

| Intent | Command | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Select one file | `git add PATH` | Stages its current content |
| Record selected changes | `git commit -m "Describe the outcome"` | Creates a local commit |
| New feature branch | `git switch -c feat/NAME` | Creates and switches branches |
| Fetch remote history | `git fetch origin` | Updates remote-tracking references; no merge |
| Update clean main | `git pull --ff-only origin main` | Stops if integration needs a divergent merge |
| First branch push | `git push -u origin feat/NAME` | Publishes the branch and sets its upstream |
| Merge current main into feature | `git merge origin/main` | Run while on the feature branch |
| Stop an unfinished merge | `git merge --abort` | Returns toward pre-merge state; begin merges clean |

A PR is created on GitHub after pushing. Follow the [repository-to-PR walkthrough](/guide/git-basics) for base/compare selection and review.

## Undo the smallest thing

**Keep edits, change staging:** `git restore --staged PATH` removes that path from the next commit while retaining working-file edits.

**Discard edits:** `git restore PATH` replaces unstaged tracked-file content from the index. This loses those edits. Review the diff and save anything needed first. It does not delete untracked files. See [restore](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-restore).

**Reverse a shared commit:** `git revert COMMIT` creates a new inverse commit; inspect and test it, then submit it for review. Reverting a merge needs an explicit parent choice and should be planned separately. See [revert](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-revert).

**Park unfinished edits:** `git stash push -u -m "Describe unfinished work"` includes untracked files, but not ignored files. Use `git stash list`, then `git stash apply` to restore while retaining the stash. Apply can conflict. Only `git stash drop` after verifying the restored work. See [stash](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-stash).

**Find a recent local pointer:** `git reflog` can help locate a previous commit. Create `git branch rescue/NAME COMMIT` to retain it before attempting recovery. Reflog is local and expires; it is not a backup. See [reflog](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-reflog).

## Cleanup with evidence

`git branch -d feat/NAME` deletes a local branch only when Git's merge checks allow it. Remote deletion (`git push origin --delete feat/NAME`) affects collaborators; verify the PR is merged and no task still uses it. Never use force deletion just to suppress an unexplained refusal.

`reset --hard`, `clean -fd`, and force pushes can discard files or rewrite shared history. They are intentionally outside this everyday workflow. Stop and identify what must survive before choosing one.

title: Git worktrees for Foundry tasks
summary: Give parallel tasks separate directories, integrate reviewed branches, and clean up safely.
body:
## When a second directory helps

Use a worktree when a task needs its own checkout while another task remains open. A branch names a line of commits; a worktree gives a branch a working directory and staging area. Linked worktrees share repository objects and references. They are not separate security boundaries.

## Create two task checkouts

This standalone Git exercise assumes a repository with a clean, committed main and an origin remote. Run it from the repository root. The sibling directories must not already exist.

```sh
git switch main
git pull --ff-only origin main
git worktree add -b feat/api-notes ../build-api-notes main
git worktree add -b feat/client-notes ../build-client-notes main
git worktree list
```

One branch normally cannot be checked out in two worktrees at once. Choose unique task names. Each checkout needs its own ignored `.env`, dependencies and distinct local ports where applicable. These do not copy automatically. See [Git worktree documentation](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-worktree).

## Match Foundry's task ownership

For a Foundry-managed task, follow [the first-task workflow](/guide/foundry-first-task) and its assigned workspace instead of creating a competing checkout. The standalone commands above explain the Git mechanism; they do not register or approve a Foundry task.

Give each agent its task, exact directory, permitted paths and acceptance criteria. Ask it to verify `pwd`, `git branch --show-current` and `git status` before editing. A separate directory prevents accidental checkout collisions; it does not prevent overlapping changes or grant deployment authority. Shared files still need coordination.

## Review and integrate

In each task directory, stage only the task's changes, run its checks and commit. Push its branch and open its PR using [the Git walkthrough](/guide/git-basics). Review against the latest main and run integration checks after merging. If conflicts appear, resolve their behavior rather than selecting one whole side blindly.

A Foundry implementation commit still needs its required review and release evidence. A Git merge or a green local test is not an owner release decision. Follow [Foundry review and release](/guide/foundry-review-release).

## Remove finished checkouts

After the corresponding PR is merged and local work is accounted for, run from the original repository:

```sh
git -C ../build-api-notes status --short
git worktree remove ../build-api-notes
git branch -d feat/api-notes
git worktree list
```

Removal deletes the linked directory. Keep any ignored local files you still need first, and never force removal to bypass unfinished work. Repeat for the second task when it is finished. Squash merges can require separate branch-cleanup review; a refusal from `branch -d` is a reason to inspect.

## Verify and troubleshoot

The original main checkout should contain the integrated behavior, and removed paths should disappear from `worktree list`. If Git says a branch is already checked out, locate its existing directory. Use `worktree remove` rather than deleting folders by hand; `worktree prune --dry-run` can preview stale metadata cleanup after a directory was removed externally.

title: Deploy Django on Heroku
summary: Prepare a Django API, release migrations, and verify the first Heroku deployment.
body:
## Scope and prerequisites

This is a reference deployment for your Django API with React delivered separately. It does not provision anything from the handbook. Use a staging app first. Heroku dynos and add-ons can incur charges; select their plans in the dashboard deliberately. No plan name or price is assumed here.

Start with a reviewed Git revision, passing tests, Heroku CLI access and a PostgreSQL-compatible application. Verify the supported Python runtime and buildpack against [Heroku's Python setup](https://devcenter.heroku.com/articles/getting-started-with-python).

## 1. Choose the deploy root

Heroku's Python build needs its dependency manifest and `Procfile` at the deploy root. With `project/backend` and `project/frontend`, either configure a reviewed monorepo build pipeline or deploy the backend subtree. The example below uses a [backend subtree](https://github.com/git/git/blob/master/contrib/subtree/git-subtree.adoc); it does not change your normal GitHub repository layout. Keep a supported `.python-version` and `requirements.txt` inside backend.

Dependencies normally include Django, Gunicorn, a PostgreSQL driver, `dj-database-url` and WhiteNoise. Record reviewed versions in your project's dependency workflow; do not copy a random version list from a tutorial.

## 2. Configure production settings

Adapt the existing settings module rather than replacing it wholesale:

```python
import os
import dj_database_url

SECRET_KEY = os.environ["DJANGO_SECRET_KEY"]
DEBUG = False
ALLOWED_HOSTS = os.environ["DJANGO_ALLOWED_HOSTS"].split(",")
DATABASES = {"default": dj_database_url.config(conn_max_age=60)}
STATIC_URL = "/static/"
STATIC_ROOT = BASE_DIR / "staticfiles"
```

Put WhiteNoise immediately after SecurityMiddleware and configure `STORAGES["staticfiles"]` to use `whitenoise.storage.CompressedManifestStaticFilesStorage`, preserving your existing default storage. Heroku's Python build runs `collectstatic`; fix missing assets instead of disabling that step. User uploads belong in durable private storage such as S3, not the dyno filesystem. See [Django configuration](https://devcenter.heroku.com/articles/django-app-configuration) and [static assets](https://devcenter.heroku.com/articles/django-assets).

Configure secure session/CSRF cookies, HTTPS handling and explicit trusted frontend origins for your actual host setup. Require the database TLS behavior specified by your selected Heroku Postgres offering. Confirm proxy-header trust before enabling forwarded-protocol settings. CORS and CSRF are separate controls: use the [CORS guide](/guide/django-cors), your authentication integration, and Django's deployment checks.

## 3. Declare processes

In `backend/Procfile`, replace `config` with your Django project package:

```procfile
web: gunicorn config.wsgi:application --bind 0.0.0.0:$PORT
release: python manage.py migrate --noinput
```

Use the appropriate ASGI server and process configuration for Channels; this WSGI example does not serve WebSockets. Release migrations run before the new release is activated, but are not automatically reversed if something later fails. Use [compatible migrations](/guide/safe-database-migrations) and serialize deployments. See [release phase](https://devcenter.heroku.com/articles/release-phase).

## 4. Prepare the Heroku app

In the dashboard, create a staging app, select its region/runtime and attach an intentionally selected Heroku Postgres plan. Set `DJANGO_SECRET_KEY` through the dashboard without exposing it in shell history. Set `DJANGO_ALLOWED_HOSTS` to the actual API hostname without a scheme, along with your application's origin settings. Postgres supplies `DATABASE_URL` when attached. Never paste config exports into issues or handbook notes.

From the monorepo root, replace YOUR-STAGING-APP:

```sh
heroku login
heroku git:remote --app YOUR-STAGING-APP
git status --short
git subtree push --prefix backend heroku main
```

This publishes the committed backend subtree and can trigger a real release and migrations. Confirm the target app and reviewed commit first. For a backend-only repository, use its configured Heroku remote and `git push heroku main` instead.

## Verify and troubleshoot

Inspect `heroku releases --app YOUR-STAGING-APP`, `heroku ps --app YOUR-STAGING-APP` and recent logs. Check an actual health endpoint, static assets, login, CORS/preflight and a synthetic database operation. Confirm the intended release and migration result before promoting the same revision.

A missing Procfile or manifest usually means the deploy root is wrong. An import error often means the project package or dependencies are wrong. A failed release command requires inspecting its logs; do not keep deploying until its database effects are understood. Continue with [Heroku operations](/guide/heroku-operations).

title: Heroku operations and command reference
summary: Inspect releases, run workers and scheduled tasks, verify backups, and plan rollback.
body:
## Confirm the app before every change

Replace YOUR-APP explicitly. These commands are a reference, not a batch script. Inspect the release, target database and recent logs before making changes. Logs and backup files can contain private data; use restricted storage and redact shared excerpts. The [CLI reference](https://devcenter.heroku.com/articles/heroku-cli-commands) documents current command options.

## Inspect and diagnose

| Intent | Command | What to verify |
| --- | --- | --- |
| App processes | `heroku ps --app YOUR-APP` | Expected process types and state |
| Recent logs | `heroku logs --num 100 --app YOUR-APP` | Startup, request and worker errors |
| Follow logs | `heroku logs --tail --app YOUR-APP` | Stop with Ctrl-C; avoid leaking request data |
| Release history | `heroku releases --app YOUR-APP` | Deployed version and failed release attempts |
| Release details | `heroku releases:info vNN --app YOUR-APP` | The candidate you actually intended |
| Release command output | `heroku releases:output vNN --app YOUR-APP` | Migration errors and partial effects |
| Database status | `heroku pg:info --app YOUR-APP` | Correct attachment and health |

## Workers and scheduled tasks

For a project already configured with Celery and a supported broker, add a Procfile entry such as `worker: celery -A config worker --loglevel=info`. Replace the package name and verify the broker configuration. Scaling it with `heroku ps:scale worker=1 --app YOUR-APP` starts a real process and can incur charges. Test an idempotent synthetic job and inspect its result, not just the worker's startup log.

Install and configure Heroku Scheduler intentionally. `heroku addons:open scheduler --app YOUR-APP` opens its dashboard after installation. For example, schedule your own `python manage.py enqueue_due_jobs` command using the interval and UTC time shown there. That management command must exist and handle retries. Scheduled work can overlap or be missed; use idempotency, execution records and alerts. Exact-once business behavior belongs in your application. See [Scheduler](https://devcenter.heroku.com/articles/scheduler) and [backup/job patterns](/guide/backup-and-scheduled-tasks).

## Backups with a recovery exercise

| Intent | Command | Consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Capture now | `heroku pg:backups:capture --app YOUR-APP` | Creates a database backup; assess load on a busy database |
| List backups | `heroku pg:backups --app YOUR-APP` | Confirm successful completion and age |
| Schedule daily | `heroku pg:backups:schedule DATABASE_URL --at '02:00 UTC' --app YOUR-APP` | Changes the selected database's backup schedule |
| Check schedules | `heroku pg:backups:schedules --app YOUR-APP` | Confirm the schedule was accepted |

Check retention and feature availability for the selected database plan. PGBackups is not supported on Heroku Postgres Advanced; evaluate the provider's continuous-protection options for production recovery. Scheduled logical backup failures do not generate automatic notifications, so verify completion and recheck schedules after changing database attachments. PostgreSQL backups do not include S3 files, secrets or all infrastructure settings. Restore into a separate recovery database and verify synthetic records, constraints and application compatibility. Treat a production restore as a separate, explicitly approved recovery operation because it replaces data. Keep backup URLs private. See [PGBackups](https://devcenter.heroku.com/articles/heroku-postgres-backups).

## Rollback is a release decision

`heroku rollback vNN --app YOUR-APP` changes the running release. Inspect the target version and confirm compatibility with today's database before executing it. It does not reverse database migrations, restore deleted records or undo external side effects. Prefer a forward fix when the old code cannot read the current schema. See [release rollback](https://devcenter.heroku.com/articles/releases).

Record the incident, target revision, database compatibility decision and owner. After recovery, verify health, login, a synthetic read/write, worker backlog and error rates. Use [operational runbooks](/guide/operational-runbooks) to capture that evidence. If a process crashed, inspect the cause before using a restart; restarting does not repair configuration or data.

title: CI/CD: how a change becomes a release
summary: Learn integration, delivery, deployment, artifacts, and gates through one small frontend/backend change.
body:
## What am I learning?

CI/CD is a way to make the journey from source change to running software repeatable and visible. Its usefulness is fast feedback and fewer forgotten steps, including when I am the only developer. A pipeline is the ordered work; GitHub Actions is one engine that can run it.

## CI, delivery, and deployment

| Term | The question it answers |
| --- | --- |
| Continuous integration, CI | Do frequently integrated changes build and pass the checks we chose? |
| Continuous delivery | Can a validated change be released through a repeatable process, with a release decision still allowed? |
| Continuous deployment | Does an eligible change proceed automatically into production after the configured checks? |

The two meanings of CD are related but different. A manual production approval can belong to continuous delivery. A single automatic upload is not, by itself, a complete CI/CD practice. [AWS explanation of CI/CD](https://aws.amazon.com/what-is/ci-cd/).

## Why frequent integration helps

Suppose my React form and Django endpoint evolve independently for weeks. Finding their mismatch at release time makes the problem larger. Integrating smaller changes and checking them early brings that feedback closer to the change that caused it. CI reports evidence from the checks it runs; missing checks remain missing. [GitHub's CI introduction](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/get-started/continuous-integration).

## Read the pipeline vocabulary

| Word | Explain it to myself |
| --- | --- |
| Event | The trigger: a pull request, push, schedule, or manual request |
| Workflow | The defined automation for that event |
| Job | A group of steps running on a runner |
| Runner | The machine executing the job |
| Step | An individual command or action inside a job |
| Dependency | A rule that another job must finish before this job can proceed |

Jobs can run in parallel when they do not depend on one another. A failed required check should prevent the release path from continuing. [GitHub Actions concepts](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/get-started/understand-github-actions).

## Follow one example change

Teaching scenario: I add a required description to a Reports form and its API contract.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  Change[Small committed change] --> Checks[Frontend and backend checks]
  Checks --> Candidate[Build a release candidate]
  Candidate --> Decision[Configured release decision]
  Decision --> Deploy[Deploy the chosen artifact]
  Deploy --> Observe[Verify the live application]
  Checks -->|failure| Fix[Fix and check again]
```

The frontend checks might catch a missing field. The API tests might catch accepting an invalid request. A browser check might catch the two sides disagreeing. These checks answer different questions; one green unit test cannot substitute for all three.

## Why artifacts matter

An **artifact** is output worth retaining: a built site, package, container image, or test report. A commit identifies source; an artifact identifies produced bytes. Cache entries help jobs run faster, but are not the same thing as release outputs. [GitHub's artifact guide](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/workflows-and-actions/workflow-artifacts).

My release-design rule: tie evidence to the candidate, and deploy the candidate I verified. Rebuilding or editing files afterward can produce different bytes. A newer green run does not prove that an older artifact was checked by that run.

## Gates and credentials

An environment can require approval before a deployment job proceeds and can restrict access to its secrets. That gate is a configured policy, not something CI invents automatically. [Deployment environments](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/workflows-and-actions/deployment-environments).

Untrusted pull-request code should not inherit production deployment credentials. Treat dependency scripts and third-party actions as executable code; give jobs only the permissions they need. [GitHub's secure-use guidance](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/security/secure-use).

## What a green pipeline cannot tell me

A completed deployment still needs live verification. The service can have a bad environment variable, incompatible database state, or unhealthy dependency. A rollback also needs a plan: redeploying yesterday's code does not automatically undo today's database migration.

Foundry can coordinate tasks and evidence. The pipeline runs configured checks. The hosting platform serves the result. For this repository's concrete process, open [checks, review, release](/guide/ci-cd-release-workflow).

## Check your understanding

- Checks passed, but production still needs a person to approve. Is this necessarily continuous deployment?
- Why retain a candidate's identity alongside its test results?
- Does a successful build prove the live endpoint works?

## Answer key

A human release gate is compatible with continuous delivery. Candidate identity connects evidence to the thing being released. A build is pre-release evidence; live behavior needs its own checks.

title: CI/CD: checks, review, release
summary: Find the checks, approval, deployment and recovery steps without confusing a green build with a live release.
body:
## Learn the concepts first

New to the terms? Read [CI/CD: how a change becomes a release](/guide/ci-cd-fundamentals) for the difference between integration, delivery, deployment, and release evidence.

## Choose the step you need

Continuous integration checks a change. Delivery prepares a candidate for release. Deployment publishes it. Your project decides which steps are automated and where an owner must approve. Use this page as the map to the existing guides.

| Question | Open |
| --- | --- |
| How do I submit a reviewed change? | [Git branches and pull requests](/guide/git-basics) |
| Which tests should block release? | [Testing strategy](/guide/testing-strategy) |
| How does Foundry handle candidate evidence and authority? | [Foundry review and release](/guide/foundry-review-release) |
| How do I deploy a Django API? | [Heroku deployment](/guide/heroku-django-deployment) |
| What do I check after deployment? | [Heroku operations](/guide/heroku-operations) |
| How do I recover when something fails? | [Operational runbooks](/guide/operational-runbooks) |

## This handbook's release path

The repository contains a GitHub Actions verification workflow for pushes, pull requests, manual runs and a weekly schedule. It checks the candidate without deployment credentials. Remote CI only runs once that workflow is published to GitHub; a local workflow file is not evidence of a remote run.

The manual publication process used for this handbook is:

```sh
npm run release:prepare
npm run release:deploy
```

Preparation requires committed, clean source, audits dependencies, builds and scans the public artifact, runs browser/security checks, and records the revision and artifact digest. Deployment refuses changed source or build files. After Netlify publishes, the checker verifies the live revision, configured headers, representative routes and local assets. A failed live check reports failure after publication; it does not automatically roll back.

## Apply the pattern to your application

Agree on required checks before merging. Keep deployment credentials out of untrusted pull-request jobs. Promote the reviewed revision, account for migrations and background processes, then verify the running application. Record the candidate, executed checks, release decision and recovery route.

Foundry coordinates build evidence; your hosting platform runs the deployed application. See [the platform map](/guide/deployment-platforms) for that boundary. A green build alone does not establish database compatibility, tenant isolation or a successful production release.
